title: Chi-Squared Statistic Mean under H₁
informal:
Under the alternative $H_1$ the chi-squared statistic is $T_n = \sum_{i=1}^n (\theta_i + z_i)^2$ with signal $\theta$.

If each $z_i \sim N(0,1)$, then $$\mathbb{E}[T_n] = n + \lVert\theta\rVert^2, \qquad \lVert\theta\rVert^2 = \sum_i \theta_i^2.$$
summary: Under the alternative, the chi-squared statistic has expectation n plus the squared signal norm.
leanSignature:
theorem chiSq_H1_mean (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P] (z : Fin n → Ω → ℝ) (θ : Fin n → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (z i))
    (hlaw : ∀ i, Measure.map (z i) P = gaussianReal 0 1) :
    ∫ ω, ∑ i, (θ i + z i ω) ^ 2 ∂P = (∑ i, (θ i) ^ 2) + (n : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: standard Gaussian noise
hypotheses.note: Each noise coordinate z_i has law N(0,1) under P.

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic originates with K. Pearson, "On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling," *Philosophical Magazine*, Series 5, **50** (1900), 157–175. Under the alternative the statistic follows a noncentral $\chi^2$ with noncentrality $\lVert\theta\rVert^2$; its mean and variance are standard computations applied in the Candès lecture notes.

title: Chi-Squared Statistic Variance under H₁
informal:
For the alternative chi-squared statistic $T_n = \sum_{i=1}^n (\theta_i + z_i)^2$:

if each $z_i \sim N(0,1)$ and the $z_i$ are jointly independent, then $$\operatorname{Var}[T_n] = 2n + 4\lVert\theta\rVert^2.$$
summary: Under the alternative, the chi-squared statistic has variance 2n plus four times the squared signal norm.
leanSignature:
theorem chiSq_H1_variance (P : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure P] (z : Fin n → Ω → ℝ)
    (θ : Fin n → ℝ)
    (hmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (z i))
    (hlaw : ∀ i, Measure.map (z i) P = gaussianReal 0 1)
    (hindep : iIndepFun z P) :
    ∫ ω, (∑ i, (θ i + z i ω) ^ 2 - ((∑ i, (θ i) ^ 2) + (n : ℝ))) ^ 2 ∂P
      = 2 * (n : ℝ) + 4 * (∑ i, (θ i) ^ 2)

hypotheses.label: standard Gaussian noise
hypotheses.note: Each noise coordinate z_i has law N(0,1) under P.

hypotheses.label: independence
hypotheses.note: The coordinates z_i are jointly independent, so cross-covariances vanish.

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic originates with K. Pearson, "On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling," *Philosophical Magazine*, Series 5, **50** (1900), 157–175. Under the alternative the statistic follows a noncentral $\chi^2$ with noncentrality $\lVert\theta\rVert^2$; its mean and variance are standard computations applied in the Candès lecture notes.

title: Split-Conformal Coverage Guarantee
informal:
Given $n+1$ nonconformity scores $S_0,\dots,S_{n-1}$ (calibration) plus a test score $S_n$, the split-conformal prediction set $\hat C$ is built from the $k$-th smallest calibration score with $k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$. The covering event $\{Y_{n+1} \in \hat C\}$ equals $\{\operatorname{rank}(S_n) \le k\}$.

If the scores are exchangeable and almost surely pairwise distinct, then $$1 - \alpha \;\le\; \mathbb{P}\bigl(\operatorname{rank}(S_n) \le k\bigr).$$
summary: For exchangeable, a.s. distinct nonconformity scores, the split-conformal prediction set built from the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))-th smallest score covers the test point with probability at least 1-alpha.
leanSignature:
theorem conformal_coverage {n : ℕ} {α : ℝ} (hα0 : 0 < α) (hα1 : α < 1)
    (S : Fin (n + 1) → Ω → ℝ) (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (S i))
    (hExch : Exchangeable S μ)
    (hdistinct : ∀ᵐ ω ∂μ, Function.Injective (fun i => S i ω)) :
    (ENNReal.ofReal (1 - α)) ≤
      μ {ω | rankOf S (Fin.last n) ω ≤ ⌈((n : ℝ) + 1) * (1 - α)⌉₊}

hypotheses.label: exchangeability
hypotheses.note: The calibration and test scores are exchangeable, making the rank of the test score uniform.

hypotheses.label: a.s. distinct
hypotheses.note: The scores are almost surely pairwise distinct, so the order statistics are unambiguous.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: Split (a.k.a. inductive) conformal prediction originates with H. Papadopoulos, K. Proedrou, V. Vovk & A. Gammerman, "Inductive Confidence Machines for Regression", *ECML 2002*, LNCS 2430, pp. 345–356, and is developed systematically in V. Vovk, A. Gammerman & G. Shafer, *Algorithmic Learning in a Random World*, Springer, 2005. The finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee proved here is Theorem 2.2 of J. Lei, M. G'Sell, A. Rinaldo, R. J. Tibshirani & L. Wasserman, "Distribution-Free Predictive Inference for Regression", *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **113**(523):1094–1111, 2018.

title: E-variable
informal: Fix a simple null hypothesis with law $\mu$ on $\Omega$. A statistic $E : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is an e-variable if it is nonnegative, measurable, and has null expectation at most one, $\mathbb{E}_\mu[E] \le 1$. Its realized values are e-values — the natural currency for optional continuation (sequential testing with data-dependent stopping), where p-values fail.
summary: An e-variable for a simple null is a nonnegative measurable statistic whose null expectation is at most one.
leanSignature:
structure IsEVariable (E : Ω → ℝ) (μ : Measure Ω) : Prop where
  nonneg : ∀ ω, 0 ≤ E ω
  measurable : Measurable E
  expectation_le_one : ∫⁻ ω, ENNReal.ofReal (E ω) ∂μ ≤ 1
formalizationNotes: The defining inequality E_μ[E] ≤ 1 is stated as a lower integral ∫⁻ ofReal(E) dμ ≤ 1 rather than a Bochner integral: for nonnegative measurable E this lower integral is the genuine (possibly +∞) expectation, so bounding it by 1 both encodes the bound and forces integrability. The Bochner form ∫ E dμ ≤ 1 would be unsound since a non-integrable nonnegative E has Bochner integral 0 ≤ 1 vacuously.

hypotheses.label: nonnegative
hypotheses.note: E(ω) ≥ 0 for all ω.

hypotheses.label: measurable
hypotheses.note: E is measurable, so the expectation is the genuine null expectation.

hypotheses.label: expectation ≤ 1
hypotheses.note: The null expectation of E is at most one (stated via the lower integral of ofReal∘E).

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The standard reference for the calibration and combination theory of e-values is V. Vovk and R. Wang, "E-values: Calibration, combination and applications," *The Annals of Statistics* **49**(3):1736–1754, 2021, where e-variables are defined as nonnegative random variables with expectation at most one under the null. The "testing by betting" viewpoint that motivates e-values as wealth processes is laid out in G. Shafer, "Testing by betting: A strategy for statistical and scientific communication," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A* **184**(2):407–431, 2021.

title: E-to-p Conversion
informal:
Let $E$ be an e-variable for a simple null with law $\mu$.

If $E$ is an e-variable and $E$ is strictly positive pointwise, then its reciprocal $1/E$ is a (conservative) p-variable: for every level $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $$ \mu\{\,1/E \le \alpha\,\} \le \alpha. $$ This is the simplest calibrator turning e-value evidence into a valid p-value, so e-values plug directly into p-value-based multiple-testing procedures.
summary: The reciprocal of a positive e-variable is a valid (conservative) p-variable, calibrating evidence on the e-value scale into a p-value.
leanSignature:
theorem isPVariable_inv_of_isEVariable {E : Ω → ℝ} {μ : Measure Ω} [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hE : IsEVariable E μ)
    (hpos : ∀ ω, 0 < E ω) :
    IsPVariable (fun ω => 1 / E ω) μ
formalizationNotes: Beyond the e-variable assumption, the formalization requires E to be strictly positive pointwise, ruling out Lean's 1/0 = 0 convention which would map the no-evidence event E = 0 (intuitively p-value 1) to 1/E = 0 and spuriously inflate the bound. E-variables arising as likelihood ratios are positive, so this is no loss of generality. The companion superUniform_inv_of_isEVariable extends the bound to all t ≥ 0, the form consumed by the BH/Holm assembly.

hypotheses.label: e-variable
hypotheses.note: E is an e-variable for the simple null μ (nonnegative, measurable, E_μ[E] ≤ 1).

hypotheses.label: strictly positive
hypotheses.note: E(ω) > 0 pointwise, so 1/E is the genuine reciprocal p-value (Lean-only).

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The reciprocal calibrator is due to Vladimir Vovk and Ruodu Wang, "E-values: Calibration, combination and applications", *The Annals of Statistics* **49**(3):1736–1754, 2021. There, calibrators from e-values to p-values are studied systematically (their §2); the map $e \mapsto \min(1, 1/e)$ — equivalently the bound used here, $\mu\{1/E \le \alpha\} \le \alpha$ — is the canonical such calibrator and follows from Markov's inequality.

title: Bayes Risk of the Gaussian Shrinkage Estimator
informal:
Consider the Gaussian sequence model with Gaussian prior: $\theta_i \sim N(0,\tau^2)$, independent noise $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$, and observations $X_i = \theta_i + \varepsilon_i$. The Bayes estimator shrinks toward zero by $s = \tau^2/(\sigma^2+\tau^2)$: $\hat\mu_{B,i} = s\,X_i$.

If each prior coordinate has law $N(0,\tau^2)$, each noise coordinate has law $N(0,\sigma^2)$, and prior and noise are independent within each coordinate, then the Bayes risk is $$\mathbb{E}\,\lVert \hat\mu_B - \theta \rVert^2 = p\,\frac{\sigma^2\tau^2}{\sigma^2 + \tau^2} = R_{\mathrm{MLE}} \cdot \frac{\tau^2}{\sigma^2 + \tau^2},$$ where $R_{\mathrm{MLE}} = p\,\sigma^2$. Since $\tau^2/(\sigma^2+\tau^2) < 1$, shrinkage strictly reduces the risk.
summary: In the normal-normal model the Bayes (posterior-mean) shrinkage estimator has risk equal to the no-shrinkage risk multiplied by the shrinkage factor, p sigma^2 tau^2 / (sigma^2 + tau^2).
leanSignature:
theorem empiricalBayes_risk {p : ℕ} {σ2 τ2 : ℝ} (hσ : 0 < σ2) (hτ : 0 < τ2)
    (μ : Measure Ω) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (θ ε : Fin p → Ω → ℝ)
    (hθmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (θ i))
    (hεmeas : ∀ i, Measurable (ε i))
    (hθlaw : ∀ i, Measure.map (θ i) μ = gaussianReal 0 ⟨τ2, hτ.le⟩)
    (hεlaw : ∀ i, Measure.map (ε i) μ = gaussianReal 0 ⟨σ2, hσ.le⟩)
    (hindep : ∀ i, IndepFun (θ i) (ε i) μ) :
    (∫ ω, ∑ i, ((τ2 / (σ2 + τ2)) * (θ i ω + ε i ω) - θ i ω) ^ 2 ∂μ)
      = (p : ℝ) * (σ2 * τ2 / (σ2 + τ2))
formalizationNotes: The book conditions on μ and takes an outer expectation; the formalization works directly with the unconditional second moments, which is equivalent and avoids conditional-expectation machinery. The Lean statement states the risk of the fixed estimator and does not separately introduce R_MLE (the identity R_MLE = pσ² is recorded only in prose).

hypotheses.label: Gaussian prior
hypotheses.note: Each prior coordinate θ_i has law N(0, τ²).

hypotheses.label: Gaussian noise
hypotheses.note: Each noise coordinate ε_i has law N(0, σ²).

hypotheses.label: prior ⊥ noise
hypotheses.note: Prior and noise are independent within each coordinate, so the cross term vanishes.

reference.formal: E. J. Candès, *STAT 300C: Theory of Statistics*, Lecture Notes, Stanford University.
reference.biblio: The normal–normal conjugate computation of this Bayes risk is classical/folklore. Its use as the *empirical-Bayes* interpretation of the James–Stein estimator — the role it plays in Candès Lecture 15 — originates with B. Efron and C. Morris, "Stein's Estimation Rule and Its Competitors—An Empirical Bayes Approach", *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **68**(341) (1973), 117–130, who recover the James–Stein rule by plugging an unbiased estimate $(p-2)\sigma^2/\lVert X\rVert^2$ of the shrinkage factor into this Bayes estimator.

title: Minimax Risk for a Distortion Loss
informal: Fix a class of distributions $\{P_\theta\}$, a functional $\theta\mapsto g(\theta)$ valued in a space with a semimetric $\rho$, and an increasing distortion $\Phi:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$. The minimax risk for estimating $g(\theta)$ under the distortion loss $\Phi\circ\rho$ is $$\mathfrak{M}\big(g(\theta);\,\Phi\circ\rho\big)=\inf_{\widehat\theta}\ \sup_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{P_\theta}\big[\Phi\big(\rho(\widehat\theta,\,g(\theta))\big)\big],$$ where the infimum ranges over all (randomized) estimators and $\rho$ is the extended distance on the functional values.
summary: The minimax risk for estimating a functional under a distortion of the semimetric: infimum over estimators of the worst-case expected loss.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def minimaxRiskDist [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω]
    (Φ : ℝ≥0∞ → ℝ≥0∞) (g : Θ → Ω) (P : Kernel Θ 𝓧) : ℝ≥0∞

hypotheses.label: data-generating model
hypotheses.note: P sends each parameter θ to its data law P_θ; the infimum is over Markov-kernel estimators.

hypotheses.label: semimetric ρ
hypotheses.note: The functional value space carries Wainwright's semimetric ρ as an extended pseudometric (edist).

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: These objects are a synthesis of the classical minimax decision-theory framework. The decision-theoretic formulation of minimax risk over a family of distributions traces to A. Wald, *Statistical Decision Functions* (Wiley, 1950). The reduction of minimax estimation to $M$-ary hypothesis testing over a separated family — the engine behind the Le Cam, Fano, and Assouad lower-bound methods — is due to L. Le Cam (*Convergence of estimates under dimensionality restrictions*, Ann. Statist. 1 (1973), 38–53; and *Asymptotic Methods in Statistical Decision Theory*, Springer, 1986), with multi-hypothesis/packing variants developed by P. Assouad (1983) and the information-theoretic Fano bound (see also Ibragimov and Has'minskii, *Statistical Estimation*, Springer, 1981).

title: From Estimation to Testing
informal: Fix an increasing distortion $\Phi$ and a finite family $\{\theta^1,\dots,\theta^M\}$ that is $2\delta$-separated in the semimetric on the functional values. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\dots,M\}$ and, given $J$, draw $Z\sim P_{\theta^J}$. Then the minimax risk for estimating $g(\theta)$ under $\Phi\circ\rho$ satisfies $$\mathfrak{M}\big(g(\theta);\,\Phi\circ\rho\big)\ \ge\ \Phi(\delta)\cdot\inf_{\psi}\ \mathbb{Q}\big[\psi(Z)\ne J\big],$$ the infimum running over all (randomized) tests $\psi$.
summary: The minimax risk is at least the distortion at the separation radius times the error probability of the induced M-ary hypothesis test.
leanSignature:
theorem minimax_ge_testing_error
    [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω] {M : ℕ} [NeZero M]
    (Φ : ℝ≥0∞ → ℝ≥0∞) (g : Θ → Ω) (P : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    (θfam : Fin M → Θ) (hθ : Measurable θfam) (δ : ℝ≥0∞)
    (hΦ : Monotone Φ)
    (hsep : IsSeparatedFamily g θfam δ) :
    Φ δ * multiwayTestingError (P.comap θfam hθ) ≤ minimaxRiskDist Φ g P

hypotheses.label: increasing distortion
hypotheses.note: Φ is nondecreasing on the extended nonnegative reals.

hypotheses.label: 2δ-separation
hypotheses.note: The functional values g(θ^j) are pairwise at semimetric distance at least 2δ.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: This estimation-to-testing reduction is folklore, the common abstract scaffold behind the Le Cam, Assouad, and Fano lower-bound methods. The idea of reducing estimation to a multiple-hypothesis test and bounding the minimax risk by a separation $\times$ testing-error product traces to L. Le Cam, *Convergence of estimates under dimensionality restrictions*, Ann. Statist. 1 (1973), 38–53, and to Ibragimov and Has'minskii, *Statistical Estimation* (Springer, 1981). The packaging follows the survey of B. Yu, *Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam* (Festschrift for Lucien Le Cam, Springer, 1997).

title: Bayes Error Equals Total Variation
informal: Consider a binary hypothesis test in which a label $J\in\{0,1\}$ is drawn uniformly and, given $J=j$, the observation $Z$ is drawn from $\mathbb{P}_j$. The Bayes error of the optimal (possibly randomized) test equals the total-variation distance between the hypotheses: $$\inf_{\psi}\ \mathbb{Q}\big[\psi(Z)\ne J\big]=\tfrac12\big(1-\|\mathbb{P}_1-\mathbb{P}_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\big).$$
summary: In a binary test with equally weighted hypotheses, the optimal error probability equals one half of one minus the total-variation distance.
leanSignature:
theorem binary_testingError_eq_tvDist (Q : Kernel (Fin 2) 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel Q] :
    multiwayTestingError Q = 2⁻¹ * (1 - tvDist (Q 0) (Q 1))

hypotheses.label: two hypotheses
hypotheses.note: Q j is the data law P_j under hypothesis j ∈ {0,1}; assumed a Markov kernel (probability laws).

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The reduction of estimation to two-point testing originates with L. Le Cam, "Convergence of Estimates Under Dimensionality Restrictions," *The Annals of Statistics* **1** (1973), no. 1, 38–53, which introduced what is now called *Le Cam's method*. The identification of the optimal binary-testing error with the total-variation distance is the classical Neyman–Pearson consequence and is folklore.

title: Le Cam's Two-Point Lower Bound
informal: For an increasing distortion $\Phi$ and a pair $\theta_0,\theta_1$ whose functional values are $2\delta$-separated, the minimax risk obeys $$\mathfrak{M}\big(g(\theta);\,\Phi\circ\rho\big)\ \ge\ \frac{\Phi(\delta)}{2}\big(1-\|P_{\theta_0}-P_{\theta_1}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\big).$$
summary: For a 2δ-separated pair of parameters, the minimax risk is at least half the distortion at δ times one minus their total-variation distance.
leanSignature:
theorem minimax_two_point [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω]
    (Φ : ℝ≥0∞ → ℝ≥0∞) (g : Θ → Ω) (P : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    (θ₀ θ₁ : Θ) (δ : ℝ≥0∞)
    (hΦ : Monotone Φ)
    (hsep : 2 * δ ≤ edist (g θ₀) (g θ₁)) :
    Φ δ / 2 * (1 - tvDist (P θ₀) (P θ₁)) ≤ minimaxRiskDist Φ g P

hypotheses.label: increasing distortion
hypotheses.note: Φ is nondecreasing.

hypotheses.label: 2δ-separation
hypotheses.note: The two functional values are at semimetric distance at least 2δ.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The reduction of estimation to two-point testing originates with L. Le Cam, "Convergence of Estimates Under Dimensionality Restrictions," *The Annals of Statistics* **1** (1973), no. 1, 38–53, which introduced *Le Cam's method* (the *two-point method*) for minimax lower bounds. The identification of the optimal binary-testing error with the total-variation distance is the classical Neyman–Pearson consequence; Wainwright Eq. (15.13)–(15.14) is the synthesis used here.

title: Hellinger Modulus of Continuity
informal: For estimating a real functional $\theta:\mathcal{F}\to\mathbb{R}$ of a density, the modulus of continuity at Hellinger radius $\varepsilon$ is $$\omega(\varepsilon;\theta,\mathcal{F})=\sup\big\{|\theta(f)-\theta(g)|:\ H^2(f\,\|\,g)\le\varepsilon^2\big\},$$ where $H^2$ is the squared Hellinger distance between the candidate densities.
summary: The largest fluctuation of a functional over a Hellinger ball of radius epsilon — the geometric object controlling Le Cam's functional bound.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def hellingerModulus (θfunc : ι → ℝ) (P : ι → Measure 𝓧) (ε : ℝ≥0∞) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨆ (i : ι) (j : ι) (_ : sqHellinger (P i) (P j) ≤ ε ^ 2), ENNReal.ofReal |θfunc i - θfunc j|

hypotheses.label: Hellinger ball
hypotheses.note: The supremum is over pairs whose squared Hellinger distance is at most ε².

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The reduction of functional estimation to the modulus of continuity of the functional with respect to Hellinger distance is due to D. L. Donoho and R. C. Liu, "Geometrizing rates of convergence, II & III," *The Annals of Statistics* **19** (1991), no. 2, 633–667 and 668–701.

title: Le Cam's Bound for Functionals
informal: For the $n$-sample i.i.d. model $P_i^{\otimes n}$ over a class of densities and an increasing, lower-semicontinuous distortion $\Phi$, the minimax risk for estimating the functional obeys $$\inf_{\widehat\theta}\ \sup_{i}\ \mathbb{E}\big[\Phi(|\widehat\theta-\theta(i)|)\big]\ \ge\ \tfrac14\,\Phi\!\Big(\tfrac12\,\omega\big(\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt n};\theta,\mathcal{F}\big)\Big),$$ with $\omega$ the Hellinger modulus of continuity.
summary: For an n-sample i.i.d. model the minimax risk of a functional is at least a quarter of the distortion at half the Hellinger modulus at the critical radius 1/(2√n).
leanSignature:
theorem minimax_functional_modulus
    [Nonempty ι]
    (θfunc : ι → ℝ) (P : ι → Measure 𝓧)
    [∀ i, IsProbabilityMeasure (P i)]
    (n : ℕ) (Pn : Kernel ι (Fin n → 𝓧)) [IsMarkovKernel Pn]
    (Φ : ℝ≥0∞ → ℝ≥0∞)
    (hΦ : Monotone Φ)
    (hΦlsc : LowerSemicontinuous Φ)
    (hPn : ∀ i, Pn i = Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => P i) :
    4⁻¹ * Φ (2⁻¹ * hellingerModulus θfunc P (ENNReal.ofReal (1 / (2 * Real.sqrt n))))
      ≤ minimaxRiskDist Φ θfunc Pn
formalizationNotes: Two technical hypotheses are added beyond the book statement: the index set is nonempty ([Nonempty ι], vacuous for any concrete family) and Φ is lower-semicontinuous (hΦlsc, used for the modulus-supremum interchange; holds for the quadratic distortion in the book's examples).

hypotheses.label: class of densities
hypotheses.note: Each P i is a probability measure (the family is a class of densities).

hypotheses.label: increasing distortion
hypotheses.note: Φ is nondecreasing.

hypotheses.label: lower semicontinuity
hypotheses.note: Lean-only regularity enabling Φ(½·sup) ≤ sup Φ(½·); satisfied by Φ = (·)².

hypotheses.leanToken: hPn : ∀ i, Pn i = Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => P i
hypotheses.label: n-fold i.i.d. product
hypotheses.note: The observed model is the n-fold i.i.d. product of the base family.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: Le Cam's two-point testing approach to minimax lower bounds originates with L. Le Cam, "Convergence of estimates under dimensionality restrictions," *The Annals of Statistics* 1 (1973), 38–53. The reduction of functional estimation to the modulus of continuity with respect to Hellinger distance is due to D. L. Donoho and R. C. Liu, "Geometrizing rates of convergence, II & III," *The Annals of Statistics* 19 (1991), no. 2, 633–667 and 668–701; Wainwright's Corollary 15.6 is the lower-bound half of that equivalence.

title: Le Cam's Convex-Hull Lower Bound
informal: Generalizing the two-point method from single pairs to pairs of classes: for an increasing distortion $\Phi$, two $2\delta$-separated subfamilies indexed by $a_0,a_1$, and any mixing priors $\pi_0,\pi_1$, the minimax risk dominates $$\frac{\Phi(\delta)}{2}\big(1-\|\bar Q_1-\bar Q_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\big),$$ where $\bar Q_0=\int P_{a_0}\,d\pi_0$ and $\bar Q_1=\int P_{a_1}\,d\pi_1$ are the mixtures over the convex hulls.
summary: For two 2δ-separated subfamilies, the minimax risk is controlled by the total variation between mixtures (convex hulls), which can be far smaller than the pointwise separation.
leanSignature:
theorem minimax_le_cam_convex_hull [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω]
    (Φ : ℝ≥0∞ → ℝ≥0∞) (g : Θ → Ω) (P : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    (δ : ℝ≥0∞) {ι₀ ι₁ : Type*} [MeasurableSpace ι₀] [MeasurableSpace ι₁]
    (a₀ : ι₀ → Θ) (a₁ : ι₁ → Θ) (ha₀ : Measurable a₀) (ha₁ : Measurable a₁)
    (π₀ : Measure ι₀) (π₁ : Measure ι₁) [IsProbabilityMeasure π₀] [IsProbabilityMeasure π₁]
    (hΦ : Monotone Φ)
    (hsep : ∀ i₀ i₁, 2 * δ ≤ edist (g (a₀ i₀)) (g (a₁ i₁))) :
    Φ δ / 2 * (1 - tvDist (P.comap a₀ ha₀ ∘ₘ π₀) (P.comap a₁ ha₁ ∘ₘ π₁))
      ≤ minimaxRiskDist Φ g P

hypotheses.label: increasing distortion
hypotheses.note: Φ is nondecreasing.

hypotheses.leanToken: hsep : ∀ i₀ i₁, 2 * δ ≤ edist (g (a₀ i₀)) (g (a₁ i₁))
hypotheses.label: class separation
hypotheses.note: Every member of subfamily 0 is at semimetric distance at least 2δ from every member of subfamily 1.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The convex-hull (mixture) refinement of the two-point method originates with L. Le Cam, "Convergence of estimates under dimensionality restrictions," *The Annals of Statistics* **1** (1973), no. 1, 38–53, where the lower bound is expressed through the affinity / total-variation distance between mixtures over the two competing subfamilies. Related expositions appear in B. Yu, "Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam" (Festschrift for Lucien Le Cam, Springer, 1997), 423–435, and A. B. Tsybakov, *Introduction to Nonparametric Estimation* (Springer, 2009), §2.

title: Mutual Information of the M-ary Testing Problem
informal: In the $M$-ary testing problem, with index $J$ uniform on $\{1,\dots,M\}$ and $Z\sim P_{\theta^J}$, the mutual information is taken in its averaged form $$I(Z;J)=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}D\big(P_{\theta^j}\,\big\|\,\bar Q\big),\qquad \bar Q=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^{M}P_{\theta^j},$$ where $D(\cdot\,\|\,\cdot)$ is the Kullback–Leibler divergence and $\bar Q$ is the uniform mixture. This equals the KL divergence between the joint law and the product of marginals.
summary: The average KL divergence between each component law and the uniform mixture — the information the observation carries about the random index.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def mutualInformation {M : ℕ} [NeZero M] (Q : Kernel (Fin M) 𝓧) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  (M : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹ * ∑ j, klDiv (Q j) (mixture Q)

hypotheses.label: KL to the mixture
hypotheses.note: Averages the KL divergence from each component law Q j to the uniform mixture.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: Mutual information originates with C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," *Bell System Technical Journal* **27** (1948), 379–423 and 623–656, where it appears (in the entropy form $H(Z)-H(Z\mid J)$, equivalent to the KL form) as the channel information rate.

title: Convexity Bound on Mutual Information
informal: The mutual information is controlled by the pairwise Kullback–Leibler divergences: $$I(Z;J)\ \le\ \frac{1}{M^2}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}D\big(P_{\theta^j}\,\big\|\,P_{\theta^k}\big).$$ This follows from convexity of the KL divergence in its second argument, since the mixture minimizes the average divergence.
summary: The mutual information of the M-ary problem is at most the average pairwise KL divergence — the key ingredient for local-packing lower bounds.
leanSignature:
theorem mutualInformation_le_avg_pairwise_kl {M : ℕ} [NeZero M] (Q : Kernel (Fin M) 𝓧)
    [IsMarkovKernel Q] :
    mutualInformation Q ≤ ((M : ℝ≥0∞) ^ 2)⁻¹ * ∑ j, ∑ k, klDiv (Q j) (Q k)

hypotheses.label: Markov kernel
hypotheses.note: Each component Q j is a probability law, so the mixture is well-defined and minimizes the average divergence.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The convexity (KL) bound is folklore: the standard "convexity of KL in the second argument" step underlying the local Fano / Has'minskii (1978) local-packing minimax machinery, with no single seminal origin beyond the joint convexity of the KL divergence itself.

title: Fano's Inequality
informal: For the $M$-ary testing problem with index $J$ uniform on $\{1,\dots,M\}$ and observation $Z$ from the $J$-th distribution, the error probability of any test obeys $$\inf_{\psi}\mathbb{P}\big[\psi(Z)\ne J\big]\ \ge\ 1-\frac{I(Z;J)+\log 2}{\log M},$$ where $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The bound is informative when there are at least two hypotheses, so that $\log M>0$.
summary: The M-ary testing error is lower bounded by one minus the mutual information plus log 2, divided by log M.
leanSignature:
theorem fano_inequality {M : ℕ} [NeZero M] (Q : Kernel (Fin M) 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel Q]
    (hM : 2 ≤ M) :
    1 - (mutualInformation Q + ENNReal.ofReal (Real.log 2)) / ENNReal.ofReal (Real.log (M : ℝ))
      ≤ multiwayTestingError Q

hypotheses.label: at least two hypotheses
hypotheses.note: M ≥ 2, so that log M > 0 and the bound is nondegenerate.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: Fano's inequality is classical information theory, originating with R. M. Fano, *Transmission of Information: A Statistical Theory of Communications*, MIT Press and Wiley, 1961 (and standard in T. M. Cover and J. A. Thomas, *Elements of Information Theory*, Wiley). Its use for statistical minimax lower bounds traces to R. Z. Has'minskii (1978) and to the systematic development by L. Birgé, "Approximation dans les espaces métriques et théorie de l'estimation," *Z. Wahrsch. Verw. Gebiete* 65 (1983), 181–237. The testing-reduction synthesis follows B. Yu, "Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam" (Festschrift for Lucien Le Cam, Springer, 1997), 423–435.

title: Fano Minimax Lower Bound
informal: For an increasing distortion $\Phi$ and a $2\delta$-separated family $\theta^1,\dots,\theta^M$ with $M\ge 2$, the minimax risk for $\Phi\circ\rho$ satisfies $$\mathfrak{M}\big(g(\theta);\Phi\circ\rho\big)\ \ge\ \Phi(\delta)\left(1-\frac{I(Z;J)+\log 2}{\log M}\right),$$ where $I(Z;J)$ is the mutual information of the induced sub-model.
summary: Combining Fano's inequality with the estimation-to-testing reduction gives a minimax lower bound in terms of the mutual information of the sub-model.
leanSignature:
theorem minimax_fano_lower_bound [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω]
    (Φ : ℝ≥0∞ → ℝ≥0∞) (g : Θ → Ω) (P : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    {M : ℕ} [NeZero M] (θfam : Fin M → Θ) (hθ : Measurable θfam) (δ : ℝ≥0∞)
    (hM : 2 ≤ M)
    (hΦ : Monotone Φ)
    (hsep : IsSeparatedFamily g θfam δ) :
    Φ δ * (1 - (mutualInformation (P.comap θfam hθ) + ENNReal.ofReal (Real.log 2))
                / ENNReal.ofReal (Real.log (M : ℝ)))
      ≤ minimaxRiskDist Φ g P

hypotheses.label: at least two hypotheses
hypotheses.note: M ≥ 2, so log M > 0.

hypotheses.label: increasing distortion
hypotheses.note: Φ is nondecreasing.

hypotheses.label: 2δ-separation
hypotheses.note: The functional values are pairwise at semimetric distance at least 2δ.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: Fano's inequality originates with R. M. Fano, *Transmission of Information*, MIT Press and Wiley, 1961. Its use for statistical minimax lower bounds traces to R. Z. Has'minskii (1978) and to L. Birgé (*Z. Wahrsch. Verw. Gebiete* 65 (1983), 181–237). The synthesis of the Fano, Assouad, and Le Cam methods follows the survey of B. Yu, "Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam" (Festschrift for Lucien Le Cam, Springer, 1997), 423–435.

title: Local-Packing Minimax Lower Bound
informal: Suppose a $2\delta$-separated family $\theta^1,\dots,\theta^M$ has pairwise KL divergences satisfying $D(P_{\theta^j}\,\|\,P_{\theta^k})\le c^2 n\delta^2$ (condition (15.35a)) and cardinality with $\log M\ge 2(c^2 n\delta^2+\log 2)$ (condition (15.35b)). Then for any increasing distortion $\Phi$, $$\mathfrak{M}\big(g(\theta);\Phi\circ\rho\big)\ \ge\ \tfrac12\,\Phi(\delta).$$
summary: The generalized Fano method: a 2δ-separated family with controlled pairwise KL and large enough cardinality forces minimax risk at least half the distortion at δ.
leanSignature:
theorem minimax_local_packing [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω]
    (Φ : ℝ≥0∞ → ℝ≥0∞) (g : Θ → Ω) (P : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    {M : ℕ} [NeZero M] (θfam : Fin M → Θ) (hθ : Measurable θfam) (δ : ℝ≥0∞) (c n : ℝ)
    (hΦ : Monotone Φ)
    (hsep : IsSeparatedFamily g θfam δ)
    (hn : 0 ≤ n)
    (h35a : ∀ j k, j ≠ k →
      klDiv ((P.comap θfam hθ) j) ((P.comap θfam hθ) k)
        ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (c ^ 2 * n * δ.toReal ^ 2))
    (h35b : 2 * (c ^ 2 * n * δ.toReal ^ 2 + Real.log 2) ≤ Real.log (M : ℝ)) :
    2⁻¹ * Φ δ ≤ minimaxRiskDist Φ g P
formalizationNotes: Uses the squared, divergence-level form D ≤ c²nδ² in place of the book's square-root form √D ≤ c√n δ (15.35a) — these are equivalent. The sample size enters as the explicit hypothesis n ≥ 0.

hypotheses.label: increasing distortion
hypotheses.note: Φ is nondecreasing.

hypotheses.label: 2δ-separation
hypotheses.note: The functional values are pairwise at distance at least 2δ.

hypotheses.label: pairwise KL control (15.35a)
hypotheses.note: Each pairwise KL divergence is at most c²nδ².

hypotheses.label: packing cardinality (15.35b)
hypotheses.note: log M ≥ 2(c²nδ² + log 2), so the family is large enough.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The local-packing / generalized-Fano scheme — combining a Fano-type lower bound with the convexity (mixture) bound on mutual information — originates with Y. Yang and A. Barron, "Information-theoretic determination of minimax rates of convergence," *Annals of Statistics* 27(5) (1999), 1564–1599. The broader Fano-method tradition traces to R. Z. Has'minskii (1978) and to L. Birgé (*Z. Wahrsch. Verw. Gebiete* 65 (1983), 181–237).

title: Yang–Barron Mutual-Information Bound
informal: Given a finite family $\{\gamma_k\}_{k$\varepsilon$-covers the model $\{Q_j\}$ in the square-root KL divergence — for each $j$ there is $k$ with $D(Q_j\,\|\,\gamma_k)\le\varepsilon^2$ — the mutual information obeys $$I(Z;J)\ \le\ \varepsilon^2+\log N.$$ Optimizing over covers gives $I(Z;J)\le\inf_{\varepsilon>0}\{\varepsilon^2+\log N_{\mathrm{KL}}(\varepsilon;\mathcal{P})\}$.
summary: The mutual information is bounded by the global metric entropy of the family in the square-root KL divergence, avoiding local packings.
leanSignature:
theorem yang_barron {M : ℕ} [NeZero M] (Q : Kernel (Fin M) 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel Q]
    {N : ℕ} (γ : Fin N → Measure 𝓧) [∀ k, IsProbabilityMeasure (γ k)] (ε : ℝ≥0∞)
    (hcover : ∀ j, ∃ k, klDiv (Q j) (γ k) ≤ ε ^ 2) :
    mutualInformation Q ≤ ε ^ 2 + ENNReal.ofReal (Real.log (N : ℝ))

hypotheses.leanToken: hcover : ∀ j, ∃ k, klDiv (Q j) (γ k) ≤ ε ^ 2
hypotheses.label: ε-cover in √KL
hypotheses.note: Every model law Q j is within squared KL ε² of some cover atom γ k.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The result originates with Y. Yang and A. Barron, "Information-theoretic determination of minimax rates of convergence," *Annals of Statistics*, 27(5):1564–1599, 1999, whose global-entropy device replacing local packings is the paper's central contribution. Wainwright's Lemma 15.21 is the presentation.

title: Pinsker–Csiszár–Kullback Inequality
informal: For probability distributions $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$, the total-variation distance is controlled by the Kullback–Leibler divergence: $$\|\mathbb{P}-\mathbb{Q}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\ \le\ \sqrt{\tfrac12\,D(\mathbb{Q}\,\|\,\mathbb{P})}.$$ The constant $\tfrac12$ (in nats) is sharp and no absolute-continuity hypothesis is needed (the bound is vacuous when the divergence is infinite).
summary: The total-variation distance between two probability distributions is at most the square root of half their KL divergence.
leanSignature:
theorem pinsker_tv_le_kl (μ ν : Measure α)
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] [IsProbabilityMeasure ν] :
    tvDist μ ν ≤ (2⁻¹ * klDiv ν μ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: probability measures
hypotheses.note: Both μ and ν are probability distributions.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The inequality is jointly attributed to three independent works. M. S. Pinsker, *Information and Information Stability of Random Variables and Processes* (trans. A. Feinstein), Holden-Day, San Francisco, 1964, first established a bound of this form (with a non-optimal constant). The sharp constant $\tfrac12$ (in nats) was obtained independently by I. Csiszár, "Information-type measures of difference of probability distributions and indirect observations," *Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica* 2 (1967), 299–318, and by S. Kullback, "A lower bound for discrimination information in terms of variation," *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory* 13(1) (1967), 126–127.

title: Le Cam's Inequality (TV ≤ Hellinger)
informal: For probability measures $\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}$, the total-variation distance is bounded by the Hellinger distance: $$\|\mathbb{P}-\mathbb{Q}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\ \le\ H(\mathbb{P}\,\|\,\mathbb{Q})\,\sqrt{1-\tfrac14\,H^2(\mathbb{P}\,\|\,\mathbb{Q})},$$ where $H=\sqrt{H^2}$ is the (unsquared) Hellinger distance and $H^2=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\xi$ against a common dominating measure $\xi$.
summary: The total-variation distance is bounded above by the Hellinger distance times the square root of one minus a quarter of the squared Hellinger distance.
leanSignature:
theorem lecam_tv_le_hellinger (μ ν : Measure α)
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] [IsProbabilityMeasure ν] :
    tvDist μ ν
      ≤ (sqHellinger μ ν) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ) * (1 - sqHellinger μ ν / 4) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: probability measures
hypotheses.note: Both μ and ν are probability distributions.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: L. Le Cam, "Convergence of Estimates Under Dimensionality Restrictions," *The Annals of Statistics* **1**(1), 38–53, 1973, introduced the Hellinger affinity / Hellinger distance as the controlling quantity for testing and estimation rates; the two-sided comparison between total variation and Hellinger distance — of which the inequality $\mathrm{TV}\le H\sqrt{1-H^2/4}$ is the upper bound — originates in this line of work. The sharp constants and clean Cauchy–Schwarz derivation are now standard material.

title: Data-Processing Inequality for KL Divergence
informal: For a measurable map $f:\alpha o eta$ and probability measures $\mu, u$, the Kullback–Leibler divergence contracts under the push-forward: $$D ig(\mu\circ f^{-1}\, ig\|\, u\circ f^{-1} ig)\ \le\ D(\mu\,\|\, u).$$ This is the deterministic-channel case of the data-processing inequality for an $f$-divergence.
summary: Pushing two laws through a measurable map can only decrease their KL divergence.
leanSignature:
theorem klDiv_map_le {f : α → β} (hf : Measurable f) (μ ν : Measure α)
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] [IsProbabilityMeasure ν] :
    klDiv (μ.map f) (ν.map f) ≤ klDiv μ ν

hypotheses.label: measurable map
hypotheses.note: The channel f is a measurable map.

hypotheses.label: probability measures
hypotheses.note: Both μ and ν are probability distributions.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The data-processing inequality for KL divergence (and more generally any $f$-divergence) is classical folklore. The general $f$-divergence statement and its convexity proof are due to I. Csiszár, "Information-type measures of difference of probability distributions and indirect observations," *Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica* **2** (1967), 299–318, and independently S. M. Ali and S. D. Silvey, "A general class of coefficients of divergence of one distribution from another," *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B*, **28** (1966), 131–142. See also T. M. Cover and J. A. Thomas, *Elements of Information Theory*, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006, Theorem 2.8.1.

title: Minimax Rate for the Gaussian Location Family
informal: For the Gaussian location family $\{\mathcal{N}(\theta,\sigma^2):\theta\in\mathbb{R}\}$ observed through $n$ i.i.d. samples, the minimax risk for estimating the mean under squared error obeys $$\inf_{\widehat\theta}\ \sup_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_\theta\big[(\widehat\theta-\theta)^2\big]\ \ge\ \frac{\sigma^2}{24\,n},$$ for fixed nonzero variance $\sigma^2$ and sample size $n\ge1$.
summary: For n i.i.d. samples from a Gaussian with unknown mean, the minimax squared-error risk for the mean is at least σ²/(24n).
leanSignature:
theorem gaussian_location_minimax_rate (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) (v : ℝ≥0) (hv : v ≠ 0)
    (P : Kernel ℝ (Fin n → ℝ)) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    (hP : ∀ θ : ℝ, P θ = Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => gaussianReal θ v) :
    ENNReal.ofReal ((v : ℝ) / (24 * n)) ≤ minimaxRiskDist (· ^ 2) id P
formalizationNotes: The book states the σ²/n order up to a universal constant; the formalization proves the explicit constant 1/24 (the two-point construction yields σ²/(16n); 1/24 is stated so the inequality holds verbatim).

hypotheses.leanToken: hP : ∀ θ : ℝ, P θ = Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => gaussianReal θ v
hypotheses.label: n-fold i.i.d. Gaussian
hypotheses.note: P θ is the n-fold product of N(θ, v).

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The $\sigma^2/n$ minimax rate for estimating a Gaussian mean under squared-error loss is classical folklore. The lower-bound technique is Le Cam's two-point method (L. Le Cam, "Convergence of estimates under dimensionality restrictions," *Annals of Statistics* 1 (1973), 38–53); Pinsker's inequality (M. S. Pinsker, *Information and Information Stability of Random Variables and Processes*, Holden-Day, 1964) converts the KL divergence into the required total-variation bound.

title: Minimax Rate for the Uniform Location Family
informal: For the uniform location family $\{\mathrm{Uniform}[\theta,\theta+1]:\theta\in\mathbb{R}\}$ observed through $n$ i.i.d. samples (with $n\ge2$), the minimax risk for estimating $\theta$ under squared error obeys $$\inf_{\widehat\theta}\ \sup_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_\theta\big[(\widehat\theta-\theta)^2\big]\ \ge\ \frac{1-1/\sqrt2}{128}\cdot\frac{1}{n^2},$$ the characteristic $n^{-2}$ rate of a non-regular problem.
summary: For n i.i.d. samples from a unit-width uniform with unknown shift, the minimax squared-error risk is at least a constant times n^{-2} — faster than the parametric rate.
leanSignature:
theorem uniform_location_minimax_rate (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n)
    (P : Kernel ℝ (Fin n → ℝ)) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    (hP : ∀ θ : ℝ, P θ = Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => volume.restrict (Set.Icc θ (θ + 1))) :
    ENNReal.ofReal ((1 - 1 / Real.sqrt 2) / 128 / (n : ℝ) ^ 2)
      ≤ minimaxRiskDist (· ^ 2) id P
formalizationNotes: Restricted to n ≥ 2 (at n=1 the two shifted unit-uniforms are a.e. disjoint, forcing TV distance 1 and a vacuous two-point bound; the book statement is an n→∞ rate). The explicit constant (1−1/√2)/128 is the provable value; the book states only the order.

hypotheses.leanToken: hP : ∀ θ : ℝ, P θ = Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => volume.restrict (Set.Icc θ (θ + 1))
hypotheses.label: n-fold i.i.d. uniform shift
hypotheses.note: P θ is the n-fold product of Uniform[θ, θ+1].

hypotheses.label: sample size n ≥ 2
hypotheses.note: At least two samples so the two-point bound is non-vacuous.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: This is a classical example. The uniform shift (location) family is the canonical illustration of a *non-regular* parametric model whose minimax rate $n^{-2}$ is faster than the parametric $n^{-1}$. The analysis via Hellinger-based two-point bounds is folklore (cf. L. Le Cam, *Asymptotic Methods in Statistical Decision Theory*, Springer, 1986; I. A. Ibragimov and R. Z. Has'minskii, *Statistical Estimation: Asymptotic Theory*, Springer, 1981).

title: Minimax Rate for Fixed-Design Linear Regression
informal: For the Gaussian linear model $y=X\theta^*+w$ with noise $w\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$ under the prediction semimetric $\rho_X(\theta,\theta')=\|X(\theta-\theta')\|_2/\sqrt n$, realized via $g(\theta)=A\theta/\sqrt n$ with $y\sim\mathcal{N}(A\theta,vI_n)$ and $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$, the minimax prediction risk obeys $$\inf_{\widehat\theta}\ \sup_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}\Big[\tfrac1n\|X(\widehat\theta-\theta)\|_2^2\Big]\ \ge\ \frac{\sigma^2}{2560}\cdot\frac{\operatorname{rank}(X)}{n}.$$
summary: For the Gaussian linear model with prediction loss, the minimax risk is at least a constant times σ²·rank(X)/n.
leanSignature:
theorem linear_regression_minimax_rate {n d : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (v : ℝ≥0) (hv : v ≠ 0) (r : ℕ)
    (hr0 : 40 ≤ r)
    (A : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) →ₗ[ℝ] EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))
    (g : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))
    (P : Kernel (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)) (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    (hg : ∀ θ, g θ = (Real.sqrt n)⁻¹ • A θ)
    (hP : ∀ θ, P θ = multivariateGaussian (A θ) ((v : ℝ) • (1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ)))
    (hr : r = Module.finrank ℝ (LinearMap.range A)) :
    ENNReal.ofReal ((v : ℝ) * r / (2560 * n)) ≤ minimaxRiskDist (· ^ 2) g P
formalizationNotes: The leading constant is the provable 1/2560 rather than the book's 1/128, forced by the r/10 Gilbert–Varshamov sphere-packing brick; the result requires rank(A) = r ≥ 40 (small-rank designs are degenerate for the Fano cardinality condition).

hypotheses.leanToken: hg : ∀ θ, g θ = (Real.sqrt n)⁻¹ • A θ
hypotheses.label: normalized prediction map
hypotheses.note: g θ = Aθ/√n realizes the prediction semimetric as a Euclidean distance.

hypotheses.leanToken: hP : ∀ θ, P θ = multivariateGaussian (A θ) ((v : ℝ) • (1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ))
hypotheses.label: Gaussian design model
hypotheses.note: y ~ N(Aθ, v Iₙ), the fixed-design Gaussian linear model.

hypotheses.label: r = rank(A)
hypotheses.note: r is the rank of the design map A.

reference.formal: M. J. Wainwright, *High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint*, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
reference.biblio: The fixed-design prediction-error minimax rates are the presentation of results from G. Raskutti, M. J. Wainwright, and B. Yu, "Minimax rates of estimation for high-dimensional linear regression over $\ell_q$-balls," *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory*, vol. 57, no. 10, pp. 6976–6994, 2011. That paper derives matching minimax upper and lower bounds, under suitable design regularity, using exactly the Fano / local-packing argument reproduced here.

title: Minimax Rate for Sparse Linear Regression
informal: For the Gaussian linear model $y=X\theta^*+w$ with the regression vector known to be $s$-sparse, taking as the parameter set the sparse Euclidean unit ball $\mathbb{S}_d(s)=\{\theta:\|\theta\|_0\le s,\ \|\theta\|_2\le1\}$, the minimax risk in squared Euclidean error obeys $$\mathfrak{M}\big(\mathbb{S}_d(s);\|\cdot\|_2^2\big)\ \ge\ \frac{1}{4096}\,\min\!\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma_{2s}^2}\cdot\frac{s\,\log((d-s)/s)}{n},\ 1\right),$$ where $\gamma_{2s}$ is the $2s$-restricted maximum singular value of $X$ and $y\sim\mathcal{N}(A\theta,vI_n)$. The $\min(\cdot,1)$ cap reflects the bounded ball.
summary: Over the s-sparse Euclidean unit ball, the minimax squared-error risk scales as σ²·s·log((d−s)/s)/(γ²n), capped at a constant.
leanSignature:
theorem sparse_linear_regression_minimax_rate {n d s : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hs0 : 10 ≤ s)
    (hds : 8 * s ≤ d)
    (v : ℝ≥0) (hv : v ≠ 0) (γ : ℝ≥0) (hγ : γ ≠ 0)
    (A : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) →ₗ[ℝ] EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))
    (hγbd : ∀ θ : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d),
        (Finset.univ.filter fun i => θ i ≠ 0).card ≤ 2 * s → ‖A θ‖ ≤ Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) * (γ : ℝ) * ‖θ‖)
    (P : Kernel (SparseBall d s) (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))) [IsMarkovKernel P]
    (hP : ∀ θ, P θ = multivariateGaussian (A (θ : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)))
            ((v : ℝ) • (1 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ))) :
    ENNReal.ofReal (4096⁻¹ *
        min ((v : ℝ) * (s : ℝ) * Real.log (((d : ℝ) - s) / s) / ((γ : ℝ) ^ 2 * n)) 1)
      ≤ minimaxRiskDist (· ^ 2) Subtype.val P

title: Convergence of Gradient Descent (O(1/t) rate)
informal: Let $f : E \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex on a real Hilbert space and $L$-smooth (its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz, with $L > 0$). Run gradient descent from $x_0$ with constant step $1/L$, i.e. $x_{t+1} = x_t - \tfrac{1}{L}\,\nabla f(x_t)$, and let $x^\star$ be a global minimizer of $f$. Then for every $t \ge 1$, $$f(x_t) - f(x^\star) \;\le\; \frac{2L\,\lVert x_0 - x^\star\rVert^2}{t},$$ so the optimality gap decays at the $O(1/t)$ rate.
summary: Gradient descent with step 1/L on a convex L-smooth function drives the optimality gap to zero at the O(1/t) rate.
leanSignature:
theorem gradientDescent_rate
    {f : E → ℝ} (hf : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ f) (hdiff : Differentiable ℝ f)
    {L : ℝ} (hL : 0 < L) (hsmooth : IsLSmooth f L)
    (x : ℕ → E) (hrec : ∀ t, x (t + 1) = x t - (1 / L) • gradient f (x t))
    {xstar : E} (hmin : ∀ y, f xstar ≤ f y)
    {t : ℕ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    f (x t) - f xstar ≤ 2 * L * ‖x 0 - xstar‖ ^ 2 / (t : ℝ)
formalizationNotes: The book constant $2L$ is kept; the telescoping recursion actually proves a slightly tighter pre-bound that is loosened to match the book exactly. The iteration is supplied abstractly as a sequence satisfying the recurrence rather than via an explicit map, and the rate is stated for $t \ge 1$.

title: Convergence of the Frank–Wolfe Algorithm (O(1/t) rate)
informal: Let $f$ be convex and $L$-smooth, minimized over a convex feasible set $X$. At each step a linear-minimization oracle returns $y_t \in X$ minimizing $z \mapsto \langle \nabla f(x_t), z\rangle$ over $X$, and the squared step lengths are bounded, $\lVert y_t - x_t\rVert^2 \le D$. The Frank–Wolfe (conditional-gradient) iterates $x_{t+1} = x_t + \tfrac{2}{t+2}\,(y_t - x_t)$ satisfy, for every $t \ge 1$, $$f(x_t) - f(x^\star) \;\le\; \frac{2\,L\,D}{t+2}.$$
summary: The projection-free Frank-Wolfe method with step 2/(t+2) achieves an O(1/t) optimality gap over a convex feasible set of bounded diameter.
leanSignature:
theorem frankWolfe_rate
    {f : E → ℝ} (hf : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ f) (hdiff : Differentiable ℝ f)
    {L : ℝ} (hL : 0 < L) (hsmooth : IsLSmooth f L)
    {X : Set E} (hX : Convex ℝ X) {D : ℝ}
    (x y : ℕ → E)
    (hxX : ∀ t, x t ∈ X)
    (hlmo : ∀ t, y t ∈ X ∧ ∀ z ∈ X, ⟪gradient f (x t), y t⟫_ℝ ≤ ⟪gradient f (x t), z⟫_ℝ)
    (hdiam : ∀ t, ‖y t - x t‖ ^ 2 ≤ D)
    (hrec : ∀ t, x (t + 1) = x t + (2 / ((t : ℝ) + 2)) • (y t - x t))
    {xstar : E} (hxsX : xstar ∈ X) (hmin : ∀ z ∈ X, f xstar ≤ f z)
    (t : ℕ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) :
    f (x t) - f xstar ≤ 2 * L * D / ((t : ℝ) + 2)
formalizationNotes: The linear-minimization oracle is supplied as a hypothesis (the genuine per-step subproblem), avoiding argmin-existence machinery; the diameter enters only through the per-step squared bound $\lVert y_t - x_t\rVert^2 \le D$, and the book's affine-invariant curvature is specialized to $L D$. Stated for $t \ge 1$: the $t = 0$ case would assert the trivial initial gap $f(x_0) - f(x^\star) \le L D$, not provable from the per-step diameter bound alone for a constrained minimizer.

title: Convergence of Proximal Gradient Descent (O(1/t) rate)
informal: Consider the composite objective $F = f + h$, where $f$ is convex and $L$-smooth ($L > 0$) and $h$ is convex. Starting from $x_0$, the proximal-gradient method with constant step $1/L$ generates the iterates $x_{t+1} = \operatorname{prox}_{(1/L)\,h}\!\bigl(x_t - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(x_t)\bigr)$, where $\operatorname{prox}_{(1/L)h}(z) = \arg\min_y \{ \tfrac1L h(y) + \tfrac12\lVert y - z\rVert^2 \}$. Then for every minimizer $x^\star$ of $F$ and every $t \ge 1$, $$F(x_t) - F(x^\star) \;\le\; \frac{L\,\lVert x_0 - x^\star\rVert^2}{2\,t}.$$
summary: Proximal gradient descent with step 1/L on a composite objective f + h drives the objective gap to zero at the O(1/t) rate.

        (x t - (1 / L) • gradient f (x t)) (x (t + 1)))
    {xstar : E} (hmin : ∀ y, f xstar + h xstar ≤ f y + h y)
    {t : ℕ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    (f (x t) + h (x t)) - (f xstar + h xstar) ≤ L * ‖x 0 - xstar‖ ^ 2 / (2 * (t : ℝ))

The proof applies the pillar inequality (Lemma 14.1) twice — for monotone descent and for a telescoping per-step bound — and the constants match the book exactly. Stated for $t \ge 1$.

title: Convergence of Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient Descent (O(1/t²) rate)
informal: Let $f$ be convex and $L$-smooth ($L > 0$), with $x^\star$ a minimizer. Run Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent from $x_0 = y_0$ with fixed step $\eta = 1/L$ and momentum schedule $\lambda_0 = 1$, $\lambda_{t+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4\lambda_t^2}\bigr)$: $x_{t+1} = y_t - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_t)$ (a plain gradient step) and $y_{t+1} = x_{t+1} + \tfrac{\lambda_t - 1}{\lambda_{t+1}}(x_{t+1} - x_t)$ (mixing in the history term). Then for every $t \ge 1$, $$f(x_t) - f(x^\star) \;\le\; \frac{2L\,\lVert x_0 - x^\star\rVert^2}{(t+1)^2},$$ the accelerated $O(1/t^2)$ rate.
summary: Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent attains the accelerated O(1/t^2) optimality-gap rate, faster than plain gradient descent.

    (x y : ℕ → E) (lam : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hxy0 : y 0 = x 0) (hlam0 : lam 0 = 1)
    (hlamrec : ∀ t, lam (t + 1) = (1 + Real.sqrt (1 + 4 * lam t ^ 2)) / 2)
    (hxrec : ∀ t, x (t + 1) = y t - (1 / L) • gradient f (y t))
    (hyrec : ∀ t, y (t + 1) = x (t + 1) + ((lam t - 1) / lam (t + 1)) • (x (t + 1) - x t))
    {xstar : E} (hmin : ∀ z, f xstar ≤ f z)
    (t : ℕ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) :
    f (x t) - f xstar ≤ 2 * L * ‖x 0 - xstar‖ ^ 2 / ((t : ℝ) + 1) ^ 2

The book states the bound for all $t$; the Lean statement restricts to $t \ge 1$ (inherited from Theorem 14.2).

hypotheses.label: momentum mixing
hypotheses.note: y_{t+1} adds the momentum term (λ_t-1)/λ_{t+1} times the iterate difference.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The algorithm and its $O(1/k^2)$ convergence rate are due to Y. E. Nesterov, "A method for solving the convex programming problem with convergence rate $O(1/k^2)$", *Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR* **269** (3), 543–547, 1983 (in Russian). This is the seminal result establishing that, for convex $L$-smooth objectives, first-order methods can accelerate the gradient-descent $O(1/k)$ rate to the optimal $O(1/k^2)$ rate; the momentum schedule $\lambda_{t+1} = (1 + \sqrt{1 + 4\lambda_t^2})/2$ originates there. The proof technique formalized here (via an estimate-sequence / proximal argument) follows the modern treatment rather than Nesterov's original presentation.

title: Convergence of Accelerated Proximal Gradient Descent / FISTA (O(1/t²) rate)
informal: Consider the composite minimization of $F = f + h$, where $f$ is convex and $L$-smooth ($L > 0$) and $h$ is convex (possibly nonsmooth). The accelerated proximal-gradient method (FISTA) uses step $1/L$ and Nesterov momentum: from $x_0 = y_0$, $\lambda_0 = 1$, $\lambda_{t+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4\lambda_t^2})$, with $x_{t+1} = \operatorname{prox}_{(1/L)h}\!\bigl(y_t - \tfrac1L\nabla f(y_t)\bigr)$ and $y_{t+1} = x_{t+1} + \tfrac{\lambda_t - 1}{\lambda_{t+1}}(x_{t+1} - x_t)$. Then for any minimizer $x^\star$ of $F$ and every $t \ge 1$, $$F(x_t) - F(x^\star) \;\le\; \frac{2L\,\lVert x_0 - x^\star\rVert^2}{(t+1)^2}.$$
summary: FISTA, the accelerated proximal gradient method with Nesterov momentum, attains the accelerated O(1/t^2) rate on a composite objective f + h.
leanSignature:
theorem acceleratedProximalGradient_rate
    {f h : E → ℝ} (hf : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ f) (hdiff : Differentiable ℝ f)
    {L : ℝ} (hL : 0 < L) (hsmooth : IsLSmooth f L) (hh : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ h)
    (x y : ℕ → E) (lam : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hxy0 : y 0 = x 0)
    (hlam0 : lam 0 = 1)
    (hlamrec : ∀ t, lam (t + 1) = (1 + Real.sqrt (1 + 4 * lam t ^ 2)) / 2)
    (hxrec : ∀ t, IsProxMinimizer ((1 / L) • h)
        (y t - (1 / L) • gradient f (y t)) (x (t + 1)))
    (hyrec : ∀ t, y (t + 1) = x (t + 1) + ((lam t - 1) / lam (t + 1)) • (x (t + 1) - x t))
    {xstar : E} (hmin : ∀ z, f xstar + h xstar ≤ f z + h z)
    (t : ℕ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) :
    (f (x t) + h (x t)) - (f xstar + h xstar)
      ≤ 2 * L * ‖x 0 - xstar‖ ^ 2 / ((t : ℝ) + 1) ^ 2
formalizationNotes: The proof is not monotone in F; it uses a non-increasing Lyapunov energy (Lemma 14.2) combined with the pillar inequality and the Nesterov-sequence lower bound λ_t ≥ (t+2)/2 and identity λ_{t+1}² - λ_{t+1} = λ_t². Stated for $t \ge 1$ (the $t = 0$ case is the trivial initial gap).

hypotheses.label: f convex L-smooth
hypotheses.note: The smooth part f is convex and L-smooth, L > 0.

hypotheses.label: h convex
hypotheses.note: The nonsmooth part h is convex.

hypotheses.label: momentum schedule
hypotheses.note: Extrapolation weights follow λ_{t+1} = (1 + √(1 + 4λ_t²))/2 with λ_0 = 1.

hypotheses.label: prox step
hypotheses.note: x_{t+1} is the prox minimizer of (1/L)·h at the gradient-stepped extrapolated point.

hypotheses.label: momentum mixing
hypotheses.note: y_{t+1} adds the Nesterov momentum term to x_{t+1}.

reference.formal: Junwei Lu, *Big Data Analysis*, Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025.
reference.biblio: The algorithm and its $O(1/t^2)$ convergence rate are due to A. Beck and M. Teboulle, "A Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm for Linear Inverse Problems," *SIAM Journal on Imaging Sciences* **2**(1):183–202, 2009. The momentum recursion $\lambda_{t+1} = \tfrac12(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4\lambda_t^2})$ appears as Eq.
