    (hERM : ∀ ξ, ∀ S ∈ C, empFrac (fun i : Fin n => X i ξ) (Sn ξ ∆ Θ) ≤
      empFrac (fun i : Fin n => X i ξ) (S ∆ Θ))
    (hRmeas : MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable
      (fun ξ => μ.real (Sn ξ ∆ Θ)) P)
    {S₀ : Set Ω}
    (hS₀ : S₀ ∈ C) :
    ∫ ξ, μ.real (Sn ξ ∆ Θ) ∂P ≤
      μ.real (S₀ ∆ Θ) + 10800 * Real.sqrt d / Real.sqrt n
formalizationNotes: The constant $10800 = 2 \times 5400$ follows from the excess-risk bound $R(S^*_n) \le R(S_0) + 2\sup_S |R_n(S) - R(S)|$ combined with the VC law of large numbers on the loss class, whose VC dimension equals that of $\mathcal{C}$ (the Boolean squared loss reduces pointwise to the indicator of the symmetric difference with $\Theta$). The class is assumed countable per the batch supremum policy, and measurability of the selected hypothesis's risk is an added regularity hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: Independence
hypotheses.note: The sample stream is jointly independent.

hypotheses.label: Common law mu
hypotheses.note: Each variable has distribution mu.

hypotheses.label: VC dimension at most d
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis class has VC dimension bounded by d.

hypotheses.label: d at least 1
hypotheses.note: The VC dimension bound is at least one.

hypotheses.label: Empirical risk minimizer
hypotheses.note: The learner output minimizes empirical risk over the class at each sample.

hypotheses.label: Competitor in class
hypotheses.note: The comparison hypothesis belongs to the class.

reference.formal: R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability: An Introduction with Applications in Data Science*, Cambridge University Press, 2018.
reference.biblio: Theorem 8.4.5 is the classical Vapnik–Chervonenkis generalization bound in in-expectation form (Theory of Probability and Its Applications 16, 1971); the reduction of Boolean squared loss to symmetric differences is folklore.

title: VC Dimension
informal: A class $\mathcal{C}$ of subsets of a space $\Omega$ (each set identified with the Boolean classifier it indicates) shatters a finite set $\Lambda \subseteq \Omega$ when every subset of $\Lambda$ arises as a trace $\Lambda \cap S$ for some $S \in \mathcal{C}$, i.e. $\{\Lambda \cap S : S \in \mathcal{C}\} = 2^\Lambda$. The VC dimension $\mathrm{vc}(\mathcal{C})$ is the largest cardinality of a shattered finite set, $$\mathrm{vc}(\mathcal{C}) \;=\; \sup\{|\Lambda| : \mathcal{C}\text{ shatters }\Lambda\},$$ valued in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, equal to $\infty$ when arbitrarily large sets are shattered. By convention the empty class shatters nothing, so $\mathrm{vc}(\varnothing) = 0$.
summary: The VC dimension of a set class is the largest cardinality of a finite set that the class shatters.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def vcDim (C : Set (Set Ω)) : ℕ∞ :=
  ⨆ (Λ : Finset Ω) (_ : Shatters C Λ), (Λ.card : ℕ∞)
formalizationNotes: Classes are encoded as `Set (Set Ω)` (a classifier identified with the set it indicates), and $\mathrm{vc}$ is valued in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ (the top element when arbitrarily large sets are shattered). Edge behavior: the empty class shatters nothing, giving the degenerate value $0$.

reference.formal: R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability: An Introduction with Applications in Data Science*, Cambridge University Press, 2018.
reference.biblio: The VC dimension is due to V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” Theory of Probability and Its Applications 16 (1971), 264–280. The growth function and its polynomial bound trace to the same paper and, independently, to N. Sauer (Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series A 13, 1972, 145–147) and S. Shelah (Pacific Journal of Mathematics 41, 1972, 247–261).

title: VC Dimension of Half-Spaces
informal: The class of closed half-spaces $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^m : \langle a, x\rangle \le b\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$, taken over all $a \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}$, has VC dimension exactly $$\mathrm{vc}(\text{half-spaces in }\mathbb{R}^m) \;=\; m + 1.$$ In particular, half-planes in $\mathbb{R}^2$ have VC dimension $3$.
summary: The class of closed half-spaces in m-dimensional Euclidean space has VC dimension exactly m plus one.
leanSignature:
theorem vcDim_halfSpaceClass (m : ℕ) :
    vcDim (halfSpaceClass m) = m + 1
formalizationNotes: The lower bound exhibits the shattered $(m+1)$-point simplex $\{0, e_0, \dots, e_{m-1}\}$ with explicit separating witnesses; the upper bound uses Radon's partition theorem to show that no $(m+2)$-point set is shattered. The equality is exact with no constant slack, and the half-plane case ($m = 2$, VC dimension $3$) is derived as an instance rather than re-proved.

reference.formal: R. Vershynin, *High-Dimensional Probability: An Introduction with Applications in Data Science*, Cambridge University Press, 2018.
reference.biblio: The half-space computation is a classical example of Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory (Theory of Probability and Its Applications 16, 1971, 264–280); the Radon-partition route to the upper bound follows J. Radon, “Mengen konvexer Körper, die einen gemeinsamen Punkt enthalten,” Mathematische Annalen 83 (1921), 113–115.

title: Bayesian Statistical Experiment
informal: A Bayesian statistical model on a parameter space $\Theta$ and a sample space $\mathcal{X}$ consists of a prior probability distribution $\pi$ on $\Theta$ together with a sampling model $\theta \mapsto f(\cdot\mid\theta)$, presented as a Markov kernel (the likelihood) assigning to each parameter $\theta$ a probability distribution on the data. The prior is required to be a genuine probability measure and each $f(\cdot\mid\theta)$ a probability distribution. From these ingredients one forms the joint law $\pi \otimes f$ on $\Theta \times \mathcal{X}$, the prior predictive (marginal) $m(x) = \int_\Theta f(x\mid\theta)\,\pi(d\theta)$ on $\mathcal{X}$, and the posterior kernel $x \mapsto \pi(\cdot\mid x)$.
summary: The core data model bundling a prior probability measure with a Markov-kernel likelihood, from which the joint, prior predictive, and posterior distributions are built.
leanSignature:
structure BayesExperiment (Θ 𝓧 : Type*) [MeasurableSpace Θ] [MeasurableSpace 𝓧] where
  /-- The prior distribution `π` on the parameter space. -/
  prior : Measure Θ
  /-- The sampling model `θ ↦ f(·|θ)`, as a Markov kernel from parameters to data. -/
  likelihood : Kernel Θ 𝓧
  /-- Constitutive: the prior is a *probability* distribution. -/
  priorIsProbability : IsProbabilityMeasure prior
  /-- Constitutive: each `f(·|θ)` is a probability distribution (Markov kernel). -/
  likelihoodIsMarkov : IsMarkovKernel likelihood
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert's Definition 1.2.1. The probability/Markov requirements are constitutive structure fields (registered as instances), because dropping either makes the object not Robert's Bayesian model. Standard-Borelness and nonemptiness of Θ, needed by Mathlib's posterior construction, attach as typeclass arguments on the derived `posterior`, not as fields; improper (non-probability) priors are a deliberate out-of-scope extension.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The measure-theoretic Bayesian model — a prior on the parameter and a regular conditional distribution for the posterior — is standard; for the kernel/disintegration formulation used here, see the regular-conditional-probability and disintegration theory of J. L. Doob (*Stochastic Processes*, Wiley, 1953).

title: Posterior Disintegrates the Joint Distribution
informal:
For a Bayesian model with prior $\pi$ and likelihood kernel $f$, form the joint law $\pi \otimes f$ of parameter and data, the prior predictive (marginal) distribution $m$ of the data, and the posterior kernel $x \mapsto \pi(\cdot\mid x)$. Then on a standard Borel, nonempty parameter space the prior predictive composed with the posterior kernel equals the joint law with its two coordinates swapped:

$$m \otimes \pi(\cdot\mid\cdot) \;=\; (\pi \otimes f)^{\mathrm{swap}}.$$

This identity is the measure-theoretic content of Bayesian conditioning — prior $\times$ likelihood $=$ predictive $\times$ posterior.
summary: The prior predictive composed with the posterior kernel reproduces the joint law of parameter and data (coordinates swapped) — the disintegration identity underlying Bayesian conditioning.
leanSignature:
theorem posterior_disintegrates_joint [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ] :
    E.predictive ⊗ₘ E.posterior = E.joint.map Prod.swap
formalizationNotes: A textbook-facing alias of Mathlib's `compProd_posterior_eq_map_swap`, specialized to the fields of a `BayesExperiment` (here `E`). Standard-Borelness and nonemptiness of the parameter space are Lean-side regularity needed to construct the posterior kernel; Robert states the identity without them.

hypotheses.label: standard Borel parameter
hypotheses.note: The parameter space Θ is standard Borel and nonempty — the regularity Mathlib requires to construct the regular conditional distribution (the posterior kernel).

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The disintegration of a joint law into a marginal and a regular conditional distribution originates with A. N. Kolmogorov (*Grundbegriffe*, 1933) and was given its standard-Borel form by J. L. Doob (*Stochastic Processes*, 1953); reading “prior × likelihood = predictive × posterior” as its statistical meaning is the standard Bayesian viewpoint.

title: Bayes' Theorem (Dominated Form)
informal:
Consider a dominated statistical model in which the sampling distribution $f(\cdot\mid\theta)$ has density $p(\theta,\cdot)$ with respect to a common dominating measure $\nu$, together with a prior $\pi$. Then for prior-predictive-almost-every observation $x$, the posterior is the prior reweighted by the normalized likelihood:

$$\pi(d\theta\mid x) \;=\; \frac{p(\theta,x)\,\pi(d\theta)}{\int_\Theta p(\theta',x)\,\pi(d\theta')}.$$

This holds provided the joint density $(\theta,x)\mapsto p(\theta,x)$ is jointly measurable (with the parameter space standard Borel and the prior finite).
summary: In a dominated model, the posterior equals the prior reweighted by the likelihood density normalized by the evidence — the density form of Bayes' theorem.
leanSignature:
theorem posterior_eq_withDensity_likelihood_div_predictive
    [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ] [IsFiniteMeasure π] [IsFiniteKernel κ] [SFinite ν]
    (hp : Measurable (Function.uncurry p))
    (hκ : ∀ θ, κ θ = ν.withDensity (p θ)) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂(κ ∘ₘ π), (κ†π) x = π.withDensity fun θ => p θ x / ∫⁻ θ', p θ' x ∂π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert eq. (1.2.3). Proved by identifying the explicit density kernel with Mathlib's abstract posterior via uniqueness of disintegration. Joint measurability of $p$ is Lean-side regularity; finiteness of the prior/kernel and σ-finiteness of ν are standing instance assumptions. No `IsMarkovKernel` on the likelihood is needed — the density self-normalizes.

hypotheses.label: joint measurability
hypotheses.note: The likelihood density $(θ,x) ↦ p(θ,x)$ is jointly measurable — a measure-theoretic regularity condition; without it the density-form posterior kernel would be Mathlib's junk zero kernel.

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: Each sampling distribution $K(θ,\cdot)$ equals $ν$ reweighted by $p(θ,\cdot)$, i.e. has density $p(θ,\cdot)$ with respect to the common σ-finite dominating measure ν. This is the defining assumption of a dominated Bayesian model.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The density form of Bayes' theorem goes back to Bayes (1763, published by R. Price) and, in the generality of “the probability of causes,” to P. S. Laplace (1774); its measure-theoretic justification rests on Kolmogorov's axiomatization of conditioning (1933) and the theory of regular conditional distributions on standard Borel spaces (J. L. Doob, 1953).

title: Prior Predictive Density (Evidence)
informal:
In a dominated model where the sampling distribution has density $p( heta,\cdot)$ with respect to a dominating measure $ u$, the marginal (prior predictive) distribution of the data — obtained by integrating the likelihood against the prior $\pi$ — itself has a density with respect to $ u$, namely the prior predictive density (the evidence)

$$m(x) \;=\; \int_\Theta p( heta,x)\,\pi(d heta).$$

That is, the data distribution equals $ u$ reweighted by $m$. This requires only joint measurability of the likelihood density.
summary: The marginal distribution of the data in a dominated model has density m(x) = ∫ p(θ,x) π(dθ) — the evidence — with respect to the dominating measure.
leanSignature:
theorem comp_eq_withDensity_predictiveDensity [SFinite π] [SFinite ν]
    (hp : Measurable (Function.uncurry p))
    (hκ : ∀ θ, κ θ = ν.withDensity (p θ)) :
    κ ∘ₘ π = ν.withDensity (predictiveDensity p π)
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert's marginal $m(x)$ (§1.4). The a.e. non-degeneracy facts $0 < m < ∞$ under a finite model are derived elsewhere in the file (not assumed — assuming them would launder a fact forced by the setup). Only σ-finiteness of π and ν plus joint measurability of $p$ are needed.

hypotheses.label: joint measurability
hypotheses.note: The likelihood density $(θ,x) ↦ p(θ,x)$ is jointly measurable (measure-theoretic regularity).

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: Each sampling distribution $K(θ,\cdot)$ equals $ν$ reweighted by $p(θ,\cdot)$: the model is dominated by the common measure ν with density $p$.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The marginal (prior predictive) density $m(x)$ is the evidence of the model; its systematic use for hypothesis comparison begins with H. Jeffreys (*Theory of Probability*, 1939), and it underlies Bayes factors, model averaging, and empirical-Bayes calibration — see R. E. Kass and A. E. Raftery, “Bayes factors,” *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 90 (1995), 773–795.

title: Posterior Expectation Formula
informal:
In a dominated model with likelihood density $p(\theta,\cdot)$ against a dominating measure $\nu$ and prior $\pi$, the posterior expectation of any nonnegative measurable functional $g(\theta)$ is the ratio of likelihood-weighted prior integrals: for prior-predictive-almost-every $x$,

$$\int_\Theta g(\theta)\,\pi(d\theta\mid x) \;=\; \frac{\int_\Theta g(\theta)\,p(\theta,x)\,\pi(d\theta)}{\int_\Theta p(\theta',x)\,\pi(d\theta')}.$$

This uses only joint measurability of the likelihood density and holds with no positivity side conditions.
summary: The posterior mean of a nonnegative functional equals the likelihood-weighted prior integral divided by the evidence.
leanSignature:
theorem posterior_lintegral_eq_div [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ]
    [IsFiniteMeasure π] [IsFiniteKernel κ] [SFinite ν]
    (hp : Measurable (Function.uncurry p))
    (hκ : ∀ θ, κ θ = ν.withDensity (p θ))
    {g : Θ → ℝ≥0∞} (hg : Measurable g) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂(κ ∘ₘ π),
      ∫⁻ θ, g θ ∂((κ†π) x) = (∫⁻ θ, g θ * p θ x ∂π) / ∫⁻ θ', p θ' x ∂π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the posterior-expectation ratio of Robert §1.4 (eq. (1.2.3) integrated against $g$). Stated for $ℝ_{≥0}^∞$-valued $g$, so no positivity or integrability hypotheses are required; the set-indicator special case gives $π(s\mid x) = \int_s p\,dπ / \int p\,dπ$ (a companion lemma in the same file).

hypotheses.label: joint measurability
hypotheses.note: The likelihood density $(θ,x) ↦ p(θ,x)$ is jointly measurable (regularity).

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: Each sampling distribution equals $ν$ reweighted by $p(θ,\cdot)$: the model is dominated by ν with density $p$.

hypotheses.label: measurable functional
hypotheses.note: The functional $g : Θ → ℝ_{≥0}^∞$ is measurable; being extended-nonnegative-real–valued, it needs no integrability or positivity conditions.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: Ratios of the form $\int g\cdot p\,dπ / \int p\,dπ$ are the computational core of Bayesian inference — already Laplace's 1774 memoir evaluates posterior expectations of this shape, and their numerical approximation motivates the Monte Carlo and Laplace-approximation methods.

title: Posterior Odds = Prior Odds × Bayes Factor
informal:
For a hypothesis represented by a measurable event $s$ (with alternative $s^c$) and observed data $d$ on a finite measure space, the posterior odds factor as the prior odds times the Bayes factor:

$$\frac{\mu[s\mid d]}{\mu[s^c\mid d]} \;=\; \frac{\mu(s)}{\mu(s^c)}\cdot\frac{\mu[d\mid s]}{\mu[d\mid s^c]}.$$

The identity holds unconditionally — every degenerate case collapses both sides under the extended-nonnegative-real conventions.
summary: Bayesian hypothesis testing: the posterior odds of an event equal its prior odds multiplied by the Bayes factor (the data's likelihood ratio).
leanSignature:
theorem posteriorOdds_eq_priorOdds_mul_bayesFactor (μ : Measure Ω) [IsFiniteMeasure μ]
    {s : Set Ω} (hs : MeasurableSet s) (d : Set Ω) :
    posteriorOdds μ s d = priorOdds μ s * bayesFactor μ s d
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert's odds form of Bayes' theorem (eq. (1.2.2)) and Definition 5.2.5. Stated unconditionally for a finite measure: all degenerate cases ($μ d$, $μ s$, or $μ s^c$ zero) collapse both sides under the $ℝ_{≥0}^∞$ division conventions. A companion lemma inverts it to express the Bayes factor as the posterior/prior odds ratio, which does require nondegenerate prior mass on $s$ and $s^c$.

hypotheses.label: hypothesis is an event
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis $s$ is a measurable set; its complement $s^c$ is the alternative hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: finite measure
hypotheses.note: $μ$ is a finite measure, which removes the $∞$ cases so the odds factorization holds without further positivity assumptions.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The odds formulation of Bayesian hypothesis comparison and the Bayes factor are due to H. Jeffreys (*Theory of Probability*, 1939), whose calibration scale — refined by I. J. Good (1958) — remains in use; the modern survey is R. E. Kass and A. E. Raftery, “Bayes factors,” *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 90 (1995), 773–795.

title: Sufficiency: Posterior Depends on Data Only Through the Statistic
informal:
Suppose the likelihood of a dominated model factorizes in the Fisher–Neyman form $p(\theta,x)=g(\theta,T(x))\,h(x)$ through a measurable statistic $T$, with the density $p$ jointly measurable and the model dominated, $f(\cdot\mid\theta)=p(\theta,\cdot)\,\nu$. Then the full-data posterior depends on the observation only through the sufficient statistic: for prior-predictive-almost-every $x$,

$$\pi(\cdot\mid x) \;=\; \pi\big(\cdot\mid T(x)\big),$$

where the right-hand side is the posterior of the experiment induced by $T$. Equivalently, the base factor $h(x)$ cancels from the posterior.
summary: Under a Fisher–Neyman factorization, the posterior given the full data equals the posterior given only the sufficient statistic T(x) — the nuisance factor h(x) cancels.
leanSignature:
theorem posterior_ae_eq_posterior_statKernel [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ]
    {π : Measure Θ} [IsFiniteMeasure π] {κ : Kernel Θ 𝓧} [IsFiniteKernel κ]
    {ν : Measure 𝓧} [SFinite ν] {p : Θ → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞} {T : 𝓧 → S}
    (hp : Measurable (Function.uncurry p)) (hT : Measurable T)
    {g : Θ → S → ℝ≥0∞} (hg : Measurable (Function.uncurry g))
    {h : 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞} (hh : Measurable h)
    (hκ : ∀ θ, κ θ = ν.withDensity (p θ))
    (hfac : IsFactorizedLikelihood p T g h) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂(κ ∘ₘ π), (κ†π) x = ((statKernel κ hT)†π) (T x)
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the Bayesian content of sufficiency (Robert §1.3.1–1.3.2): the base factor $h$ cancels and the posterior reduces to the statistic experiment's posterior. Joint measurability of $g$ and measurability of $h$ are additional Lean-side regularity; the exceptional-set transport uses that $h \in (0,∞)$ holds predictive-a.e. (forced, not assumed). The likelihood-principle statement (proportional likelihoods give equal posteriors) is a companion result in the same file.

hypotheses.label: joint measurability
hypotheses.note: The likelihood density $(θ,x) ↦ p(θ,x)$ is jointly measurable (regularity).

hypotheses.label: measurable statistic
hypotheses.note: $T : 𝓧 → S$ is measurable; it defines the statistic experiment, the pushforward of the likelihood along $T$.

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: Each sampling distribution equals $ν$ reweighted by $p(θ,\cdot)$: the model is dominated by the common measure ν with density $p$.

hypotheses.label: factorized likelihood
hypotheses.note: The density factorizes as $p(θ,x) = g(θ, T x)\cdot h(x)$: the part depending on $θ$ enters only through $T(x)$. This is the Fisher–Neyman sufficiency criterion.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.pointer: §1.3.1, Definition 1.3.1 and the factorization theorem, p. 14; §1.3.2, pp. 15–16
reference.biblio: Sufficiency is due to R. A. Fisher (1922); the factorization criterion to J. Neyman (1935) and, in measure-theoretic form, to P. R. Halmos and L. J. Savage (*Ann. Math. Statist.* 20 (1949), 225–241). The Likelihood Principle — which Bayesian inference automatically obeys — was given its modern form by A. Birnbaum (1962) and defended by J. O. Berger and R. L. Wolpert (*The Likelihood Principle*, 1988).

title: The i.i.d. Posterior (Product Likelihood)
informal:
For an i.i.d. sample $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ drawn from a dominated model in which each observation has density $p(\theta,\cdot)$ with respect to a dominating measure $\nu$, with prior $\pi$, the posterior is the prior reweighted by the normalized product likelihood: for prior-predictive-almost-every sample,

$$\pi(d\theta\mid x_{1:n}) \;=\; \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n p(\theta,x_i)\,\pi(d\theta)}{\int_\Theta \prod_{i=1}^n p(\theta',x_i)\,\pi(d\theta')}.$$

This requires joint measurability of the per-observation density.
summary: For an i.i.d. sample, the posterior is the prior reweighted by the product of the per-observation likelihoods, normalized by the evidence.
leanSignature:
theorem posterior_iid_eq_withDensity_prod_likelihood
    [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ] {π : Measure Θ} [IsFiniteMeasure π]
    {κ : Kernel Θ 𝓧} [IsMarkovKernel κ] {ν : Measure 𝓧} [SigmaFinite ν]
    {p : Θ → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞}
    (hp : Measurable (Function.uncurry p))
    (hκ : ∀ θ, κ θ = ν.withDensity (p θ)) (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂(iidKernel κ n ∘ₘ π),
      ((iidKernel κ n)†π) x
        = π.withDensity fun θ => (∏ i, p θ (x i)) / ∫⁻ θ', ∏ i, p θ' (x i) ∂π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes posterior $∝$ prior $×$ i.i.d. likelihood (Gelman §1.3) as a one-shot application of the dominated Bayes theorem to the i.i.d. product kernel `iidKernel κ n`; the dominating measure is the product measure `Measure.pi (fun _ => ν)`. Here the likelihood is a Markov kernel (a genuine sampling model) and ν is σ-finite.

hypotheses.label: joint measurability
hypotheses.note: The per-observation likelihood density $(θ,x) ↦ p(θ,x)$ is jointly measurable (regularity).

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: Each single-observation sampling distribution equals $ν$ reweighted by $p(θ,\cdot)$; the sample of size $n$ is i.i.d. from this model.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Posterior updating on an i.i.d. sample is the original setting of both Bayes (1763, binomial counts) and Laplace (1774); the product-likelihood form is implicit in every conjugate analysis.

title: Posterior Predictive = Conditional Law of the Future
informal:
Consider the joint Bayesian model in which the parameter is drawn from the prior $\pi$ and, given the parameter, the observed data $X$ and a future observation $Y$ are conditionally independent, with $X\sim K_X(\theta,\cdot)$ and $Y\sim K_Y(\theta,\cdot)$. Then on standard Borel parameter and future spaces the conditional law of the future given the data is the posterior predictive distribution: for prior-predictive-almost-every $x$,

$$\mathcal{L}(Y\mid X=x) \;=\; \int_\Theta K_Y(\theta,\cdot)\,\pi(d\theta\mid x).$$

The future's distribution is obtained by averaging its sampling law over the posterior.
summary: In the joint model over parameter, data, and a conditionally-independent future, the conditional law of the future given the data is exactly the posterior predictive.
leanSignature:
theorem condDistrib_ae_eq_posteriorPredictive
    [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ] [StandardBorelSpace 𝓨] [Nonempty 𝓨]
    {π : Measure Θ} [IsFiniteMeasure π]
    (KX : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel KX] (KY : Kernel Θ 𝓨) [IsMarkovKernel KY] :
    condDistrib (fun ω : Θ × 𝓧 × 𝓨 => ω.2.2) (fun ω => ω.2.1) (π ⊗ₘ (KX ×ₖ KY))
      =ᵐ[KX ∘ₘ π] posteriorPredictive KX KY π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the posterior predictive distribution of Gelman §1.3 by identifying Mathlib's `condDistrib` of the future given the data with `posteriorPredictive KX KY π = KY ∘ₖ (KX†π)`. Conditional independence of $X$ and $Y$ given $θ$ is encoded by the product kernel $K_X ×_k K_Y$ (a constitutive modeling choice). The future space must be standard Borel for `condDistrib` to exist; the pivot is the disintegration “data ⊗ predictive = joint of the pair.”

hypotheses.label: conditional independence
hypotheses.note: Data and future are modeled by the product kernel $K_X ×_k K_Y$, encoding that $X$ and $Y$ are conditionally independent given $θ$ — a constitutive modeling choice, not a regularity assumption.

hypotheses.label: standard Borel spaces
hypotheses.note: The parameter space $Θ$ and the future space $𝓨$ are standard Borel and nonempty, as required for the posterior kernel and for the conditional distribution `condDistrib` to exist.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Reading prediction as conditioning in a joint model over parameter, data, and future is the de Finetti–Geisser predictivist program (B. de Finetti, *Theory of Probability*, 1974; S. Geisser, *Predictive Inference*, 1993) and the semantic basis of probabilistic programming; the disintegration technology is Kolmogorov (1933) and Doob (1953).

title: The Conjugacy Criterion (Normalization Principle)
informal:
This is the engine behind every conjugate-prior computation: the working principle that one may recognize the posterior up to its normalizing constant. Let $\pi$ be a prior (a finite measure) on a parameter space $\Theta$, and let the observation model be a likelihood kernel $\kappa$ that is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\nu$, so that each observation law $\kappa(\theta,\cdot)$ has density $p(\theta,\cdot)$ against $\nu$, where the density $p(\theta,x)$ is jointly measurable in the parameter and the data.

Suppose that at every data point $x$ the unnormalized posterior $p(\cdot,x)\,\pi(d\theta)$ equals a scalar multiple $c(x)\cdot\rho_x$ of a candidate measure, where each candidate $\rho_x$ is a probability measure. Then the posterior coincides with the candidate, $$\pi(d\theta \mid x) = \rho_x,$$ for prior-predictive-almost-every data point $x$. Remarkably, no positivity or finiteness assumption on the constant $c(x)$ is required: evaluating the recognized identity on the whole parameter space forces $c(x)$ to equal the marginal density $m(x)=\int_\Theta p(\theta,x)\,\pi(d\theta)$, which the dominated-model machinery guarantees is strictly positive and finite almost everywhere.
summary: The normalization principle behind conjugacy: if the unnormalized posterior is a scalar multiple of a probability measure, the posterior is exactly that measure, for predictive-almost-every data point.
formalizationNotes: Robert states conjugacy informally as `the posterior is proportional to f(x|θ)π(θ)'; this packages that slogan as a reusable measure-theoretic lemma, so each concrete conjugate pair below reduces to a single pointwise density identity. The predictive-almost-everywhere qualifier and the joint-measurability hypothesis on p are Lean-side regularity. Notably the recognized constant c(x) needs no side conditions — the whole-space evaluation forces c(x) = m(x), and the dominated Bayes machinery supplies 0 < m(x) < ∞ almost everywhere. A pointwise companion, generalizedPosterior_eq_of_withDensity_eq_smul, gives an everywhere (non-a.e.) identity at the cost of assuming c ∈ (0, ∞) explicitly.

hypotheses.label: measurable likelihood density
hypotheses.note: The likelihood density p(θ, x) is jointly measurable in the parameter and the data.

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: Each observation law κ(θ, ·) has a density p(θ, ·) against a common σ-finite measure ν.

hypotheses.label: probability candidates
hypotheses.note: Each candidate posterior ρ_x is a probability measure.

hypotheses.label: recognized form
hypotheses.note: At every data point x, the unnormalized posterior p(·, x)·π equals a scalar multiple c(x)·ρ_x of the candidate measure.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.pointer: §3.3.2, Definition 3.3.1 (conjugate families) and the proportionality computations of §3.3–§4.2.
reference.biblio: The `recognize the posterior up to its normalizing constant' principle traces to H. Raiffa and R. Schlaifer, *Applied Statistical Decision Theory* (Harvard, 1961).

title: Beta–Bernoulli Conjugacy and Laplace's Rule of Succession
informal:
Model an unknown success probability with a Beta prior, $\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$ with $\alpha > 0$ and $\beta > 0$, and observe $n$ independent Bernoulli trials $y_1, \dots, y_n$. Writing $s = \sum_{i} y_i$ for the number of successes, the posterior is again a Beta law, obtained by adding the successes and the failures to the two parameters: $$\theta \mid y_{1:n} \sim \mathrm{Beta}\big(\alpha + s,\ \beta + (n - s)\big),$$ for prior-predictive-almost-every sample.

The celebrated corollary is Laplace's rule of succession (companion theorem beta_bernoulli_posteriorPredictive_true_ae): the posterior predictive probability of one further success is $$P(y_{n+1} = 1 \mid y_{1:n}) = \frac{\alpha + s}{\alpha + \beta + n}.$$ Laplace's original form $(n+1)/(n+2)$ — the odds the sun rises again after $n$ risings — is the uniform-prior case $\alpha = \beta = 1$, $s = n$. This is the first posterior predictive computation in history and the standard `add-one' (Laplace) smoothing device of modern categorical modeling.
summary: For i.i.d. Bernoulli data with a Beta prior, the posterior is Beta with successes and failures added to the parameters, yielding Laplace's rule of succession for the next-success probability.
leanSignature:
theorem beta_bernoulli_posterior_ae {α β : ℝ}
    (hα : 0 < α) (hβ : 0 < β)
    [IsFiniteMeasure (betaMeasure α β)] (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ᵐ y ∂(iidKernel bernoulliKernel n ∘ₘ betaMeasure α β),
      ((iidKernel bernoulliKernel n)†(betaMeasure α β)) y
        = betaMeasure (α + successes y) (β + ((n - successes y : ℕ) : ℝ)) := by ...
formalizationNotes: Gelman §2.4 gives the update for a single binomial count; here the likelihood is the i.i.d. Bernoulli product, whose exponents are the success count s and failure count n−s. Positivity α, β > 0 is required for the Beta prior to be a genuine probability measure (Lean-side [IsFiniteMeasure ...] plumbing is discharged from it). The result holds for prior-predictive-almost-every sample — the a.e. qualifier is the measure-theoretic rendering of `for all observed data', excluding the marginal null set.

hypotheses.label: positive shape α
hypotheses.note: The first Beta parameter is strictly positive.

hypotheses.label: positive shape β
hypotheses.note: The second Beta parameter is strictly positive.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.pointer: §2.1 and §2.4 (binomial model with conjugate Beta prior), pp. 29, 34.
reference.biblio: The rule of succession is P. S. Laplace, `Mémoire sur la probabilité des causes par les événements' (1774); the representation theorem of B. de Finetti (1937) explains the exchangeable-data reduction.

title: Beta–Binomial Conjugacy
informal:
The classical first example of Bayes' theorem. Place a Beta prior $\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$ on a success probability, with $\alpha > 0$ and $\beta > 0$, and take a single Binomial observation $k \sim \mathcal{B}(n, \theta)$ recording $k$ successes in $n$ trials. The posterior is again Beta, with the successes and the failures added to the two parameters: $$\theta \mid k \sim \mathrm{Beta}\big(\alpha + k,\ \beta + (n - k)\big),$$ for prior-predictive-almost-every $k$.

The prior predictive (marginal) law is the Beta–Binomial pmf (companion theorem beta_binomial_predictiveDensity): $$P(k) = \binom{n}{k}\,\frac{B(\alpha + k,\ \beta + n - k)}{B(\alpha, \beta)}.$$ Bayes's 1763 essay treats exactly the uniform-prior case $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$.
summary: A Beta prior on a success probability updated by a single Binomial observation gives a Beta posterior with the successes and failures added to the two parameters.
leanSignature:
theorem beta_binomial_posterior_ae {α β : ℝ}
    (hα : 0 < α) (hβ : 0 < β)
    [IsFiniteMeasure (betaMeasure α β)] (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ᵐ k ∂(binomialKernel n ∘ₘ betaMeasure α β),
      ((binomialKernel n)†(betaMeasure α β)) k
        = betaMeasure (α + (k : ℕ)) (β + ((n - (k : ℕ) : ℕ) : ℝ)) := by ...
formalizationNotes: Matches Gelman §2.4 exactly. The success probability is internally clamped to [0, 1] so that the Binomial kernel is a total Markov kernel over all real parameters; the clamp is invisible under the Beta prior, whose density vanishes off [0, 1]. The Markov property of the kernel is the binomial theorem evaluated at clamp(θ) + (1 − clamp(θ)) = 1. The predictive-a.e. qualifier is the Lean rendering of `for every observed count k'.

hypotheses.label: positive shape α
hypotheses.note: The first Beta parameter is strictly positive.

hypotheses.label: positive shape β
hypotheses.note: The second Beta parameter is strictly positive.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: The original Bayesian computation: T. Bayes's 1763 essay treats the uniform-prior case Beta(1,1); the modern conjugate-family reading is Raiffa–Schlaifer (1961), with the Beta–Binomial as Diaconis–Ylvisaker's (1985) canonical worked example.

title: Gamma–Poisson Conjugacy
informal:
For an unknown Poisson rate with a Gamma prior in the shape–rate parametrization, $\lambda \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(a, r)$ with shape $a > 0$ and rate $r > 0$, observe $n$ independent counts $y_1, \dots, y_n \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$. The posterior is again a Gamma law, adding the total observed count to the shape and the sample size to the rate: $$\lambda \mid y_{1:n} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\Big(a + \sum_{i} y_i,\ r + n\Big),$$ for prior-predictive-almost-every sample.

This is the count-data workhorse of Bayesian practice, from actuarial credibility theory to empirical-Bayes shrinkage of rates; the negative-binomial marginal it induces is the classical overdispersed count model.
summary: For i.i.d. Poisson counts with a Gamma prior on the rate, the posterior is Gamma with the total count added to the shape and the sample size added to the rate.
leanSignature:
theorem gamma_poisson_posterior_ae {a r : ℝ}
    (ha : 0 < a) (hr : 0 < r)
    [IsFiniteMeasure (gammaMeasure a r)] (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ᵐ y ∂(iidKernel poissonKernel n ∘ₘ gammaMeasure a r),
      ((iidKernel poissonKernel n)†(gammaMeasure a r)) y
        = gammaMeasure (a + ∑ i, (y i : ℝ)) (r + n) := by ...
formalizationNotes: The pinned Gamma measure is shape/RATE, matching Gelman's parametrization with the second argument a rate, so the update reads Gamma(a + Σy_i, r + n) with no reparametrization. Positivity of shape and rate makes the prior a genuine probability measure. The Poisson rate is internally clamped to [0, ∞) (invisible under the Gamma prior, whose density vanishes on θ ≤ 0); the Poisson kernel is Markov for every real parameter since the Poisson pmf sums to one at every nonnegative rate. Holds for prior-predictive-almost-every sample.

hypotheses.label: positive shape
hypotheses.note: The Gamma shape parameter is strictly positive.

hypotheses.label: positive rate
hypotheses.note: The Gamma rate parameter is strictly positive.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: The Gamma prior for Poisson intensities appears in actuarial credibility theory (Bühlmann 1967) and empirical-Bayes rate shrinkage (Robbins 1956; Efron–Morris 1975); it is one of the Raiffa–Schlaifer (1961) natural conjugate pairs.

title: Normal–Normal Conjugacy (Known Variance)
informal:
For an unknown Gaussian mean with a Gaussian prior $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, t_0)$ and $n$ independent observations $x_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, v)$ of known noise variance $v$, assuming the prior variance $t_0$ is nonzero and the noise variance $v$ is nonzero, the posterior is again Gaussian: $$\mu \mid x_{1:n} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n,\ \tau_n), \qquad \tau_n = \Big(t_0^{-1} + n\,v^{-1}\Big)^{-1}, \qquad \mu_n = \tau_n\Big(\frac{m_0}{t_0} + \frac{\sum_{i} x_i}{v}\Big).$$ In words, the posterior precision is the sum of the prior precision and the $n$ data precisions, and the posterior mean is the corresponding precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the observations. This holds for prior-predictive-almost-every sample.

A future observation then has posterior predictive law $\mathcal{N}(\mu_n,\ \tau_n + v)$ — the posterior uncertainty plus the observation noise (companion theorem normal_normal_posteriorPredictive_ae). The precision-weighted update is the static basis of the Kalman filter.
summary: For i.i.d. Gaussian observations of known variance with a Gaussian prior on the mean, the posterior is Gaussian with precision-weighted mean and summed precisions.
leanSignature:
theorem normal_normal_posterior_ae {m₀ : ℝ} {t₀ v : ℝ≥0}
    (ht₀ : t₀ ≠ 0) (hv : v ≠ 0)
    [IsMarkovKernel (gaussKernel v)] (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂(iidKernel (gaussKernel v) n ∘ₘ gaussianReal m₀ t₀),
      ((iidKernel (gaussKernel v) n)†(gaussianReal m₀ t₀)) x
        = gaussianReal (postMean m₀ t₀ v x) (postVar t₀ v n) := by ...
formalizationNotes: Matches Gelman §2.5. Variances t₀, v are encoded as nonnegative reals, and the nondegeneracy hypotheses t₀ ≠ 0, v ≠ 0 replace the book's implicit positivity; at v = 0 the Gaussian likelihood kernel degenerates to the zero kernel, so the Markov-kernel instance carries v ≠ 0 (a Lean-side plumbing argument, discharged by isMarkovKernel_gaussKernel, not a statistical assumption beyond nondegeneracy). The proof's heart is a completing-the-square identity. Holds for prior-predictive-almost-every sample.

hypotheses.label: nonzero prior variance
hypotheses.note: The prior variance is nonzero, i.e. the prior is nondegenerate.

hypotheses.label: nonzero noise variance
hypotheses.note: The known observation-noise variance is nonzero; at zero variance the Gaussian likelihood kernel degenerates to the zero kernel.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: The Gaussian-mean update with Gaussian prior is Gauss's combination-of-observations calculus (*Theoria motus*, 1809) read as Bayesian shrinkage; the precision-weighted form is the basis of the Kalman filter (Kalman 1960).

title: Dirichlet–Multinomial Conjugacy
informal:
The categorical generalization of Beta–Binomial conjugacy. For category probabilities over $k + 1$ categories with a Dirichlet prior $\theta \sim \mathcal{D}_{k+1}(\alpha)$, where every concentration parameter satisfies $\alpha_i > 0$, and a single Multinomial observation of $n$ trials producing the count vector $v = (v_0, \dots, v_k)$, the posterior is again Dirichlet, obtained by adding the counts to the concentrations: $$\theta \mid v \sim \mathcal{D}_{k+1}(\alpha + v),$$ for prior-predictive-almost-every count vector.

This `add the counts to the concentrations' rule is the categorical analogue of Laplace smoothing and the conjugate core of finite mixture models, latent Dirichlet allocation, and (in the infinite limit) the Dirichlet-process machinery of Bayesian nonparametrics.
summary: A Dirichlet prior on category probabilities updated by a Multinomial count vector gives a Dirichlet posterior with the counts added to the concentration parameters.
leanSignature:
theorem dirichlet_multinomial_posterior_ae {α : Fin (k + 1) → ℝ}
    (hα : ∀ i, 0 < α i)
    [IsFiniteMeasure (dirichletMeasure α)] (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ᵐ v ∂(dmKernel k n ∘ₘ dirichletMeasure α),
      ((dmKernel k n)†(dirichletMeasure α)) v
        = dirichletMeasure (α + fun i => (v i : ℝ)) := by ...
formalizationNotes: Gelman §3.4 writes the Dirichlet density in k+1 symmetric coordinates on the simplex null set; here it uses the standard Lebesgue-absolutely-continuous corner parametrization (drop the last coordinate, keeping all measure theory on Fin k → ℝ). Positivity of every concentration makes both prior and posterior genuine probability measures. The conjugacy kernel is the Multinomial kernel pulled back along the simplex embedding, dominated by counting measure on the countable count space; the observed counts satisfy Σ v_i = n. Holds predictive-a.e.

hypotheses.label: positive concentrations
hypotheses.note: Every Dirichlet concentration parameter is strictly positive.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Dirichlet-multinomial updating underlies latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei–Ng–Jordan 2003) and, in the infinite limit, the Dirichlet-process prior of T. S. Ferguson (*Ann. Statist.* 1 (1973), 209–230); it is one of the Raiffa–Schlaifer (1961) natural conjugate families.

title: Exponential-Family Conjugacy (Diaconis–Ylvisaker)
informal:
The single most reusable conjugacy theorem, from which all the concrete pairs specialize. Let the sampling model be a natural exponential family: each observation law has density $p( heta, x) = h(x)\,\exp ig(\langle \eta( heta), T(x) angle - A( heta) ig)$ against a $\sigma$-finite base measure, with natural parameter $\eta( heta) \in \mathbb{R}^d$, sufficient statistic $T(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d$, log-partition $A( heta)$, and finite base factor $h(x) < \infty$; the family components are measurable. Equip it with the Diaconis–Ylvisaker conjugate prior $$\pi_{\chi, u_0}(d heta) \propto \exp ig(\langle \chi, \eta( heta) angle - u_0\,A( heta) ig)\,\mu_0(d heta),$$ assumed proper ($Z(\chi, u_0) eq 0$ and $Z(\chi, u_0) < \infty$).

If every updated prior is likewise proper, then after $n$ independent observations $x_1, \dots, x_n$ the posterior stays in the conjugate family with updated hyperparameters $$\pi_{\chi, u_0}(\cdot \mid x_{1:n}) = \pi_{\chi + \sum_{i} T(x_i),\ u_0 + n},$$ for prior-predictive-almost-every sample: the sufficient statistics are accumulated into $\chi$ and the pseudo-count $ u_0$ is incremented by the sample size $n$. In modern practice this update is the tractable primitive behind variational inference and natural-gradient methods.
summary: For any natural exponential family with its Diaconis-Ylvisaker conjugate prior, the posterior stays conjugate with the sufficient statistics accumulated and the pseudo-count incremented by the sample size.

title: The Dirichlet Normalizing Constant
informal:
The exact closed form of the normalizing constant of the Dirichlet distribution over $k + 1$ categories. For strictly positive concentration parameters $\alpha_i > 0$, the integral of the unnormalized Dirichlet density over the probability simplex evaluates to a ratio of Gamma functions: $$Z(\alpha) = \int_{\Delta} \prod_{i=0}^{k} \theta_i^{\alpha_i - 1}\,d\theta = \frac{\prod_{i=0}^{k} \Gamma(\alpha_i)}{\Gamma\!\big(\sum_{i=0}^{k} \alpha_i\big)}.$$ Equivalently, this is the multivariate Beta function $B(\alpha)$.

The identity follows by peeling one coordinate at a time, reducing to the one-dimensional Beta integral $B(a, b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a + b)$ and telescoping. As immediate corollaries, the normalizer is finite ($Z(\alpha) < \infty$) and the Dirichlet measure is a genuine probability measure — the two facts the Dirichlet–Multinomial conjugacy result consumes. The evaluation goes back to Dirichlet's 1839 computation of the multivariate simplex integral.
summary: The Dirichlet normalizing constant equals the product of the Gamma functions of the parameters divided by the Gamma function of their sum.
formalizationNotes: Closes the closed-form Dirichlet normalizer that the conjugacy results otherwise needed only abstractly (0 < Z < ∞). The integral is taken in the corner parametrization on ℝ^k against Lebesgue measure, equivalent to the symmetric simplex integral of Gelman §3.4. The proof uses the pinned real Beta–Gamma identity B(a,b) = Γ(a)Γ(b)/Γ(a+b) telescoped through a coordinate-peel recursion Z(α) = B(α₀, Σ_{i≥1} α_i)·Z(tail α). Finiteness dirichletZ_lt_top and the probability-measure property are immediate corollaries.

hypotheses.label: positive concentrations
hypotheses.note: Every Dirichlet concentration parameter is strictly positive.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: The normalizing constant is P. G. L. Dirichlet's evaluation of the multivariate simplex integral ∫ ∏ x_i^{α_i−1} (*J. Math. Pures Appl.* 4 (1839), 164–168); as the multinomial's conjugate prior it enters via Raiffa–Schlaifer (1961) and underlies Ferguson's (1973) Dirichlet process.

title: Bayes Estimator via Posterior-Risk Minimization
informal: Consider a statistical decision problem with parameter $\theta$, data $x$, and a loss $\ell(\theta, y)\in[0,\infty]$ for taking action $y$; let $\pi(\cdot\mid x)$ be the posterior for a prior $\pi$ and data-generating model $P$. If the decision rule $\delta$ is measurable and for almost every observation $x$ (under the marginal $m = P\pi$) the action $\delta(x)$ minimizes the posterior expected loss $\int_\Theta \ell(\theta, y)\,\pi(d\theta\mid x)$ over all actions $y$, then $\delta$ is a Bayes estimator: it attains the Bayes risk $r(\pi) = \inf_{\widehat\theta} r(\pi, \widehat\theta)$. The proof rests on the Fubini identity $r(\pi,\delta) = \int_{\mathcal X}\big(\int_\Theta \ell(\theta,\delta(x))\,\pi(d\theta\mid x)\big)\,m(dx)$, so pointwise optimality gives global optimality. Here the loss is jointly measurable in $(\theta, y)$.
summary: A decision rule that minimizes the posterior expected loss at almost every observation attains the Bayes risk, hence is a Bayes estimator.

title: Posterior Mean is Bayes under Squared Loss
informal: Under the quadratic (squared-error) loss $\ell(\theta, a) = (\theta - a)^2$ on $\mathbb R$, the Bayes action given data $x$ is the posterior mean $$\widehat\theta(x) = \mathbb E[\theta \mid x] = \int_{\mathbb R} \theta\,\pi(d\theta\mid x),$$ and the resulting estimator attains the Bayes risk. Remarkably, no integrability assumption is needed: if the posterior lacks a finite second moment at $x$, then every action incurs infinite posterior quadratic risk there, so the claim holds vacuously; otherwise the mean is the unique minimizer by the bias–variance identity. This subsumes Robert's "provided the expectation exists" proviso.
summary: Under quadratic loss the posterior mean is a Bayes estimator, with no integrability assumption required.
leanSignature:
theorem posteriorMean_isBayesEstimator_sqLoss (P : Kernel ℝ 𝓧) [IsFiniteKernel P]
    (π : Measure ℝ) [IsFiniteMeasure π] :
    IsBayesEstimator sqLoss P
      (Kernel.deterministic (posteriorMean P π) (measurable_posteriorMean P π)) π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert Proposition 2.5.1. The proof case-splits on whether the posterior has a finite second moment (MemLp id 2): in the degenerate branch every action has infinite posterior quadratic risk, so even the junk value of `posteriorMean` (the Bochner integral, which is 0 when no first moment) minimizes; otherwise the bias–variance inequality selects the mean. The loss is encoded as ‖θ − a‖ₑ² to reuse Mathlib's variance API.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: Quadratic loss is the founding loss function of statistics, from the least-squares theory of A. M. Legendre (1805) and C. F. Gauss (1809); that the posterior mean minimizes posterior quadratic loss was already implicit in Laplace's probability-of-causes computations (1774). The bias–variance decomposition used here is textbook folklore.

title: Posterior Mode (MAP) is Bayes under 0–1 Loss
informal: On a finite parameter space $\Theta$, under the 0–1 loss $\ell(\theta, a) = \mathbf 1[\theta \neq a]$, the Bayes action given data $x$ is the posterior mode — the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator $$\widehat\theta(x) = \arg\max_{a\in\Theta}\ \pi(\{a\}\mid x).$$ The mechanism is that the posterior $0$–$1$ risk of action $a$ equals $1 - \pi(\{a\}\mid x)$, so minimizing the risk is exactly maximizing the posterior mass; the most probable parameter value is optimal, and the estimator attains the Bayes risk.
summary: Under 0–1 loss on a finite parameter space, the posterior mode (the MAP estimator) is a Bayes estimator.
leanSignature:
theorem posteriorMode_isBayesEstimator_zeroOneLoss [Fintype Θ] [Nonempty Θ]
    [DiscreteMeasurableSpace Θ]
    (P : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsFiniteKernel P] (π : Measure Θ) [IsFiniteMeasure π] :
    IsBayesEstimator zeroOneLoss P
      (Kernel.deterministic (posteriorMode P π) (measurable_posteriorMode P π)) π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert Proposition 2.5.7 / §4.1.2 (MAP = posterior mode). The mode is built from a choice-free finite argmax (`fintypeArgmax`, taking the least maximizer in the canonical enumeration) so that the estimator is genuinely measurable, rather than an unmeasurable `Exists.choose`. Finiteness plus the discrete σ-algebra makes StandardBorelSpace automatic.

hypotheses.label: finite parameter space
hypotheses.note: The parameter space Θ is finite and carries the discrete σ-algebra, so the MAP argmax is well defined and measurable.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.pointer: §2.5.3, Eq. (2.5.5) and Proposition 2.5.7, p. 81; §4.1.2 (MAP estimator), p. 166
reference.biblio: The 0–1 loss is the decision-theoretic formulation of hypothesis selection, tied to the testing theory of J. Neyman and E. S. Pearson (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 231 (1933), 289–337). That the Bayes rule under 0–1 loss is the maximum a posteriori estimator is standard; the MAP estimator also reads as penalized maximum likelihood.

title: Constant-Risk Bayes Estimator is Minimax
informal: Let $\kappa$ be a (randomized) estimator and $\pi$ a proper prior. If $\kappa$ is a Bayes estimator for $\pi$ and its frequentist risk $R(\theta, \kappa)$ is constant in $\theta$, then $\kappa$ is minimax: it minimizes the worst-case risk $\sup_\theta R(\theta, \widehat\theta)$ over all estimators. This is the classical device for certifying minimaxity from above — a Bayes rule with flat risk has risk equal to its own Bayes risk, and the Bayes risk always lower-bounds the minimax risk. The associated prior $\pi$ is then least favorable.
summary: A Bayes estimator whose frequentist risk is constant across all parameters is minimax.
leanSignature:
theorem isMinimaxEstimator_of_isBayesEstimator_of_risk_const
    {κ : Kernel 𝓧 𝓨} [IsMarkovKernel κ] {π : Measure Θ} [IsProbabilityMeasure π]
    (hB : IsBayesEstimator ℓ P κ π)
    (hconst : ∀ θ θ', risk ℓ P κ θ = risk ℓ P κ θ') :
    IsMinimaxEstimator ℓ P κ
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the principle of Robert Example 2.4.14 (a special case of Lemma 2.4.13). It reduces to the global-domination form (risk ≤ Bayes risk everywhere, `isMinimaxEstimator_of_isBayesEstimator_of_risk_le`): a constant-risk Bayes rule has risk equal to its integrated = Bayes risk. Complements the Minimaxity area (which lower-bounds minimax risk); here Bayes rules certify minimax risk from above.

Constant-risk Bayes rules and least favorable priors are the standard devices for exhibiting minimax estimators, e.g. the Beta(√n/2, √n/2) binomial example.

title: Flat-Prior Normal Mean Posterior
informal: Let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be i.i.d. observations from $\mathcal N(\mu, v)$ with known positive variance $v$, and place the improper flat prior $\pi(d\mu) = d\mu$ (Lebesgue measure) on the mean. Provided there is at least one observation, the generalized posterior is a proper Gaussian distribution $$\mu \mid x_{1:n} \sim \mathcal N\!\Big(\bar x,\ \frac{v}{n}\Big), \qquad \bar x = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.$$ The posterior is centered at the sample mean with variance $v/n$, reproducing the frequentist answer — the classical reconciliation between Bayesian and frequentist inference for a location parameter.
summary: Under the improper flat prior, the posterior for a normal mean from n i.i.d. observations is Normal, centered at the sample mean with variance v/n.
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the noninformative-prior normal-mean result of Gelman §2.5 / §3.2. Because Lebesgue measure is not finite, Mathlib's abstract posterior κ†π does not exist; the statement is genuinely about `generalizedPosterior` (the withDensity construction that works for improper σ-finite priors). The proof completes the square in the product Gaussian likelihood, exhibiting the unnormalized posterior as a positive finite multiple of the 𝒩(x̄, v/n) probability measure.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate variance
hypotheses.note: The known observation variance v is nonzero (positive).

hypotheses.label: at least one observation
hypotheses.note: n ≥ 1; required for posterior propriety under the improper flat prior.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.pointer: §2.5 (normal, known variance) and §3.2 (noninformative prior, N(ȳ, σ²/n)), pp. 39, 64
reference.biblio: The flat prior on a location parameter is Laplace's original principle of insufficient reason (1774) and the simplest Jeffreys prior (H. Jeffreys, *Theory of Probability*, 1939). That it reproduces the frequentist answer 𝒩(x̄, v/n) — with credible intervals numerically equal to confidence intervals — is the classical reconciliation example; it is safe for estimation but the arbitrary normalizing constant wrecks Bayes factors.

title: Bayes Factors Scale with Improper-Prior Constants
informal: The Bayes factor of model $0$ against model $1$ is the ratio of marginal (predictive) densities $B_{01}(x) = m_0(x)/m_1(x)$. Rescaling the null model's prior $\pi_0$ by an arbitrary constant $c \in (0, \infty)$ — as one is free to do with an improper prior, defined only up to a multiplicative constant — multiplies the Bayes factor by exactly the same $c$, whenever the alternative marginal is nonzero and finite at $x$: $$B_{01}^{\,c\pi_0}(x) = c \cdot B_{01}^{\,\pi_0}(x).$$ Since $c$ is arbitrary, the Bayes factor is undetermined. This is the precise reason improper priors are safe for estimation but meaningless for testing and model choice — by contrast, the generalized posterior itself is scale-invariant.
summary: Rescaling an improper null prior by an arbitrary constant multiplies the Bayes factor by that constant, so improper priors cannot be used for model comparison.
leanSignature:
theorem bayesFactorM_smul_left {p₀ : Θ₀' → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞} {π₀ : Measure Θ₀'}
    {p₁ : Θ₁' → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞} {π₁ : Measure Θ₁'} {x : 𝓧} (c : ℝ≥0∞)
    (h1 : predictiveDensity p₁ π₁ x ≠ 0) (h1' : predictiveDensity p₁ π₁ x ≠ ∞) :
    bayesFactorM p₀ (c • π₀) p₁ π₁ x = c * bayesFactorM p₀ π₀ p₁ π₁ x
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the improper-prior indeterminacy warning of Robert §1.5 (pp. 28–29, pointing to Chapter 5). The pseudo-marginal m(x) = ∫ p(θ,x) π(dθ) scales linearly in the prior, so the ratio inherits the constant. Companion results in the same file prove the generalized posterior is scale-invariant (so estimation is unaffected) and characterize posterior propriety.

hypotheses.label: alternative marginal nonzero
hypotheses.note: The alternative model's marginal (predictive) density at x is nonzero.

hypotheses.label: alternative marginal finite
hypotheses.note: The alternative model's marginal density at x is finite, so the ratio is well defined.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The scale-invariance of generalized posteriors and the resulting indeterminacy of Bayes factors under improper priors were emphasized by H. Jeffreys (1939) and motivate pseudo-Bayes-factor proposals — intrinsic and fractional Bayes factors (J. O. Berger and L. R. Pericchi, JASA 91 (1996), 109–122; A. O'Hagan, JRSS-B 57 (1995), 99–138). The marginalization paradoxes of Dawid, Stone and Zidek (JRSS-B 35 (1973), 189–233) delimit the safe zone.

title: Posterior Model Probabilities
informal: Consider a finite family of competing models indexed by $m$, with prior model probabilities $\varpi(\{m\})$ and, for each model, a marginal (predictive) data density $q_m(x)$. Then for almost every observation $x$, the posterior probability of model $m$ is, simultaneously across all $m$, $$P(M = m \mid x) = \frac{\varpi(\{m\})\,q_m(x)}{\sum_j \varpi(\{j\})\,q_j(x)}.$$ Each model's posterior weight is its prior weight times its marginal likelihood, renormalized over the family — the basis of Bayesian model comparison and model averaging. Here the densities are assumed jointly measurable.
summary: Over a finite family of models, the posterior probability of each model is its prior probability times its marginal likelihood, renormalized across the family.
leanSignature:
theorem posteriorModelProb_eq_div [Fintype M] [MeasurableSingletonClass M] [Nonempty M]
    {Q : Kernel M 𝓧} [IsFiniteKernel Q] {ϖ : Measure M} [IsFiniteMeasure ϖ]
    {ν : Measure 𝓧} [SFinite ν] {q : M → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞}
    (hq : Measurable (Function.uncurry q))
    (hQ : ∀ m, Q m = ν.withDensity (q m)) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂(Q ∘ₘ ϖ), ∀ m,
      posteriorModelProb Q ϖ x m = ϖ {m} * q m x / ∑ j, ϖ {j} * q j x
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert Eq. (7.2.2). The model index M is treated as a new finite-discrete parameter space (StandardBorelSpace from the countable-discrete instance), and the dominated-Bayes posterior-density theorem is applied, computing the posterior singleton mass and the predictive density as the finite sum ∑ⱼ ϖ({j}) qⱼ(x). Feeding q m := predictiveDensity (p m) (π m) recovers genuine within-model marginal likelihoods.

title: Bayes Test Threshold Rule
informal: Consider testing $H_0 : \theta \in \Theta_0$ against $H_1 : \theta \notin \Theta_0$ under the asymmetric $a_0$–$a_1$ loss, where wrongly rejecting $H_0$ costs $a_0$ and wrongly accepting costs $a_1$, and $\Theta_0$ is a measurable event. Whenever the combined weight $a_0 + a_1$ is nonzero and finite, the Bayes decision rule accepts $H_0$ exactly when the posterior null probability exceeds the loss-determined threshold: $$\text{accept } H_0 \iff \pi(\Theta_0 \mid x) \ge \frac{a_1}{a_0 + a_1}.$$ The optimal test is a threshold rule on the posterior probability of the null, with the threshold fixed by the ratio of the two error costs.
summary: Under the asymmetric a₀–a₁ testing loss, the Bayes test accepts the null exactly when its posterior probability exceeds the threshold a₁/(a₀+a₁).
formalizationNotes: Formalizes Robert Proposition 5.2.2 / Eq. (5.2.3). The rule `bayesTest` is defined directly by comparing the two posterior expected losses a₁·π(Θ₀ᶜ|x) and a₀·π(Θ₀|x); this theorem rewrites that comparison as the posterior-probability threshold via ℝ≥0∞ division algebra. A companion theorem (isBayesEstimator_bayesTest) shows the rule is a Bayes estimator for the loss.

hypotheses.label: the null hypothesis is an event
hypotheses.note: The null region Θ₀ ⊆ Θ is a measurable set.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate loss weights (nonzero)
hypotheses.note: The combined loss weight a₀ + a₁ is nonzero.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate loss weights (finite)
hypotheses.note: The combined loss weight a₀ + a₁ is finite, so the threshold a₁/(a₀+a₁) is well defined.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The threshold structure of Bayes tests is the Bayesian counterpart of the Neyman–Pearson lemma (1933) and appears with the a₀–a₁ loss following Wald's (1950) decision theory. Point-null refinements were sharpened into calibration results by J. O. Berger and T. Sellke (JASA 82 (1987), 112–122).

title: Point-Null Posterior Probability
informal: To test a point null $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$, use the mixture prior $w\,\delta_{\theta_0} + (1 - w)\,\pi_1$ that places an atom of mass $w \in [0, 1]$ at $\theta_0$ and spreads the remaining mass over a continuous alternative $\pi_1$ giving no mass to $\theta_0$. For a dominated model with likelihood $p(\theta, x)$, the posterior probability of the null is, for almost every $x$, $$\pi(\{\theta_0\} \mid x) = \frac{w\,p(\theta_0, x)}{w\,p(\theta_0, x) + (1 - w)\int_\Theta p(\theta, x)\,\pi_1(d\theta)}.$$ The null atom survives conditioning; its posterior weight compares the null likelihood against the alternative likelihood averaged over $\pi_1$.
summary: Under a point-mass-plus-continuous mixture prior, the posterior probability of the null point has an explicit ratio form comparing the null likelihood to the averaged alternative likelihood.
leanSignature:
theorem pointNull_posterior_singleton_ae [StandardBorelSpace Θ] [Nonempty Θ]
    [MeasurableSingletonClass Θ]
    {κ : Kernel Θ 𝓧} [IsFiniteKernel κ] {ν : Measure 𝓧} [SFinite ν] {p : Θ → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞}
    (hp : Measurable (Function.uncurry p))
    (hκ : ∀ θ, κ θ = ν.withDensity (p θ))
    {w : ℝ≥0}
    (hw : w ≤ 1) {θ₀ : Θ} {π₁ : Measure Θ} [IsProbabilityMeasure π₁]
    (hπ₁ : π₁ {θ₀} = 0) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂(κ ∘ₘ (w • Measure.dirac θ₀ + (1 - w) • π₁)),
      (κ†(w • Measure.dirac θ₀ + (1 - w) • π₁)) x {θ₀}
        = (w : ℝ≥0∞) * p θ₀ x
            / ((w : ℝ≥0∞) * p θ₀ x + ((1 - w : ℝ≥0) : ℝ≥0∞) * ∫⁻ θ, p θ x ∂π₁)
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the point-null posterior formula of Robert §5.2.4 (p. 231, stated but unnumbered). The mixture prior is finite by construction; the predictive density splits additively over the Dirac atom and the continuous part, and the hypothesis π₁({θ₀}) = 0 keeps the alternative from contaminating the null atom's posterior mass.

title: Metropolis–Hastings Reversibility (Detailed Balance)
informal: On a countable state space, fix a finite target measure $\pi$ and a proposal kernel $q$. The Metropolis–Hastings kernel — propose $y \sim q(x, \cdot)$, accept with probability $$\alpha(x, y) = \min\Big\{1,\ \frac{\pi\{y\}\,q(y, \{x\})}{\pi\{x\}\,q(x, \{y\})}\Big\},$$ otherwise stay at $x$ — satisfies detailed balance with respect to $\pi$: $$\pi\{x\}\,K(x, \{y\}) = \pi\{y\}\,K(y, \{x\}) \qquad \text{for all } x, y.$$ The chain is reversible for its target distribution — the structural property from which stationarity follows.
summary: The Metropolis–Hastings transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with respect to its target distribution, hence is reversible.
leanSignature:
theorem isReversible_mhKernel (π : Measure S) [IsFiniteMeasure π] (q : Kernel S S)
    [IsMarkovKernel q] :
    Kernel.IsReversible (mhKernel π q) π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the detailed-balance property of Gelman §11.2. The core is a pointwise symmetry lemma π{x}·q(x,{y})·α(x,y) = π{y}·q(y,{x})·α(y,x), proved via the ℝ≥0∞ identity c·min(1, d/c) = min(c, d); reversibility integrates it over pairs using Tonelli for tsums, and the diagonal-supported rejection mass is symmetric by construction. Reversibility is Mathlib's `Kernel.IsReversible`.

hypotheses.label: finite target measure
hypotheses.note: The target π is a finite measure (a probability distribution after normalization).

hypotheses.label: proposal is a Markov kernel
hypotheses.note: The proposal q(x, ·) is a probability distribution for every current state x.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: The Metropolis algorithm is N. Metropolis, A. W. Rosenbluth, M. N. Rosenbluth, A. H. Teller and E. Teller (J. Chem. Phys. 21 (1953), 1087–1092), generalized to asymmetric proposals by W. K. Hastings (Biometrika 57 (1970), 97–109). That detailed balance suffices for stationarity is the classical reversible-chain argument (A. N. Kolmogorov's reversibility criterion, 1936).

title: Metropolis–Hastings Stationarity
informal: On a countable state space, with a finite target measure $\pi$ and a Markov proposal kernel $q$, the target $\pi$ is invariant (stationary) for the Metropolis–Hastings kernel $K$: $$\pi K = \pi, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad \int K(x, A)\,\pi(dx) = \pi(A) \ \text{ for every event } A.$$ Once the chain reaches its target distribution it stays there — the correctness guarantee that makes Metropolis–Hastings a valid sampler for $\pi$. Stationarity is a direct consequence of detailed balance (reversibility).
summary: The target distribution is invariant for the Metropolis–Hastings kernel, so the chain correctly samples from it in the stationary regime.
leanSignature:
theorem invariant_mhKernel (π : Measure S) [IsFiniteMeasure π] (q : Kernel S S)
    [IsMarkovKernel q] :
    Kernel.Invariant (mhKernel π q) π
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the stationarity conclusion of Gelman §11.2. It is derived from reversibility (`isReversible_mhKernel`) via the standard implication that detailed balance implies invariance (Mathlib's `Kernel.IsReversible.invariant`). The MH kernel's Markov property — acceptance mass plus rejection mass equals one — is established separately (`isMarkovKernel_mhKernel`).
