reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Metropolis et al. (1953) introduced the symmetric-proposal algorithm for statistical mechanics; Hastings (1970) the general ratio. That reversibility implies stationarity is the classical reversible-chain argument (Kolmogorov, 1936); convergence theory (irreducibility, Harris recurrence, ergodic theorems) is Meyn–Tweedie (1993)-style analysis beyond this scope.

title: Gibbs Sampler Stationarity
informal: Let $\rho$ be a target distribution on a product space $A \times B$, where $A$ and $B$ are standard Borel spaces so the exact conditionals $\rho(da \mid b)$ and $\rho(db \mid a)$ exist. The two-block Gibbs sweep — first refresh the $A$-coordinate from its exact conditional $\rho(da \mid b)$, then refresh the $B$-coordinate from its exact conditional $\rho(db \mid a)$ — leaves $\rho$ invariant: applying the sweep to a $\rho$-distributed state returns a $\rho$-distributed state. Each single-coordinate update already preserves $\rho$ (the exact conditional preserves the joint), and composing invariant kernels preserves invariance.
summary: The systematic two-block Gibbs sweep, refreshing each coordinate from its exact conditional, leaves the joint target distribution invariant.
leanSignature:
theorem invariant_twoBlockGibbs (ρ : Measure (A × B)) [IsFiniteMeasure ρ]
    [StandardBorelSpace A] [Nonempty A] [StandardBorelSpace B] [Nonempty B] :
    Kernel.Invariant (gibbsSnd ρ ∘ₖ gibbsFst ρ) ρ
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the validity core of the Gibbs sampler (Gelman §11.1). Each one-coordinate update is shown invariant using Mathlib's measure disintegration ρ.fst ⊗ₘ ρ.condKernel = ρ (the exact conditional preserves the joint law); the two-block sweep is then `Kernel.Invariant.comp` of the two single-site updates. A companion result covers the random-scan (mixture) sweep.

hypotheses.label: first block is standard Borel
hypotheses.note: The first coordinate space A is standard Borel (and nonempty), so its exact conditional exists via disintegration.

hypotheses.label: second block is standard Borel
hypotheses.note: The second coordinate space B is standard Borel (and nonempty), so its exact conditional exists via disintegration.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: The Gibbs sampler is S. Geman and D. Geman (IEEE Trans. PAMI 6 (1984), 721–741), named for the Gibbs distributions of statistical mechanics; its data-augmentation form is M. A. Tanner and W. H. Wong (1987), and its statistical mainstreaming A. E. Gelfand and A. F. M. Smith (JASA 85 (1990), 398–409). Convergence rates and ergodicity are beyond this scope.

title: Rao–Blackwellization (Variance Reduction by Conditioning)
informal: Let $T$ be a square-integrable statistic and let $\mathcal G$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra — the retained information. Replacing $T$ by its conditional expectation $\mathbb E[T \mid \mathcal G]$ never increases its quadratic risk about any center $c$: $$\mathbb E\big[(\mathbb E[T \mid \mathcal G] - c)^2\big] \le \mathbb E\big[(T - c)^2\big].$$ This is the Rao–Blackwell inequality. In MCMC practice it justifies Rao–Blackwellization: replacing sampled values in an ergodic average by their conditional expectations given the retained coordinates reduces Monte Carlo variance at no bias cost.
summary: Conditioning a square-integrable statistic on a sub-σ-algebra cannot increase its quadratic risk, which justifies variance reduction by conditioning in MCMC.
formalizationNotes: Formalizes the Rao–Blackwell inequality behind MCMC Rao–Blackwellization (Robert §6.3.4, pp. 309–310, unnumbered). The proof uses L² contractivity of conditional expectation (Mathlib's `eLpNorm_condExp_le`) applied to the centered statistic T − c, bridged to the ∫⁻ sqLoss form; `condExp_sub` and `condExp_const` move the center c through the conditional expectation.

hypotheses.label: square-integrable statistic
hypotheses.note: The statistic T has a finite second moment (lies in L²).

hypotheses.label: conditioning sub-σ-algebra
hypotheses.note: m is a sub-σ-algebra of the ambient measurable structure — the retained information one conditions on.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: The Rao–Blackwell theorem is C. R. Rao (Bull. Calcutta Math. Soc. 37 (1945), 81–91) and D. Blackwell (Ann. Math. Statist. 18 (1947), 105–110). Its use as an MCMC variance-reduction device is A. E. Gelfand and A. F. M. Smith (1990), extended by J. S. Liu, W. H. Wong and A. Kong (Biometrika 81 (1994), 27–40).

title: The Hierarchical Bayesian Model
informal:
A two-level hierarchical Bayesian model on a hyperparameter space $\Lambda$, a parameter space $\Theta$, and a sample space $\mathcal{X}$ bundles three ingredients:

  • a hyperprior $\rho$, a probability distribution on $\Lambda$;
  • a prior kernel $\lambda \mapsto \Pi_\lambda$, assigning to each hyperparameter a probability distribution on $\Theta$;
  • a likelihood kernel $\theta \mapsto K_\theta$, assigning to each parameter a probability distribution on $\mathcal{X}$.

Together they realize the three-stage generative process $$\lambda \sim \rho, \qquad \theta \mid \lambda \sim \Pi_\lambda, \qquad X \mid \theta \sim K_\theta.$$ From these three pieces one derives every downstream object: the mixed (marginal) prior $\Pi = \int \Pi_\lambda\,\rho(d\lambda)$ on $\Theta$, the prior predictive on $\mathcal{X}$, the hyperposterior $\rho(\cdot \mid x)$ on $\Lambda$, and the conditional posteriors $\Pi_\lambda(\cdot \mid x)$ on $\Theta$.
summary: The data model bundling a hyperprior, a prior kernel, and a likelihood kernel into a two-level hierarchical Bayesian experiment.
leanSignature:
structure HierBayesExperiment (Λ Θ 𝓧 : Type*) [MeasurableSpace Λ] [MeasurableSpace Θ]
    [MeasurableSpace 𝓧] where
  hyperPrior : Measure Λ
  priorKernel : Kernel Λ Θ
  likelihood : Kernel Θ 𝓧
  hyperPriorIsProbability : IsProbabilityMeasure hyperPrior
  priorKernelIsMarkov : IsMarkovKernel priorKernel
  likelihoodIsMarkov : IsMarkovKernel likelihood
formalizationNotes: Definition-only data model (Gelman §5.2). The probability/Markov requirements are carried as constitutive instance-typed fields: Gelman's hierarchical model demands a probability hyperprior and Markov prior and likelihood kernels, and dropping any makes the object not the model. The standard-Borel and nonemptiness regularity that Mathlib's posterior needs is attached at the derived objects (hyperposterior, conditional posterior), not as structure fields.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Hierarchical priors: I. J. Good, *The Estimation of Probabilities* (MIT Press, 1965); the Bayesian linear-model form: D. V. Lindley and A. F. M. Smith, *J. Roy. Statist. Soc. Ser. B* 34 (1972), 1–41.

title: The Hierarchical Posterior Mixture Identity
informal: The mixture identity for hierarchical posteriors — the single most important decomposition of the two-level model. Suppose the likelihood is dominated, each $K_\theta$ having density $p(\theta, \cdot)$ against a common $\sigma$-finite base measure $\nu$, with the density $(\theta, x) \mapsto p(\theta, x)$ jointly measurable. Then for prior-predictive-almost-every observation $x$ and every measurable parameter set $s \subseteq \Theta$, $$\Pi(s \mid x) = \int_\Lambda \Pi_\lambda(s \mid x)\,\rho(d\lambda \mid x).$$ The marginal posterior of $s$ is the hyperposterior average of the fixed-hyperparameter conditional posteriors $\Pi_\lambda(s \mid x)$, weighted by the hyperposterior $\rho(\cdot \mid x)$ on the hyperparameter. Equivalently, the parameter posterior is a mixture of the conditional posteriors over the posterior on $\lambda$ — the measure-theoretic content of the law of total conditional probability for the hierarchy.
summary: The marginal parameter posterior is the hyperposterior-weighted mixture of the fixed-hyperparameter conditional posteriors.
leanSignature:
theorem thetaPosterior_apply_eq_lintegral_hyperPosterior
    {ν : Measure 𝓧} [SFinite ν] {p : Θ → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞}
    (hp : Measurable (Function.uncurry p))
    (hlik : ∀ θ, H.likelihood θ = ν.withDensity (p θ))
    {s : Set Θ} (hs : MeasurableSet s) :
    ∀ᵐ x ∂H.dataMarginal,
      (H.likelihood † H.mixPrior) x s
        = ∫⁻ lam, generalizedPosterior p (H.priorKernel lam) x s ∂(H.hyperPosterior x) := by
  ...
formalizationNotes: Gelman §5.3 (eq. 5.3), labeled 3A.6 in the source. Stated for a dominated likelihood — the setting the whole Bayesian area uses — while the prior kernel stays abstract; only the likelihood domination is assumed, no prior density is needed. The joint measurability of $p$ is a Lean-side regularity condition absent from the book. Derived by specializing the general posterior tower identity to the indicator of the set $s$.

hypotheses.label: jointly measurable density
hypotheses.note: Lean-side regularity (not in the book): $(\theta, x) \mapsto p(\theta, x)$ is measurable.

hypotheses.label: dominated likelihood
hypotheses.note: Each likelihood $K_\theta$ equals the base measure $\nu$ weighted by the density $p(\theta, \cdot)$; $\nu$ is a common $\sigma$-finite measure.

hypotheses.label: measurable parameter set
hypotheses.note: $s \subseteq \Theta$ is a measurable set.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Conditional decomposition into a hyperposterior and per-hyperparameter conditional posteriors: D. V. Lindley and A. F. M. Smith, *J. Roy. Statist. Soc. Ser. B* 34 (1972), 1–41; computational basis of the hierarchical Gibbs sampler of A. E. Gelfand and A. F. M. Smith, *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 85 (1990), 398–409.

title: Conditionally I.I.D. Implies Exchangeable
informal: Conditionally i.i.d. samples are exchangeable — the elementary (“if”) direction of de Finetti's theorem. Fix a likelihood, given as a Markov kernel $\theta \mapsto f(\cdot \mid \theta)$ on the sample space, a sample size $n$, and a prior probability distribution $\pi$ on the parameter. Draw the parameter $\theta \sim \pi$ and then, conditionally on $\theta$, draw $X_1, \dots, X_n$ independently and identically from $f(\cdot \mid \theta)$. Integrating out $\theta$, the resulting joint law of $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ is exchangeable: it is invariant under every permutation $\sigma$ of the coordinates, $$(X_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, X_{\sigma(n)}) \stackrel{d}{=} (X_1, \dots, X_n).$$ This is the foundation of the Bayesian reading of hierarchical models: exchangeability of the observables is exactly what a conditionally i.i.d. mixture produces.
summary: Mixing an i.i.d. product likelihood over a prior yields an exchangeable joint law -- the easy direction of de Finetti's theorem.
leanSignature:
theorem conditionallyIID_implies_exchangeable (κ : Kernel Θ 𝓧) [IsMarkovKernel κ] (n : ℕ)
    (π : Measure Θ) [IsProbabilityMeasure π] :
    IsExchangeable (iidKernel κ n ∘ₘ π) := by
  ...
formalizationNotes: Gelman §5.2, labeled 3B.2. `IsExchangeable` is defined as invariance of the law under every coordinate permutation, and `iidKernel κ n θ` is the $n$-fold product $(\kappa_\theta)^{\otimes n}$. Only the forward (conditionally-i.i.d. ⇒ exchangeable) direction is formalized; the full de Finetti representation of an exchangeable sequence as a mixture of i.i.d. sequences is left as future work.

hypotheses.label: Markov likelihood kernel
hypotheses.note: $\theta \mapsto f(\cdot \mid \theta)$ is a probability (Markov) kernel from the parameter space to the sample space.

hypotheses.label: prior probability measure
hypotheses.note: the mixing prior $\pi$ is a probability measure on the parameter space.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Exchangeability and the i.i.d.-mixture representation: B. de Finetti (*Atti Accad. Naz. Lincei* 4 (1931), 251–299; *Ann. Inst. H. Poincaré* 7 (1937), 1–68); general Polish-space form: E. Hewitt and L. J. Savage, *Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.* 80 (1955), 470–501.

title: Partial Pooling in the Normal Hierarchy
informal: Partial pooling in the normal one-way hierarchy. In the model $$Y_j \mid \theta_j \sim N(\theta_j, \sigma^2), \qquad \theta_j \mid \mu, \tau^2 \sim N(\mu, \tau^2),$$ with a nondegenerate sampling variance $\sigma^2 > 0$ and a nondegenerate prior variance $\tau^2 > 0$, the posterior mean of a group effect $\theta_j$ given its observation $y$ is the convex combination $$\mathbb{E}[\theta_j \mid y] = (1 - B)\, y + B\, \mu, \qquad B = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + \tau^2}.$$ The estimate is shrunk from the raw observation $y$ toward the grand mean $\mu$ by the shrinkage weight $B \in [0, 1]$: strong when the noise $\sigma^2$ dominates the between-group spread $\tau^2$, and negligible when it does not.
summary: In the normal one-way hierarchy the posterior mean of a group effect is a convex combination of its observation and the grand mean, shrinking by the weight sigma-squared over sigma-squared plus tau-squared.
leanSignature:
theorem normalHier_posteriorMean_convexCombination (μ : ℝ) (τ2 σ2 : ℝ≥0)
    (hτ : τ2 ≠ 0) (hσ : σ2 ≠ 0) (y : ℝ) :
    postMean μ τ2 σ2 (fun _ : Fin 1 => y)
      = (1 - shrinkageWeight σ2 τ2) * y + shrinkageWeight σ2 τ2 * μ := by
  ...
formalizationNotes: Gelman §5.4, labeled 3C.3. `postMean` and `shrinkageWeight` are the scalar Normal–Normal posterior mean and the weight $B = \sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + \tau^2)$; a single observation is encoded as a length-one vector. Both nondegeneracy hypotheses are load-bearing: they clear the denominators in the closed-form posterior. That $B \in [0, 1]$ (so this is a genuine convex combination) is proved as a companion lemma.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate prior variance
hypotheses.note: $\tau^2 \neq 0$: the between-group prior variance is strictly positive.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate sampling variance
hypotheses.note: $\sigma^2 \neq 0$: the within-group sampling variance is strictly positive.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Partial pooling / shrinkage of group means toward a grand mean: C. Stein (1956) read hierarchically; D. V. Lindley and A. F. M. Smith (1972); B. Efron and C. Morris, *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 68 (1973), 117–130.

title: Posterior Variance Reduction
informal: Variance reduction from partial pooling. In the normal one-way hierarchy $Y_j \mid \theta_j \sim N(\theta_j, \sigma^2)$, $\theta_j \mid \mu, \tau^2 \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)$, with a nondegenerate sampling variance $\sigma^2 > 0$ and a nondegenerate prior variance $\tau^2 > 0$, the posterior variance of a group effect is strictly smaller than the sampling variance: $$\operatorname{Var}(\theta_j \mid y) = \frac{\sigma^2 \tau^2}{\sigma^2 + \tau^2} < \sigma^2.$$ Borrowing strength across groups through the shared prior always sharpens the estimate of each group effect relative to using its single observation alone.
summary: The posterior variance of a group effect in the normal one-way hierarchy is strictly below the sampling variance.
leanSignature:
theorem normalHier_posteriorVar_lt_samplingVar (τ2 σ2 : ℝ≥0)
    (hτ : τ2 ≠ 0) (hσ : σ2 ≠ 0) :
    (postVar τ2 σ2 1 : ℝ) < (σ2 : ℝ) := by
  ...
formalizationNotes: Gelman §5.4, labeled 3C.4. `postVar τ2 σ2 1` is the scalar Normal–Normal posterior variance with a single observation, equal to $\sigma^2\tau^2/(\sigma^2 + \tau^2)$ (the reciprocal-sum combination of prior precision and one unit of data precision). Both variances must be nonzero for the strict inequality; the proof is real algebra after clearing denominators.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate prior variance
hypotheses.note: $\tau^2 \neq 0$: the between-group prior variance is strictly positive.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate sampling variance
hypotheses.note: $\sigma^2 \neq 0$: the within-group sampling variance is strictly positive.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Variance reduction from hierarchical borrowing of strength: D. V. Lindley and A. F. M. Smith (1972); B. Efron and C. Morris (1973).

title: The James–Stein Risk Identity
informal: The James–Stein risk identity. Let $X \sim N(\theta, \sigma^2 I_p)$ be a $p$-dimensional normal vector with a nondegenerate coordinate variance $\sigma^2 > 0$ and dimension $p \geq 3$, and consider the James–Stein estimator $$\delta^{\mathrm{JS}}(X) = \Bigl(1 - \frac{(p-2)\sigma^2}{\lVert X \rVert^2}\Bigr) X.$$ Its expected squared-error risk is given exactly by $$\mathbb{E}\,\lVert \delta^{\mathrm{JS}}(X) - \theta \rVert^2 = p\,\sigma^2 - (p-2)^2 \sigma^4 \, \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{\lVert X \rVert^2}\right].$$ The first term $p\sigma^2$ is the risk of the maximum-likelihood estimator $X$ itself; the second, always nonnegative, is the improvement obtained by shrinking toward the origin. The proof is a Gaussian integration by parts (Stein's lemma), and $p \geq 3$ is exactly what makes $\mathbb{E}\lVert X\rVert^{-2}$ finite.
summary: The James-Stein estimator's squared-error risk equals the MLE risk p-sigma-squared minus (p minus two) squared times sigma-to-the-fourth times the expected inverse squared norm.
leanSignature:
theorem jamesStein_risk_difference {p : ℕ}
    (hp : 3 ≤ p) (θ : Fin p → ℝ) (σ2 : ℝ≥0)
    (hσ : σ2 ≠ 0) :
    (∫ x, ∑ i, (jamesSteinEstimator (σ2 : ℝ) x i - θ i) ^ 2
        ∂(Measure.pi fun i => gaussianReal (θ i) σ2))
      = (p : ℝ) * (σ2 : ℝ) - ((p : ℝ) - 2) ^ 2 * (σ2 : ℝ) ^ 2
          * (∫ x, 1 / (∑ i, (x i) ^ 2) ∂(Measure.pi fun i => gaussianReal (θ i) σ2)) := by
  ...
formalizationNotes: Robert Note 2.8.2 / §10.5, labeled 3D.4. The estimator and the loss are stated over the product Gaussian $\bigotimes_i N(\theta_i, \sigma^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}^p$. The identity is proved via a one-dimensional Gaussian Stein integration by parts applied coordinatewise, plus the divergence identity $\sum_i \partial_i(x_i/\lVert x\rVert^2) = (p-2)/\lVert x\rVert^2$; the hypothesis $p \ge 3$ is load-bearing, guaranteeing finiteness of $\mathbb{E}\lVert X\rVert^{-2}$ (finite precisely because the radial integral $\int_0^1 r^{p-3}\,dr$ converges).

hypotheses.label: dimension ≥ 3
hypotheses.note: $p \ge 3$: the Stein effect is dimension-driven; three or more coordinates are needed, and $p \ge 3$ makes $\mathbb{E}\lVert X\rVert^{-2}$ finite.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate noise variance
hypotheses.note: $\sigma^2 \neq 0$: the coordinate noise variance is strictly positive.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.pointer: Note 2.8.2 (the Stein effect), p. 96; §10.5 (empirical-Bayes justifications), p. 484
reference.biblio: The dominating estimator and its risk: W. James and C. Stein, “Estimation with quadratic loss,” *Proc. Fourth Berkeley Symp.* 1 (1961), 361–379; the tool is C. Stein's Gaussian integration-by-parts lemma.

title: James–Stein Dominates the MLE
informal: The Stein effect: James–Stein strictly dominates the MLE. For $X \sim N(\theta, \sigma^2 I_p)$ with a nondegenerate coordinate variance $\sigma^2 > 0$ in dimension $p \geq 3$, the James–Stein estimator has strictly smaller risk than the maximum-likelihood estimator $X$ at every parameter value $\theta$: $$\mathbb{E}\,\lVert \delta^{\mathrm{JS}}(X) - \theta \rVert^2 < p\,\sigma^2 = \mathbb{E}\,\lVert X - \theta \rVert^2.$$ Hence the sample mean is inadmissible under squared-error loss once $p \geq 3$ — the celebrated Stein paradox. The strict gap is the term $(p-2)^2\sigma^4\,\mathbb{E}\lVert X\rVert^{-2}$ from the risk identity, which is strictly positive because the product Gaussian is atomless (so $\lVert X\rVert^2 > 0$ almost surely) and $p \geq 3$.
summary: In dimension at least three the James-Stein estimator has strictly smaller squared-error risk than the sample mean at every parameter, so the MLE is inadmissible.
leanSignature:
theorem jamesStein_dominates_mle {p : ℕ}
    (hp : 3 ≤ p) (θ : Fin p → ℝ) (σ2 : ℝ≥0)
    (hσ : σ2 ≠ 0) :
    (∫ x, ∑ i, (jamesSteinEstimator (σ2 : ℝ) x i - θ i) ^ 2
        ∂(Measure.pi fun i => gaussianReal (θ i) σ2))
      < (p : ℝ) * (σ2 : ℝ) := by
  ...
formalizationNotes: Robert Note 2.8.2 / §10.5, labeled 3D.4 (stretch). An immediate corollary of the James–Stein risk identity: the subtracted term $(p-2)^2\sigma^4\,\mathbb{E}\lVert X\rVert^{-2}$ is strictly positive. Both $p \ge 3$ and $\sigma^2 \ne 0$ are load-bearing — positivity of the coefficient $(p-2)^2$ needs $p > 2$, and atomlessness of the Gaussian gives $\lVert X\rVert^2 > 0$ almost surely, so the expectation is strictly positive.

hypotheses.label: dimension ≥ 3
hypotheses.note: $p \ge 3$: dominance fails in dimensions 1 and 2; the coefficient $(p-2)^2$ requires $p > 2$.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate noise variance
hypotheses.note: $\sigma^2 \neq 0$: the coordinate noise variance is strictly positive.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: Inadmissibility of the sample mean for $p \ge 3$: C. Stein, *Proc. Third Berkeley Symp.* 1 (1956), 197–206; explicit dominating estimator: W. James and C. Stein (1961); empirical-Bayes reading: B. Efron and C. Morris (1973).

title: Stationarity of Hierarchical Gibbs
informal: Stationarity of the two-block hierarchical Gibbs sampler. Consider a hierarchical model with joint posterior $\pi$ on hyperparameter–parameter pairs $(\lambda, \theta)$, sampled by alternately updating the two blocks: refresh $\theta$ from its full conditional $\theta \mid \lambda, x$, then refresh $\lambda$ from its full conditional $\lambda \mid \theta, x$. If the $\theta$-block update leaves the joint posterior $\pi$ invariant and the $\lambda$-block update leaves $\pi$ invariant, then the composed sweep also leaves $\pi$ invariant: $$\pi\, K_\lambda K_\theta = \pi.$$ Thus $\pi$ is a stationary distribution of the block Gibbs chain — the correctness guarantee that makes Gibbs sampling a valid Monte Carlo method for hierarchical posteriors.
summary: If each full-conditional block update leaves the joint hierarchical posterior invariant, then so does one full sweep of the two-block Gibbs sampler.
leanSignature:
theorem hierarchicalGibbs_stationary (Kθ Klam : Kernel (Λ × Θ) (Λ × Θ)) (π : Measure (Λ × Θ))
    (hθ : Kernel.Invariant Kθ π)
    (hlam : Kernel.Invariant Klam π) :
    Kernel.Invariant (Klam ∘ₖ Kθ) π :=
  hlam.comp hθ
formalizationNotes: Gelman §11.1, labeled 3H.3. A direct consequence of the invariance calculus: the composition of two $\pi$-invariant kernels is $\pi$-invariant. Stated with the two block kernels and their per-block invariance as inputs; the concrete full-conditional kernels for a specific hierarchy (drawn from the tower decomposition) are supplied separately. Each full-conditional update is invariant for the joint posterior by construction of a Gibbs step.

hypotheses.label: θ-block leaves posterior invariant
hypotheses.note: the parameter-block full-conditional update $K_\theta$ has the joint posterior $\pi$ as an invariant measure.

hypotheses.label: λ-block leaves posterior invariant
hypotheses.note: the hyperparameter-block full-conditional update $K_\lambda$ has $\pi$ as an invariant measure.

reference.formal: A. Gelman, J. B. Carlin, H. S. Stern, D. B. Dunson, A. Vehtari, and D. B. Rubin, *Bayesian Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2014.
reference.biblio: Data-augmentation / block Gibbs for hierarchical models: M. A. Tanner and W. H. Wong, *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 82 (1987), 528–540; A. E. Gelfand and A. F. M. Smith, *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 85 (1990), 398–409.

title: Tweedie's Formula (Posterior Mean)
informal: Let $G$ be a prior distribution on a location parameter $\theta$, and suppose the observation is Gaussian, $X\mid\theta\sim N(\theta, v)$, with known variance $v$. Write $f_G(x)=\int \varphi_v(x-\theta)\,dG(\theta)$ for the resulting marginal (mixture) density of $X$, where $\varphi_v$ is the $N(0,v)$ density. Provided the variance is nondegenerate, $v>0$, the prior has a finite first moment, and the marginal density is strictly positive at $x$, the posterior mean of $\theta$ given $X=x$ is given by Tweedie's formula: $$\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid X=x]=\frac{\int \theta\,\varphi_v(x-\theta)\,dG(\theta)}{f_G(x)} = x + v\,\frac{d}{dx}\log f_G(x).$$ The posterior mean depends on the prior $G$ only through the marginal $f_G$, which is directly estimable from data — the empirical-Bayes principle behind shrinkage estimation.
summary: For a Gaussian likelihood with any prior, the posterior mean of the location equals the observation plus the variance times the derivative of the log marginal density.
leanSignature:
theorem tweedie_normal_posteriorMean (G : Measure ℝ) [IsProbabilityMeasure G] (v : ℝ≥0)
    (hv : v ≠ 0)
    (hmean : Integrable (fun θ => θ) G)
    (x : ℝ) (hpos : 0 < gaussianMarginalPDF G v x) :
    (∫ θ, θ * gaussianPDFReal θ v x ∂G) / gaussianMarginalPDF G v x = tweedieEstimator G v x
formalizationNotes: The Lean statement matches Efron's Eq. (1.26) exactly. Beyond `G` being a probability measure, the three hypotheses are genuine analytic side-conditions, not laundered assumptions: `v ≠ 0` (a nondegenerate Gaussian), a finite prior first moment (`Integrable (fun θ => θ) G`, needed to differentiate the marginal under the integral sign — it supplies an integrable envelope for the Gaussian score, established in `hasDerivAt_gaussianMarginalPDF`), and strict positivity of the marginal at `x` (needed both to divide and to form the logarithmic derivative). Here `gaussianMarginalPDF G v x = ∫ N(x; θ, v) dG(θ)` and `tweedieEstimator G v x = x + v·(log f_G)'(x)`.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate variance
hypotheses.note: v ≠ 0: the Gaussian likelihood N(θ, v) is nondegenerate (v > 0).

hypotheses.label: finite prior first moment
hypotheses.note: Integrable (fun θ => θ) G: the prior has a finite mean, giving an integrable envelope for the Gaussian score so the marginal may be differentiated under the integral sign.

hypotheses.label: positive marginal at x
hypotheses.note: 0 < gaussianMarginalPDF G v x: the marginal density is strictly positive at x, needed to divide by f_G(x) and to form the logarithmic derivative.

reference.formal: B. Efron, *Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction*, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
reference.biblio: Tweedie's formula is the exponential-family posterior-mean identity attributed by H. Robbins ("An empirical Bayes approach to statistics," *Proc. Third Berkeley Symp. Math. Statist. Probab.* 1 (1956), 157–163) to M. C. K. Tweedie; its empirical-Bayes and selection-bias applications are developed in B. Efron, "Tweedie's formula and selection bias," *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 106 (2011), 1602–1614. It underlies g-modeling (Efron 2016) and the general-maximum-likelihood empirical Bayes of W. Jiang and C.-H. Zhang (*Ann. Statist.* 37 (2009), 1647–1684).

title: Tweedie's Formula (Posterior Variance)
informal: In the Gaussian location model $X\mid\theta\sim N(\theta, v)$ with prior $G$ and marginal density $f_G(x)=\int\varphi_v(x-\theta)\,dG(\theta)$, the posterior variance admits a companion to Tweedie's mean formula. Provided the variance is nondegenerate, $v>0$, the prior has a finite second moment, and the marginal is strictly positive at $x$, $$\mathrm{Var}[\theta\mid X=x]=\frac{\int(\theta-m(x))^2\,\varphi_v(x-\theta)\,dG(\theta)}{f_G(x)} = v + v^2\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\log f_G(x),$$ where $m(x)=x+v\,(\log f_G)'(x)$ is the Tweedie posterior mean. Like the mean, the posterior variance is recovered from the marginal density alone, so it too is estimable from data without knowing the prior.
summary: The posterior variance in the Gaussian location model equals the variance plus its square times the second derivative of the log marginal density.
leanSignature:
theorem tweedie_normal_posteriorVariance (G : Measure ℝ) [IsProbabilityMeasure G] (v : ℝ≥0)
    (hv : v ≠ 0)
    (hsq : Integrable (fun θ => θ ^ 2) G)
    (x : ℝ) (hpos : 0 < gaussianMarginalPDF G v x) :
    (∫ θ, (θ - tweedieEstimator G v x) ^ 2 * gaussianPDFReal θ v x ∂G) / gaussianMarginalPDF G v x
      = (v : ℝ) + (v : ℝ) ^ 2 * deriv (deriv (fun y => Real.log (gaussianMarginalPDF G v y))) x
formalizationNotes: Companion to the posterior-mean formula, matching Efron §1.5. The finite-second-moment hypothesis `Integrable (fun θ => θ^2) G` is the genuine side-condition for the second differentiation under the integral (it dominates the second-order Gaussian score); the first-moment integrability needed for the mean is derived from it internally. `tweedieEstimator G v x` denotes the Tweedie posterior mean m(x), so the left-hand side is a genuine second central moment of the posterior.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate variance
hypotheses.note: v ≠ 0: the Gaussian likelihood is nondegenerate (v > 0).

hypotheses.label: finite prior second moment
hypotheses.note: Integrable (fun θ => θ^2) G: a finite second moment dominates the second-order Gaussian score, allowing the second differentiation of the marginal under the integral; the first-moment integrability is derived from it internally.

hypotheses.label: positive marginal at x
hypotheses.note: 0 < gaussianMarginalPDF G v x: the marginal is strictly positive at x, needed to divide and to take the second logarithmic derivative.

reference.formal: B. Efron, *Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction*, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
reference.biblio: The posterior-variance companion to Tweedie's formula follows the same marginal-to-posterior differentiation as the mean; both are systematized in B. Efron, "Tweedie's formula and selection bias," *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 106 (2011), 1602–1614, building on the identity attributed by H. Robbins (1956) to M. C. K. Tweedie.

title: Robbins's Poisson Empirical-Bayes Rule
informal: Suppose the count $Y\mid\theta\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$ is Poisson with rate $\theta$ drawn from an arbitrary mixing distribution $G$, and let $f_G(y)=\int p_y(\theta)\,dG(\theta)$ denote the marginal probability mass function of $Y$, where $p_y(\theta)=e^{-\theta}\theta^y/y!$. Provided the prior charges only nonnegative rates, the numerator of the posterior mean satisfies Robbins's identity $$\int \theta\,p_y(\theta)\,dG(\theta) = (y+1)\,f_G(y+1),$$ so that the posterior mean of the rate given the count $y$ is $$\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid Y=y]=(y+1)\,\frac{f_G(y+1)}{f_G(y)}.$$ The rule is expressed entirely through the marginal pmf, which empirical Bayes estimates from the observed counts — no knowledge of the prior $G$ is required.
summary: For a Poisson likelihood with any mixing distribution, the posterior mean of the rate given count y equals (y+1) times the ratio of the marginal pmf at y+1 to its value at y.
leanSignature:
theorem robbins_poisson_posteriorMean (G : Measure ℝ) [IsProbabilityMeasure G]
    (hG : ∀ᵐ θ ∂G, 0 ≤ θ) (y : ℕ) :
    ∫⁻ θ, ENNReal.ofReal θ * poissonDensity θ y ∂G
      = ((y : ℝ≥0∞) + 1) * mixtureDensity poissonDensity G (y + 1)
formalizationNotes: The theorem states Robbins's numerator identity `∫ θ·p_y(θ) dG = (y+1)·f_G(y+1)`; dividing by the marginal `f_G(y)` yields the Robbins estimator `robbinsPoissonEstimator G y = (y+1)·f_G(y+1)/f_G(y)`. It rests on the pure Poisson pmf recursion `(y+1)·p_{y+1}(θ) = θ·p_y(θ)` (`poissonDensity_succ_mul`). The single hypothesis — that the prior charges only nonnegative rates — is intrinsic to the Poisson model. A companion result (`robbinsEstimator_tendsto_oracle`) establishes consistency of the plug-in estimator built from the empirical pmf.

hypotheses.label: prior on nonnegative rates
hypotheses.note: ∀ᵐ θ ∂G, 0 ≤ θ: the mixing measure charges only nonnegative Poisson rates — intrinsic to the Poisson model.

reference.formal: B. Efron, *Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction*, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
reference.biblio: Empirical Bayes originates with H. Robbins, "An empirical Bayes approach to statistics," *Proc. Third Berkeley Symp. Math. Statist. Probab.* 1 (1956), 157–163 (the Poisson formula is Eq. (5)); the compound-decision precursor is Robbins (*Proc. Second Berkeley Symp.*, 1951, 131–148). Its modern nonparametric and g-modeling forms are due to B. Efron ("Empirical Bayes deconvolution estimates," *Biometrika* 103 (2016), 1–20) and W. Jiang and C.-H. Zhang (*Ann. Statist.* 37 (2009), 1647–1684).

title: Local FDR is the Posterior Null Probability
informal: In Efron's two-groups model for large-scale testing, each case is null with prior probability $\pi_0$ (yielding null density $f_0$) or non-null with probability $1-\pi_0$ (density $f_1$), so the marginal density of the test statistic is the mixture $f(x)=\pi_0 f_0(x)+(1-\pi_0)f_1(x)$. The local false discovery rate is $\mathrm{fdr}(x)=\pi_0 f_0(x)/f(x)$. Provided the null proportion $\pi_0$ is a genuine probability ($\pi_0\le 1$), this ratio is exactly the posterior probability that a case with statistic $x$ belongs to the null group: $$\mathrm{fdr}(x)=\Pr(\text{null}\mid X=x)=\frac{\pi_0 f_0(x)}{\pi_0 f_0(x)+(1-\pi_0)f_1(x)}.$$ The Bayes decision rule rejects the null exactly when $\mathrm{fdr}(x)$ falls below a chosen threshold, connecting large-scale testing to empirical-Bayes shrinkage.
summary: In the two-groups model, the local false discovery rate equals the posterior probability that a case with the observed statistic belongs to the null group.
leanSignature:
theorem localFDR_eq_posteriorNullProb (π₀ : ℝ≥0∞)
    (hπ₀ : π₀ ≤ 1) (f₀ f₁ : 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞) (x : 𝓧) :
    localFDR π₀ f₀ f₁ x = (π₀ * f₀ x) / (π₀ * f₀ x + (1 - π₀) * f₁ x)
formalizationNotes: The identity `localFDR π₀ f₀ f₁ x = π₀f₀(x)/(π₀f₀(x)+(1−π₀)f₁(x))` is definitional (`rfl`) once the two-groups marginal is unfolded; the hypothesis `π₀ ≤ 1` is included so that `π₀` and `1−π₀` are genuine complementary probabilities (giving the ratio its posterior-null-probability reading), though the algebraic identity itself does not consume it. Extended-nonnegative (ℝ≥0∞) division is used, taking the junk value 0 where the marginal degenerates. A companion result (`localFDR_bayesRule_threshold`) turns the threshold `fdr(x) ≤ t` into the weighted-density comparison `π₀f₀(x) ≤ t·f(x)`.

hypotheses.label: null proportion is a probability
hypotheses.note: π₀ ≤ 1: the null fraction π₀ (and its complement 1−π₀) are genuine probabilities, giving the ratio its posterior-null-probability reading. The algebraic identity itself holds by definitional unfolding.

reference.formal: B. Efron, *Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction*, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
reference.biblio: The two-groups model and local false discovery rate are B. Efron's empirical-Bayes formulation (Efron, Tibshirani, Storey, Tusher, *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 96 (2001), 1151–1160; Efron 2010); the local FDR as a posterior null probability is the Bayesian reading of the tail-area false-discovery-rate framework of Y. Benjamini and Y. Hochberg ("Controlling the false discovery rate," *J. Roy. Statist. Soc. Ser. B* 57 (1995), 289–300).

title: Lindsay's Finite-Support NPMLE Theorem
informal: The nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimator (NPMLE) maximizes the marginal likelihood $\prod_{i=1}^n f_G(x_i)$ over all mixing distributions $G$, where $f_G(x)=\int p(\theta,x)\,dG(\theta)$. Because this likelihood is linear in $G$, the problem is convex, and Lindsay's theorem shows the maximizer can be taken with finite support. Formalized in the discrete-regular setting: for a finite, nonempty parameter space $\Theta$ with finite likelihoods $p(\theta, x_i)<\infty$, there exists a mixing probability measure $\widehat{G}$ that attains the maximum marginal likelihood and is supported on a finite set $S$ of at most $n+1$ points: $$\widehat{G}\big(S^{c}\big)=0,\qquad |S|\le n+1.$$ Geometrically, the likelihood vector $G\mapsto\big(f_G(x_1),\dots,f_G(x_n)\big)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is the $G$-barycenter of the $n$-dimensional likelihood curve $\theta\mapsto\big(p(\theta,x_1),\dots\big)$, and Carathéodory's theorem writes any boundary maximizer as a positive convex combination of at most $n+1$ extreme points (Dirac masses).
summary: The nonparametric MLE of a mixing distribution can be taken supported on at most n+1 points, by Lindsay's convex-geometry argument.
leanSignature:
theorem NPMLE_exists_finiteSupport_le_card_add_one {n : ℕ}
    [MeasurableSingletonClass Θ] [Finite Θ] [Nonempty Θ]
    (p : Θ → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞) (x : Fin n → 𝓧)
    (hpfin : ∀ θ i, p θ (x i) ≠ ∞) :
    ∃ (Ghat : Measure Θ) (S : Finset Θ),
      IsNPMLE p x Ghat ∧ Ghat ((↑S : Set Θ)ᶜ) = 0 ∧ S.card ≤ n + 1
formalizationNotes: Formalized in Lindsay's discrete-regular setting: `Θ` finite (the discrete-and-compact case) with finite likelihoods `hpfin`, so the geometric `n+1` Carathéodory bound is preserved exactly. Existence of a maximizer is *derived* internally (in `NPMLE_exists_of_finite`) rather than assumed — the marginal likelihood is a continuous function of the weight vector on the compact probability simplex `stdSimplex ℝ Θ`, hence attains its maximum — closing what would otherwise be a provider-style `∃ Ghat, IsNPMLE` hypothesis. `IsNPMLE p x Ghat` is the optimality predicate: `Ghat` is a probability measure maximizing `∏ᵢ f_G(xᵢ)` over all mixing probability measures on `Θ`. The linearity of `f_G` in `G` behind the convexity is the separate lemma `mixtureDensity_linear_in_mixing`.

hypotheses.label: finite parameter space
hypotheses.note: Θ is finite, nonempty, with measurable singletons — Lindsay's discrete-regular (discrete-and-compact) setting, in which the n+1 Carathéodory bound is preserved exactly.

hypotheses.label: finite likelihoods
hypotheses.note: ∀ θ i, p θ (x i) ≠ ∞: the likelihoods p(θ, xᵢ) are finite — Lindsay's regularity condition.

reference.formal: B. Efron, *Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction*, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
reference.biblio: The finite-support NPMLE is B. G. Lindsay's theorem ("The geometry of mixture likelihoods: a general theory," *Ann. Statist.* 11 (1983), 86–94), refining the consistency result of J. Kiefer and J. Wolfowitz ("Consistency of the maximum likelihood estimator in the presence of infinitely many incidental parameters," *Ann. Math. Statist.* 27 (1956), 887–906). Its use for normal-means estimation (GMLEB) is W. Jiang and C.-H. Zhang (*Ann. Statist.* 37 (2009), 1647–1684); it is the nonparametric backbone of modern empirical-Bayes deconvolution (Efron 2010, §5).

title: Oracle Bayes Rule Minimizes Compound Risk
informal: In the compound decision problem underlying nonparametric empirical Bayes, the oracle posterior for a mixing distribution $G$ is the ordinary (generalized) posterior $\Pi(\cdot\mid x)$ of the likelihood against $G$. Given two decision rules $d_0, d_1$ mapping each observation $x$ to an action, suppose $d_0$ dominates $d_1$ in posterior expected loss pointwise at every $x$, i.e. $$\int \ell\big(\theta, d_0(x)\big)\,d\Pi(\theta\mid x)\ \le\ \int \ell\big(\theta, d_1(x)\big)\,d\Pi(\theta\mid x)\quad\text{for all }x.$$ Then $d_0$ also has smaller compound risk — the posterior loss integrated over the data marginal $m$: $$\int\!\!\left(\int \ell(\theta, d_0(x))\,d\Pi(\theta\mid x)\right)dm(x)\ \le\ \int\!\!\left(\int \ell(\theta, d_1(x))\,d\Pi(\theta\mid x)\right)dm(x).$$ The pointwise Bayes optimality of the oracle rule integrates to compound optimality; empirical Bayes approximates this oracle by estimating $G$ (or the marginal) from data.
summary: A decision rule with pointwise smaller posterior expected loss also has smaller compound risk integrated over the data marginal.
leanSignature:
theorem oracleBayesRule_minimizes_compoundRisk {ℓ : Θ → Θ → ℝ≥0∞} (p : Θ → 𝓧 → ℝ≥0∞)
    (G : Measure Θ) (m : Measure 𝓧) (d₀ d₁ : 𝓧 → Θ)
    (hpoint : ∀ x, ∫⁻ θ, ℓ θ (d₀ x) ∂(generalizedPosterior p G x)
      ≤ ∫⁻ θ, ℓ θ (d₁ x) ∂(generalizedPosterior p G x)) :
    ∫⁻ x, (∫⁻ θ, ℓ θ (d₀ x) ∂(generalizedPosterior p G x)) ∂m
      ≤ ∫⁻ x, (∫⁻ θ, ℓ θ (d₁ x) ∂(generalizedPosterior p G x)) ∂m
formalizationNotes: A clean consequence of `lintegral_mono`: pointwise domination of posterior expected loss integrates (over the data marginal `m`) to domination of compound risk — the decision-theoretic content of Fubini's theorem. The hypothesis `hpoint` is a genuine external input (it is precisely what the pointwise oracle Bayes rule supplies for `d₀` against any competitor `d₁`). `generalizedPosterior p G x` is the Batch-1/2 dominated-Bayes posterior; the definitional bridges `mixtureDensity = predictiveDensity` (`mixtureDensity_eq_predictiveDensity`) and the oracle posterior as a `withDensity` (`npEB_oraclePosterior_eq_withDensity`) are established alongside in the same file.

hypotheses.label: pointwise posterior-risk domination
hypotheses.note: For every x, the oracle rule d₀ has posterior expected loss no larger than the competitor d₁ — what the pointwise oracle Bayes rule supplies. A genuine external input, not laundered content.

reference.formal: B. Efron, *Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction*, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
reference.biblio: The compound decision problem and its empirical-Bayes solution are due to H. Robbins ("Asymptotically subminimax solutions of compound statistical decision problems," *Proc. Second Berkeley Symp.*, 1951, 131–148; and "An empirical Bayes approach to statistics," 1956); the "oracle" terminology and modern large-scale reading are B. Efron's (2010). The equivalence of pointwise (posterior) and compound (frequentist, integrated) Bayes optimality is the decision-theoretic content of Fubini's theorem.

title: Parametric Empirical-Bayes Shrinkage Attains the Oracle Weight
informal: In the normal random-effects model $Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N(\theta_j,\sigma^2)$ with $\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$, the parametric empirical-Bayes estimator shrinks each $Y_j$ toward the sample mean with the plug-in weight $\widehat B = \widehat\tau^2/(\widehat\tau^2+\sigma^2)$, using the method-of-moments variance estimate $\widehat\tau^2=\max(0,\, s^2-\sigma^2)$. Provided the noise and effect variances are positive ($\sigma^2,\tau^2>0$) and the sample variance is consistent for the marginal variance $\sigma^2+\tau^2$, the plug-in shrinkage weight converges to the oracle Bayes weight: $$\frac{\max(0,\, s_n^2-\sigma^2)}{\max(0,\, s_n^2-\sigma^2)+\sigma^2}\ \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\ \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2}.$$ Thus the empirical-Bayes rule, which knows neither $\mu$ nor $\tau^2$, attains the oracle shrinkage in the large-sample limit.
summary: The plug-in method-of-moments shrinkage weight in the normal random-effects model converges to the oracle Bayes shrinkage weight.
leanSignature:
theorem normalParamEB_shrinkageWeight_tendsto_oracle (τ2 σ2 : ℝ)
    (hσ : 0 < σ2) (hτ : 0 < τ2) (vn : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hv : Tendsto vn atTop (𝓝 (τ2 + σ2))) :
    Tendsto (fun n => max 0 (vn n - σ2) / (max 0 (vn n - σ2) + σ2)) atTop
      (𝓝 (τ2 / (τ2 + σ2)))
formalizationNotes: Consistency is cut to the normal method-of-moments estimator per the formalization plan: this is a continuous-mapping limit of the plug-in shrinkage weight, given a consistent sample variance `vn → σ²+τ²` (which the strong law supplies as a genuine external input `hv`). The `max(0, ·)` truncation reflects the estimate `τ̂² = max(0, s²−σ²)`. General-family marginal-MLE consistency is deferred; the closely related Fisher identity for the normal marginal (`fisherIdentity_normalMarginal`), the EM monotonicity of the marginal likelihood (`EM_monotonicity_marginalLikelihood`), and the N(μ, σ²+τ²) marginal (`normalRandomEffects_marginal`) are proved separately in the same file.

hypotheses.label: positive variances
hypotheses.note: 0 < σ² and 0 < τ²: the noise and random-effect variances are nondegenerate, so the oracle shrinkage weight τ²/(τ²+σ²) is well-defined and strictly between 0 and 1.

hypotheses.label: consistent sample variance
hypotheses.note: vn → σ²+τ²: the sample variance is consistent for the marginal variance (supplied by the strong law) — the genuine external input driving the continuous-mapping limit.

reference.formal: C. P. Robert, *The Bayesian Choice: From Decision-Theoretic Foundations to Computational Implementation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer, 2007.
reference.biblio: Parametric empirical Bayes is H. Robbins's (1956) subject made parametric; the normal random-effects (James–Stein) analysis is B. Efron and C. Morris (*J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 68 (1973), 117–130, and companion papers 1972–1975). The method-of-moments shrinkage estimate and its consistency are standard empirical Bayes; the general marginal-MLE computation rests on R. A. Fisher's missing-information identity and the EM algorithm of A. P. Dempster, N. M. Laird, and D. B. Rubin (*J. Roy. Statist. Soc. Ser. B* 39 (1977), 1–38).

title: Spatial Derivative of the Gaussian Density (Score Identity)
informal: The Gaussian density $\varphi_{\theta,v}(x)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp\!\big(-(x-\theta)^2/(2v)\big)$, viewed as a function of the observation $x$, satisfies the Gaussian score identity. Provided the variance is nondegenerate, $v>0$, $$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\,\varphi_{\theta,v}(x)=\frac{\theta-x}{v}\,\varphi_{\theta,v}(x),$$ equivalently $(\theta-x)\,\varphi_{\theta,v}(x)=v\,\partial_x\varphi_{\theta,v}(x)$. This elementary but load-bearing identity — the one-dimensional case of Stein's lemma — converts the numerator $\int\theta\,\varphi_{\theta,v}(x)\,dG(\theta)$ of a posterior mean into $x\,f_G(x)+v\,f_G'(x)$, which is the algebraic engine behind Tweedie's formula.
summary: The spatial derivative of the Gaussian density equals (theta minus x)/v times the density, the score identity behind Tweedie's formula.
leanSignature:
theorem hasDerivAt_gaussianPDFReal (θ : ℝ) (v : ℝ≥0) (hv : v ≠ 0) (x : ℝ) :
    HasDerivAt (gaussianPDFReal θ v)
      ((θ - x) / (v : ℝ) * gaussianPDFReal θ v x) x
formalizationNotes: The pin (Mathlib's Gaussian file) has Gaussian moments and mgf but not the spatial derivative of `gaussianPDFReal`; this supplies it directly. `gaussianPDFReal θ v` is `const · exp ∘ g` with `g x = −(x−θ)²/(2v)`, so `HasDerivAt` follows from the chain rule (`HasDerivAt.exp`) and simplifies via `field_simp`/`ring` using `v ≠ 0`. The single hypothesis `v ≠ 0` is the nondegeneracy of the Gaussian. The `deriv`-form corollary (`deriv_gaussianPDFReal`) and pointwise differentiability (`differentiable_gaussianPDFReal`) accompany it.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate variance
hypotheses.note: v ≠ 0: the Gaussian density N(θ, v) is nondegenerate (v > 0), so the score (θ−x)/v is finite.

reference.formal: B. Efron, *Large-Scale Inference: Empirical Bayes Methods for Estimation, Testing, and Prediction*, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
reference.biblio: The identity $\partial_x\varphi=-(x/\sigma^2)\varphi$ for the standard normal density is classical (it makes the Hermite functions eigenfunctions of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator); its statistical exploitation is C. M. Stein's integration-by-parts / unbiased-risk lemma (*Proc. Sixth Berkeley Symp.*, 1972; *Ann. Statist.* 9 (1981), 1135–1151), and, for empirical-Bayes shrinkage, the marginal-to-posterior formula of H. Robbins (1956) and M. C. K. Tweedie popularized by B. Efron ("Tweedie's formula and selection bias," *J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.* 106 (2011), 1602–1614).

title: Posterior Compressibility of the Dirichlet–Laplace Prior
informal: Consider the normal-means model $y \sim N_n(\theta_0, I_n)$ with the Dirichlet–Laplace prior in product form: $\theta_j \mid \psi_j \sim \mathrm{DE}(\psi_j)$ and $\psi_j \sim \mathrm{Ga}(a_n, 1/2)$ independently across coordinates, at the scale $a_n = n^{-(1+\beta)}$ for a fixed $\beta > 0$. Let the sparsity level satisfy $q_n \ge 1$ and $q_n = o(n)$, let the truth $\theta_0$ have at most $q_n$ nonzero coordinates, and let $(\delta_n)$ be any significance-threshold sequence with $n^{-2} \le \delta_n \le 1/2$ for all large $n$. Writing $\mathrm{supp}_{\delta}(\theta) = \{j : |\theta_j| > \delta\}$ for the set of $\delta$-significant coordinates, there is a constant $A > 0$ such that the expected posterior probability $E_{\theta_0}\,\Pi\bigl(\,|\mathrm{supp}_{\delta_n}(\theta)| > A\,q_n \;\big|\; y\bigr) \longrightarrow 0$. In words: although a continuous shrinkage prior never produces exact zeros, the posterior concentrates on vectors whose effective dimension — the number of coordinates exceeding $\delta_n$ in magnitude — is at most a constant multiple of the true sparsity. The same conclusion holds at the scale $a_n = 1/n$ under the additional assumption $q_n \ge C_0 \log n$.
summary: The posterior effective dimension (number of coordinates above a small threshold) stays within a constant multiple of the true sparsity, in both prior-scale regimes.
formalizationNotes: The paper states the theorem at the fixed threshold δₙ = qₙ/n; the formalization proves it uniformly over any threshold window n⁻² ≤ δₙ ≤ 1/2, which is what the proof of Theorem 3.1 actually consumes (it applies the result at δₙ = rₙ/n, and the support-count monotonicity runs the wrong way when qₙ > log n). Two repairs to the paper's proof: its internal radius rₙ² = qₙ leaves a failure term e^{−qₙ} that need not vanish in the β-regime (where qₙ may stay bounded) — the formalization uses rₙ² = qₙ log n with the explicit threshold constant A = 3 + 2/β and tilt cₙ = n^{β/2}; and the auxiliary inequality Γ(x) ≥ 1/x quoted on p. 9 is false — the intended consequence survives as 1/Γ(a) ≤ e·a. The aₙ = 1/n regime is dl_theorem34_recip (A = 3 + (4e(e−1)+2e)/C₀, constant tilt c = e). All six DL headline declarations carry clean axioms (no sorryAx). A full deviation ledger (D1–D14) lives in the module headers.

hypotheses.label: prior-scale exponent
hypotheses.note: The Dirichlet–Laplace concentration parameter is aₙ = n^{−(1+β)} for a fixed β > 0. (The 1/n scale is the companion dl_theorem34_recip.)

hypotheses.label: nonempty sparsity level
hypotheses.note: qₙ ≥ 1 — implicit in the paper and necessary: for qₙ = 0 the event |supp| > 0 has posterior probability one under any continuous prior.

hypotheses.label: sub-linear sparsity
hypotheses.note: qₙ/n → 0: the true model dimension is negligible relative to the ambient dimension.

hypotheses.label: sparse truth
hypotheses.note: θ₀ has at most qₙ nonzero coordinates (θ₀ ∈ ℓ₀[qₙ; n]).

hypotheses.label: threshold window
hypotheses.note: The significance thresholds satisfy n^{−2} ≤ δₙ ≤ 1/2 eventually. The paper fixes δₙ = qₙ/n; the free window is a strengthening needed where Theorem 3.1's proof consumes this result at δₙ = rₙ/n.

reference.formal: A. Bhattacharya, D. Pati, N. S. Pillai, and D. B. Dunson, “Dirichlet–Laplace priors for optimal shrinkage,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **110**(512), 2015, pp. 1479–1490 (arXiv:1401.5398).
reference.biblio: Posterior compressibility — an effective-dimension bound for continuous shrinkage priors — is the entry point of the posterior-contraction program of S. Ghosal, J. K. Ghosh, and A. W. van der Vaart (*Ann. Statist.* **28**, 2000) as adapted to sparse sequence models by I. Castillo and A. W. van der Vaart (*Ann. Statist.* **40**, 2012).

title: Posterior Contraction of the Dirichlet–Laplace Prior
informal: In the normal-means model $y \sim N_n(\theta_0, I_n)$ with the Dirichlet–Laplace prior at scale $a_n = n^{-(1+\beta)}$ ($\beta > 0$), let $q_n \ge 1$, $q_n = o(n)$, let $\theta_0$ have at most $q_n$ nonzero coordinates, and assume the signal-growth condition $\|\theta_0\|_2^2 \le q_n \log^4 n$ — each nonzero signal may grow at a $\log^2 n$ rate. Then there is a constant $M > 0$ such that the expected posterior mass outside the ball of radius $M\sqrt{q_n \log n}$ vanishes: $E_{\theta_0}\, \Pi\bigl(\|\theta - \theta_0\|_2 > M\sqrt{q_n \log n} \;\big|\; y\bigr) \longrightarrow 0$. Equivalently, the posterior distribution contracts around the truth at the near-minimax rate $\sqrt{q_n \log n}$ for $q_n$-sparse means — the first such guarantee for a fully continuous shrinkage prior. Under the polynomial-sparsity condition $q_n \le n^{1-c}$ the rate improves to the exact minimax rate $\sqrt{q_n \log(n/q_n)}$, and the same conclusion holds at the scale $a_n = 1/n$ when $q_n \ge C_0 \log n$.
summary: The posterior contracts around a qₙ-sparse truth at the near-minimax rate √(qₙ log n), in both prior-scale regimes; the exact minimax rate follows under polynomial sparsity.
formalizationNotes: The paper's Theorem 3.1 states the rate sₙ = √(qₙ log(n/qₙ)), but its proof fixes rₙ² = qₙ log n and only yields that; the formal headline states the proved rate, and the paper's sₙ is recovered exactly under qₙ ≤ n^{1−c} (dl_theorem31_paper_rate). The proof is formalized following the paper's own composition (p. 15): the compressibility event is discharged by Theorem 3.4 as a black box carrying its own internal radius, while the denominator event and the shell/testing series run at rₙ² = qₙ log n — a single-radius reading is provably impossible in the 1/n regime. The testing geometry is repaired (the paper's jrₙ-nets of the full ball admit pieces with nonpositive test margin): jrₙ/4-nets with at most 33^{|S|} pieces, explicit midpoint tests with errors e^{−j²r²/12}. Companions: the ball form dl_theorem31_ball (paper's eq. (12)), dl_theorem31_paper_rate, and the aₙ = 1/n regime dl_theorem31_recip (under qₙ ≥ C₀ log n). All constants are explicit and deliberately roomy; the deviation ledger (D1–D14) lives in the module headers, with a full discussion in notes/bayesian/dl_contraction.

hypotheses.note: The Dirichlet–Laplace concentration parameter is aₙ = n^{−(1+β)} for a fixed β > 0. (The 1/n scale is the companion dl_theorem31_recip.)

hypotheses.label: nonempty sparsity level
hypotheses.note: qₙ ≥ 1 — implicit in the paper and necessary (the internal radius rₙ² = qₙ log n must tend to infinity).

hypotheses.label: sub-linear sparsity
hypotheses.note: qₙ/n → 0: the true model dimension is negligible relative to the ambient dimension.

hypotheses.label: sparse truth

title: The Kernel Density Estimator
informal:
Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. real-valued random variables with common density $p$ with respect to Lebesgue measure. Given a function $K : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ (the kernel) and a number $h > 0$ (the bandwidth), the kernel density estimator, or Parzen–Rosenblatt estimator, of $p$ at a point $x \in \mathbb{R}$ is the normalized kernel average $$\hat p_n(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{nh} \sum_{i=1}^{n} K\!\left(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\right).$$

Classically the kernel is an integrable function with $\int K(u)\,du = 1$; if moreover $K \ge 0$, the function $x \mapsto \hat p_n(x)$ is itself a probability density. The definition places no conditions on $K$ or $h$ — each risk bound for $\hat p_n$ states its own.

title: Kernel of Order ℓ
informal:
Let $\ell$ be a nonnegative integer. A function $K : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a kernel of order $\ell$ if the functions $u \mapsto u^j K(u)$ are integrable for $j = 0, 1, \dots, \ell$ and they satisfy $\int K(u)\,du = 1$ and $\int u^j K(u)\,du = 0$ for $j = 1, \dots, \ell$ (vanishing moments of orders $1$ through $\ell$). Following the classical convention, nothing is assumed about the $(\ell+1)$-st moment.

Vanishing moments are the classical bias-reduction device: smoothing a $\beta$-smooth density with a kernel of order $\ell = \lceil\beta\rceil - 1$ kills every Taylor term of the bias below order $\beta$. Any symmetric probability-density kernel with finite first absolute moment (rectangular, triangular, Epanechnikov, Gaussian, …) is a kernel of order $1$, whereas kernels of order $\ell \ge 2$ necessarily take negative values on a set of positive Lebesgue measure.
summary: A kernel of order ℓ integrates to one and has vanishing moments of orders 1, …, ℓ — the classical bias-reduction device for kernel estimators.

  integral_eq_one : ∫ u, K u = 1
  moment_eq_zero : ∀ j : ℕ, 1 ≤ j → j ≤ ℓ → ∫ u, u ^ j * K u = 0
formalizationNotes: The book defines kernels of order ℓ only for integers ℓ ≥ 1; the Lean structure reads verbatim for every natural ℓ, order 0 meaning simply an integrable function with $\int K = 1$, and all downstream statements specialize correctly. As in the book, no condition is placed on the $(\ell+1)$-st moment. In the bias and rate theorems the order is instantiated at ℓ = `holderIndex β` $= \lceil\beta\rceil - 1$, the greatest integer strictly less than the smoothness $\beta$. Existence of bounded kernels of every order — needed inside Theorem 1.1's proof — is established constructively in `exists_bounded_kernel_of_order` (box superposition plus a Vandermonde argument, replacing the book's Legendre-polynomial construction).

title: Hölder Classes and Hölder Densities
informal:
Let $\beta$ and $L$ be positive numbers and let $\ell = \lceil\beta\rceil - 1$ be the greatest integer strictly smaller than $\beta$ (so $\ell = \beta - 1$ for integer $\beta$, and $\ell = \lfloor\beta\rfloor$ for non-integer $\beta$). The Hölder class $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on a set $T \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ (classically an interval) is the set of functions $f$ that are $\ell$ times continuously differentiable on $T$ and whose $\ell$-th derivative is Hölder of exponent $\beta - \ell$ with constant $L$: $\;|f^{(\ell)}(x) - f^{(\ell)}(x^\prime)| \le L\,|x - x^\prime|^{\beta - \ell}$ for all $x, x^\prime \in T$.

The kernel-estimator risk bounds are proved uniformly over the associated Hölder density class $\mathcal{P}(\beta, L)$: the probability densities on $\mathbb{R}$ — nonnegative and integrating to one — that belong to $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
summary: The Hölder class Σ(β,L) of ℓ-times continuously differentiable functions with (β−ℓ)-Hölder top derivative, ℓ = ⌈β⌉−1, and the density class P(β,L) over which the KDE risk bounds are uniform.

noncomputable def holderIndex (β : ℝ) : ℕ := ⌈β⌉₊ - 1

structure MemHolderOn (β L : ℝ) (f : ℝ → ℝ) (T : Set ℝ) : Prop where
  contDiffOn : ContDiffOn ℝ (holderIndex β) f T
  deriv_holder : ∀ x ∈ T, ∀ y ∈ T,
    |iteratedDerivWithin (holderIndex β) f T x - iteratedDerivWithin (holderIndex β) f T y|
      ≤ L * |x - y| ^ (β - (holderIndex β : ℝ))

def MemHolder (β L : ℝ) (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop := MemHolderOn β L f Set.univ
formalizationNotes: The smoothness index `holderIndex β` $= \lceil\beta\rceil - 1$ is exactly the book's "greatest integer strictly less than $\beta$" ($\beta - 1$ for integer $\beta$, the usual floor otherwise). Differentiability is stated as `ContDiffOn` — continuity of the $\ell$-th derivative included — which carves out the same class as the book's "$\ell$ times differentiable", because the Hölder bound itself forces continuity of $f^{(\ell)}$ and lower-order derivatives are continuous wherever the next one exists. `MemHolder` is the global case $T = \mathbb{R}$; the density class $\mathcal{P}(\beta, L)$ is `IsHolderDensity` in the same file, packaging nonnegativity, $\int p = 1$, and global Hölder smoothness. The structure reads verbatim for arbitrary real $\beta, L$; membership is meaningful for $\beta > 0$ and $L \ge 0$ (the bias theorems relax the book's $L > 0$ to $L \ge 0$).

title: Pointwise Variance of the Kernel Density Estimator
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. random variables with a measurable density $p$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and suppose $p(x) \le p_{\max} < \infty$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $K$ be a measurable kernel with $\int K^2(u)\,du < \infty$. Then for every point $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, every bandwidth $h > 0$, and every sample size $n \ge 1$, the variance $\sigma^2(x_0) = \mathbb{E}_p\big[\big(\hat p_n(x_0) - \mathbb{E}_p[\hat p_n(x_0)]\big)^2\big]$ of the kernel density estimator satisfies $$\sigma^2(x_0) \;\le\; \frac{C_1}{nh}, \qquad C_1 = p_{\max} \int K^2(u)\,du.$$
summary: For a density bounded by p_max and a square-integrable kernel, the pointwise variance of the kernel density estimator is at most C₁/(nh) with C₁ = p_max ∫K².

    (hp : Measurable p) (h0 : ∀ x, 0 ≤ p x)
    (hbdd : ∀ x, p x ≤ pmax)
    (hK : Measurable K)
    (hK2 : Integrable fun u => (K u) ^ 2) :

      ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (kdeVarianceConst K pmax / ((n : ℝ) * h))

title: Pointwise Bias of the Kernel Density Estimator
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with density $p$, where $p$ belongs to the Hölder density class $\mathcal{P}(\beta, L)$ — nonnegative, integrating to one, and in $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ — for some $\beta > 0$ and $L \ge 0$. title: Pointwise Rate of the Kernel Density Estimator over a Hölder Class
informal: Fix $\beta > 0$, $L > 0$, and a bandwidth scale $\alpha > 0$. Let $K$ be a kernel of order $\ell = \lceil\beta\rceil - 1$ which is square-integrable and has finite $\beta$-moment, $\int |u|^{\beta}|K(u)|\,du < \infty$. informal: Let $K$ be a measurable kernel with $\int K^2(u)\,du < \infty$. title: Integrated Squared Bias over a Nikol'skii Class
informal:
The Nikol’skii class $H(\beta, L)$ ($\beta > 0$, $L \ge 0$) is the $L^2$ analogue of the Hölder class: with $\ell = \lceil\beta\rceil - 1$ the greatest integer strictly less than $\beta$, it consists of the $\ell$-times continuously differentiable functions $f$ whose top derivative satisfies the translated $L^2$ bound $\big(\int \big(f^{(\ell)}(x+t) - f^{(\ell)}(x)\big)^2 dx\big)^{1/2} \le L\,|t|^{\beta-\ell}$ for every shift $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

Suppose $p$ is a probability density belonging to $H(\beta, L)$, and let $K$ be a kernel of order $\ell$ with $\int |u|^{\beta}|K(u)|\,du < \infty$. Then for every bandwidth $h > 0$ and every sample size $n \ge 1$, the integrated squared bias of the kernel density estimator satisfies $$\int b^2(x)\,dx \;\le\; C_2^2\, h^{2\beta}, \qquad C_2 = \frac{L}{\ell!} \int |u|^{\beta}|K(u)|\,du$$ — the same constant as in the pointwise bias bound.
summary: Over the Nikol'skii density class H(β,L), a kernel of order ℓ = ⌈β⌉−1 with finite β-moment gives integrated squared bias at most C₂²h^(2β), with the same constant C₂ as the pointwise bound.

title: Exact Asymptotic MISE of the Kernel Density Estimator
informal:
Let $p$ be a probability density on $\mathbb{R}$ which is differentiable with absolutely continuous derivative $p^\prime$ — witnessed by a measurable function $w$ (an almost-everywhere second derivative of $p$) with $p^\prime(b) - p^\prime(a) = \int_a^b w(s)\,ds$ for all $a, b$ — such that $\int w^2(x)\,dx < \infty$ and, in addition, $\int p^2(x)\,dx < \infty$. Let $K$ be a kernel of order $1$, square-integrable with $\int u^2 |K(u)|\,du < \infty$ and with nonvanishing second moment $S_K = \int u^2 K(u)\,du \neq 0$. Write $$A(n, h) \;=\; \frac{1}{nh} \int K^2(u)\,du \;+\; \frac{h^4}{4}\, S_K^2 \int w^2(x)\,dx$$ for the main term of the mean integrated squared error $\mathrm{MISE} = \mathbb{E}_p \int \big(\hat p_n(x) - p(x)\big)^2 dx$.

Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a threshold $h_0 > 0$ — depending only on $\varepsilon$, $p$, and $K$, not on $n$ — such that for every bandwidth $0 < h < h_0$ and every i.i.d. sample of any size $n \ge 1$ drawn from $p$, $$\bigl|\mathrm{MISE} - A(n, h)\bigr| \;\le\; \varepsilon \left(\frac{1}{nh} + h^4\right).$$
summary: For a twice weakly differentiable density and an order-1 kernel with S_K ≠ 0, the MISE equals (nh)⁻¹∫K² + (h⁴/4)S_K²∫(p″)² up to an error ε((nh)⁻¹ + h⁴), for all bandwidths below an n-independent threshold h₀(ε) and all n ≥ 1.

title: The Nadaraya–Watson Estimator as a Ratio of Density Estimates
informal:
Consider data pairs $(X_1, Y_1), \dots, (X_n, Y_n)$. Given a kernel $K$ and a bandwidth $h$, the Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression estimator of the regression function $f(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]$ is the locally weighted average $$f_n^{NW}(x) \;=\; \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\, K\!\left(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} K\!\left(\frac{X_j - x}{h}\right)},$$ defined to be $0$ whenever the denominator vanishes.

Let $\hat p_n(x) = \frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K\big(\tfrac{X_i - x}{h}\big)$ be the kernel density estimator built from $X_1, \dots, X_n$, and let $\hat p_n(x, y) = \frac{1}{nh^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K\big(\tfrac{X_i - x}{h}\big) K\big(\tfrac{Y_i - y}{h}\big)$ be the bivariate product-kernel estimator built from the pairs. If $K$ is a kernel of order $1$ — that is, $u \mapsto u\,K(u)$ is integrable, $\int K(u)\,du = 1$, and $\int u\,K(u)\,du = 0$ — the bandwidth $h$ is positive, and $\hat p_n(x) \neq 0$ at the point $x$, then $$f_n^{NW}(x) \;=\; \frac{\int y\,\hat p_n(x, y)\,dy}{\hat p_n(x)}.$$ The locally weighted average is thus exactly the plug-in estimate of the conditional-mean formula $f(x) = \int y\,p(x, y)\,dy \,\big/\, p(x)$.
summary: The Nadaraya–Watson locally weighted average equals the ratio ∫y·p̂ₙ(x,y)dy / p̂ₙ(x) of the bivariate and marginal kernel density estimates when the kernel has order 1 and p̂ₙ(x) ≠ 0.
formalizationNotes: Proved as a purely algebraic identity in the data vectors — no probability model is invoked, so it covers both the random-design and fixed-design settings. The heart is the change-of-variables identity $\int y\,K((Y_i - y)/h)\,dy = h\,Y_i$, which uses exactly the order-$1$ moment conditions; integrability of $y \mapsto y\,K((Y_i - y)/h)$ is derived from the kernel's order-$1$ integrability rather than assumed. `0 < h` is a Lean-side side condition (the chapter's standing convention, made explicit). The formalized estimator `nadarayaWatson` is total, set to $0$ when the denominator vanishes exactly as in the book; the hypothesis $\hat p_n(x) \neq 0$ rules that case out.

title: The Local Polynomial Estimator
informal:
In the nonparametric regression model $Y_i = f(X_i) + \xi_i$, fix a kernel $K$, a bandwidth $h > 0$, and an integer order $\ell \ge 0$. Writing $U(u) = \big(1,\, u,\, u^2/2!,\, \dots,\, u^\ell/\ell!\big)^{T}$, a vector $\hat\theta_n(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell+1}$ minimizing the kernel-localized least-squares criterion $$\hat\theta_n(x) \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell+1}}\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big(Y_i - \theta^{T} U\Big(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\Big)\Big)^{2} K\Big(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\Big)$$ is a local polynomial estimator of order $\ell$ of $\theta(x)$, and its first coordinate $\hat f_n(x) = U(0)^{T}\hat\theta_n(x)$ is the LP($\ell$) estimator of $f(x)$.

The criterion is a weighted least-squares problem with normal equations $\mathcal{B}_{nx}\theta = a_{nx}$, where $\mathcal{B}_{nx} = \frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i} U(z_i)U(z_i)^{T}K(z_i)$ and $a_{nx} = \frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i} Y_i\,U(z_i)K(z_i)$ with $z_i = (X_i - x)/h$. When $\mathcal{B}_{nx}$ is positive definite the minimizer is unique, $\hat\theta_n(x) = \mathcal{B}_{nx}^{-1}a_{nx}$, and the estimator takes the closed weight form $$\hat f_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\,W_{ni}^{*}(x), \qquad W_{ni}^{*}(x) = \frac{1}{nh}\, U(0)^{T} \mathcal{B}_{nx}^{-1} U\Big(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\Big)\, K\Big(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\Big).$$ The formalized estimator is defined directly by these closed-form weights, applied to the design points and the response vector; it agrees with any minimizer of the criterion whenever $\mathcal{B}_{nx} \succ 0$.
summary: The LP(ℓ) estimator fits a degree-ℓ polynomial by kernel-localized weighted least squares; formalized in the closed weight form W*ᵢ(x) = (nh)⁻¹U(0)ᵀB⁻¹U(zᵢ)K(zᵢ), total via the zero-matrix convention at singular B.

title: Linearity of the Local Polynomial Estimator
informal:
An estimator $\hat f_n$ of the regression function is a linear nonparametric regression estimator if it can be written as $\hat f_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\,W_{ni}(x)$, where the weights $W_{ni}(x)$ depend only on $n$, $i$, $x$ and the design points $X_1, \dots, X_n$ — not on the responses. The local polynomial estimator of order $\ell$, built from a kernel $K$ and a bandwidth $h$, is a linear estimator: $$\hat f_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\,W^{*}_{ni}(x), \qquad W^{*}_{ni}(x) = \frac{1}{nh}\, U(0)^{T} \mathcal{B}_{nx}^{-1}\, U\Big(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\Big)\, K\Big(\frac{X_i - x}{h}\Big).$$

In the book this is stated for positive definite $\mathcal{B}_{nx}$, where the localized least-squares minimizer is unique and equals $\mathcal{B}_{nx}^{-1} a_{nx}$. The accompanying formal development proves exactly this identification: under $\mathcal{B}_{nx} \succ 0$ and $h > 0$, a coefficient vector minimizes the criterion if and only if it solves the normal equations $\mathcal{B}_{nx}\theta = a_{nx}$, the minimizer is unique, and the closed-form estimator equals its first coordinate.
summary: The LP(ℓ) estimator is a linear estimator — a response-free weighted sum Σ YᵢW*ᵢ(x) — with the closed-form weights tied to the least-squares minimizer by the normal equations when B ≻ 0.

title: Polynomial Reproduction by Local Polynomial Weights
informal:
Fix a point $x$ at which the local design matrix $\mathcal{B}_{nx}$ is positive definite, and let the bandwidth $h$ be nonzero. The weights $W^{*}_{ni}(x)$ of the LP($\ell$) estimator then reproduce every polynomial of degree at most $\ell$ exactly: for any sample $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ and any polynomial $Q$ of degree $\le \ell$, $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} Q(X_i)\, W^{*}_{ni}(x) \;=\; Q(x).$$ In particular the weights sum to one, $\sum_{i=1}^{n} W^{*}_{ni}(x) = 1$, and their centered moments vanish: $\sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - x)^k\, W^{*}_{ni}(x) = 0$ for $k = 1, \dots, \ell$.

The root statement formalized here is the centered-monomial form: for each degree $k \le \ell$, the weighted sum $\sum_{i} (X_i - x)^k\, W^{*}_{ni}(x)$ equals $1$ if $k = 0$ and $0$ otherwise. Since every polynomial of degree $\le \ell$ expands in the centered basis $(z - x)^k$, this is equivalent to the general display above. This exact cancellation of the Taylor terms of orders $1, \dots, \ell$ is the mechanism driving the bias analysis of the estimator.
summary: When the local design matrix is positive definite, the LP(ℓ) weights reproduce every polynomial of degree ≤ ℓ exactly: they sum to 1 and their centered moments of orders 1,…,ℓ vanish.

title: Bounds on the Local Polynomial Weights
informal:
Consider the LP($\ell$) weights $W^{*}_{ni}(x)$ over the unit interval, under the three standing assumptions of the local polynomial risk analysis: (LP1) the smallest eigenvalue of the local design matrix satisfies $\lambda_{\min}(\mathcal{B}_{nx}) \ge \lambda_0$ uniformly over $x \in [0,1]$, with $\lambda_0 > 0$; (LP2) the design is spread out — every interval $A$ contains at most $a_0\, n \max(\mathrm{Leb}(A),\, 1/n)$ of the points $X_i$, for a constant $a_0 \ge 0$ (the regular design $X_i = i/n$ satisfies this with $a_0 = 2$); and (LP3) the kernel $K$ is supported in $[-1, 1]$ and bounded, $|K(u)| \le K_{\max}$. Set $$C_* \;=\; \max\Big\{\frac{2 K_{\max}}{\lambda_0},\; \frac{4 K_{\max}\, a_0}{\lambda_0}\Big\}.$$

Then for every $x \in [0,1]$ the weights satisfy: (i) $\;|W^{*}_{ni}(x)| \le \dfrac{C_*}{nh}$ for every $i$ — the bound formalized as this entry's root statement, which needs only (LP1), (LP3), the sign conditions $\lambda_0 > 0$ and $a_0 \ge 0$, and $n, h > 0$; (ii) $\;\sum_{i=1}^{n} |W^{*}_{ni}(x)| \le C_*$, which additionally uses (LP2) and the bandwidth range $h \ge 1/(2n)$; and (iii) $\;W^{*}_{ni}(x) = 0$ whenever $|X_i - x| > h$, which needs only (LP3) and $h > 0$.
summary: Under the eigenvalue, design-density and boxed-kernel assumptions, each LP weight is at most C*/(nh), their absolute sum is at most C*, and weights vanish beyond distance h, with C* = max{2Kmax/λ₀, 4Kmax·a₀/λ₀}.

title: Pointwise Bias and Variance of the Local Polynomial Estimator
informal:
Consider the fixed-design nonparametric regression model $Y_i = f(X_i) + \xi_i$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, with deterministic design points $X_1, \dots, X_n \in [0,1]$, where $f$ belongs to the Hölder class $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on $[0,1]$ — it is $\ell$ times continuously differentiable with $|f^{(\ell)}(x) - f^{(\ell)}(x')| \le L\,|x - x'|^{\beta - \ell}$, $\ell$ being the greatest integer strictly less than $\beta$ — and the noise variables $\xi_i$ are independent with $\mathbb{E}[\xi_i] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[\xi_i^2] \le \sigma^2_{\max}$. Let $\hat f_n$ be the local polynomial estimator of order $\ell$, and assume the eigenvalue bound (LP1): $\lambda_{\min}(\mathcal{B}_{nx}) \ge \lambda_0 > 0$ uniformly over $x \in [0,1]$, the design density bound (LP2): every interval $[a, b]$ contains at most $a_0\, n \max(b - a,\, 1/n)$ design points, and the boxed-kernel assumption (LP3): $K$ is supported in $[-1, 1]$ with $|K| \le K_{\max}$.

Then for every $x_0 \in [0,1]$ and every bandwidth $h \ge 1/(2n)$, the bias $b(x_0) = \mathbb{E}\big[\hat f_n(x_0)\big] - f(x_0)$ and the variance $\sigma^2(x_0) = \mathbb{E}\big[\big(\hat f_n(x_0) - \mathbb{E}[\hat f_n(x_0)]\big)^2\big]$ satisfy $$|b(x_0)| \le q_1\, h^{\beta}, \qquad \sigma^2(x_0) \le \frac{q_2}{nh}, \qquad q_1 = \frac{C_* L}{\ell!},\quad q_2 = \sigma^2_{\max} C_*^{\,2},$$ with $C_*$ the weight constant of Lemma 1.3, and consequently the mean squared error obeys $$\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\hat f_n(x_0) - f(x_0)\big)^2\Big] \;\le\; q_1^2\, h^{2\beta} + \frac{q_2}{nh}.$$
summary: Over the Hölder class Σ(β,L) with independent centered noise, the LP(ℓ) estimator has bias ≤ q₁h^β and variance ≤ q₂/(nh), hence pointwise MSE ≤ q₁²h^{2β} + q₂/(nh), with q₁ = C*L/ℓ! and q₂ = σ²maxC*².

title: Pointwise Convergence Rate of the Local Polynomial Estimator
informal: In the setting of the bias–variance bound (Proposition 1.13) — fixed design in $[0,1]$ satisfying the eigenvalue bound (LP1) and the design density bound (LP2), a bounded kernel supported in $[-1,1]$ (LP3), independent centered noise with second moments at most $\sigma^2_{\max}$, and $f$ in the Hölder class $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on $[0,1]$ — choose the bandwidth $h = \alpha\, n^{-\frac{1}{2\beta+1}}$ for some $\alpha > 0$. informal: Let $f$ belong to the Hölder class $\Sigma(\beta, L)$ on $[0,1]$ with $\beta > 0$, and let $\hat f_n$ be the LP($\ell$) estimator, $\ell$ the greatest integer strictly less than $\beta$, with the sup-norm bandwidth $h = \alpha \left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\beta+1}}$, $\alpha > 0$. title: Projection Estimator on the Trigonometric Basis
informal:
Consider the nonparametric regression model $Y_i = f(x_i) + \xi_i$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, observed at the regular design $x_i = i/n$, and let $\{\varphi_j\}_{j \ge 1}$ be the trigonometric basis of $L^2[0,1]$: $$\varphi_1(x) \equiv 1, \qquad \varphi_{2k}(x) = \sqrt{2}\,\cos(2\pi k x), \qquad \varphi_{2k+1}(x) = \sqrt{2}\,\sin(2\pi k x), \qquad k = 1, 2, \dots$$ From the observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$ one estimates the Fourier coefficients $\theta_j = \int_0^1 f \varphi_j$ of $f$ by the empirical averages $$\hat\theta_j \;=\; \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\, \varphi_j(x_i).$$

For an integer order $N \ge 1$, the projection estimator (or orthogonal series estimator) of the regression function $f$ at a point $x$ is $$\hat f_{nN}(x) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N} \hat\theta_j\, \varphi_j(x).$$ The order $N$ plays the same smoothing role as the bandwidth of a kernel estimator: it governs the balance between bias (small $N$, oversmoothing) and variance (large $N$, undersmoothing).
summary: The projection estimator f̂_nN = Σ_{j≤N} θ̂ⱼφⱼ with coefficient estimates θ̂ⱼ = n⁻¹ Σᵢ Yᵢφⱼ(i/n), on the trigonometric basis at the regular design i/n.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def coeffEstimator {n : ℕ} (Y : Fin n → ℝ) (j : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ i, Y i * trigBasis j (regularDesign n i)

noncomputable def projEstimator {n : ℕ} (Y : Fin n → ℝ) (N : ℕ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, coeffEstimator Y j * trigBasis j x
formalizationNotes: `trigBasis` is 1-indexed exactly as in the classical display: `trigBasis 1` is the constant $1$, and for $j \ge 2$ the frequency is the natural-number quotient $j/2$, giving $\sqrt2\cos(2\pi kx)$ at $j = 2k$ and $\sqrt2\sin(2\pi kx)$ at $j = 2k+1$; index $0$ is inert (`trigBasis 0 = 0`), so all sums run over $j = 1, \dots, N$ (`Finset.Icc 1 N`). The regular design is encoded as `regularDesign n i = (i+1)/n` for `i : Fin n`, i.e. the design points $1/n, 2/n, \dots, 1$. In the surrounding risk analysis the coefficient sequence $\theta$ is the primitive object and the target is defined as `seriesFun θ`, the pointwise sum $\sum_j \theta_j \varphi_j$ — membership of $f$ in a smoothness class becomes a statement about its coefficient sequence, which keeps every risk theorem self-contained without invoking completeness of the trigonometric system.

hypotheses.label: regular design
hypotheses.note: The equispaced design points i/n, i = 1, …, n, at which the basis is sampled.

hypotheses.label: trigonometric basis
hypotheses.note: The orthonormal trigonometric system φ₁ ≡ 1, φ₂ₖ = √2 cos(2πkx), φ₂ₖ₊₁ = √2 sin(2πkx) of L²[0,1].

reference.formal: A. B. Tsybakov, *Introduction to Nonparametric Estimation*, Springer, New York, 2009.
reference.biblio: Orthogonal series (projection) estimation was introduced by N. N. Čencov (Soviet Math.
